Finally, we discuss implications of user adaptivity for the interpretation of experiments and show that adaptivity creates a common mechanism leading to common evaluation challenges, such as reward hacking and novelty effects. Together, this work highlights the necessity of measuring both model performance as well as changes in the user behavior that the model induces.

Title: HEIR: Harness Egocentric Intent for Human-Robot Interactions
Author: Yichi Zhang, Bo Wang, Zhenghan Zhu, Yutong Han, Jiayin Zou, Gao Kejun, Chang Liu, Shaoxuan Xie, Chi Zhang, Shi Haoyang, Zongxuan Lai, Sen Cui, Guocai Yao, Miao Liu
Text_Content: For robots to assist, serve, and collaborate with humans, they must not only interpret human requests conveyed through language and multimodal intentional cues, but also execute long-horizon tasks that interleave navigation and manipulation. In this paper, we introduce HEIR, a resource for studying how to Harness Egocentric Intent for Human-Robot Interaction. HEIR pairs human speech, measured gaze, and egocentric video with robot observations and teleoperated navigation-manipulation trajectories, while each session preserves successive episodes, with each request fulfilled through multiple execution subtasks. The captured data, together with human-authored annotations, support the study of intent grounding, execution planning, and task completion within a unified interaction setting. To demonstrate the value of HEIR, we conduct extensive offline experiments to evaluate how models benefit from additional human-centric context across these tasks, together with real-robot experiments that assess execution task completion. HEIR thus provides a valuable resource for studying user-centric robot interaction in naturalistic household environments. Our demo and dataset are available online.

Title: Al-Ghasali: A Computational Framework for Simulating Islamic Jurisprudential Rulings via Finite State Automata and Large Language Models
Author: Elnaserledinellah Mahmoud Abdelwahab
Text_Content: This paper presents Al Ghasali, a computational framework designed to formalize and simulate Islamic jurisprudential (Fiqh) rulings. Building upon recent set theoretic formalizations of al sabr wa al Taqsim that extract minimal operational rules as simple Horn clause logical programs, this work proves that the semantics of closed Fiqh chapters collapse completely to deterministic Finite State Automata (FSA). We establish a formal computational hierarchy, demonstrating that restricting formalization to finite propositional Horn theories guarantees decidability and constant time (O(1)) verdict extraction after offline compilation. The framework formally proves that hierarchical compositions of sub-chapter FSAs preserve this O(1) complexity, and that temporal juristic requirements, such as Tartib (order), are deterministically flattened into static ontological states, preserving the memoryless property of the automaton. To generate human-readable juristic summaries, Al Ghasali incorporates Large Language Models (LLMs) via an architecture where the deterministic FSA strictly controls the probabilistic LLM. Crucially, the paper formulates sufficient design safety conditions for this FSA LLM integration, ensuring strict adherence to the epistemological boundaries of Usul al Fiqh. To neutralize the risk of LLM hallucination, the system employs a Grammar Guided Constrained Decoding mechanism. We formally define the mapping function that dynamically constructs unambiguous right linear grammars from the FSA execution history. The paper mathematically proves that this architecture, augmented by a Bounded Neutral Lexicon and Valence Locking, guarantees the absolute absence of Decisional Hallucination, Juristic Factual Hallucination, and Semantic Inversion reducing the LLM to a pure linguistic transformer of deterministic juristic facts

Title: Assessing the Reliability of Longitudinal Bibliometric Rankings under Incomplete Citation Histories
Author: João Paulo Papa
Text_Content: Longitudinal bibliometric analyses rely on annual citation histories, yet missing annual observations are frequently difficult to distinguish from true zero-citation years. We present a reproducible case-study framework for auditing citation-history gaps, tracing retrieval provenance, and quantifying the sensitivity of longitudinal indicators and rankings to explicit missing-data assumptions. The case study comprises 595 consolidated publications derived from 616 Google Scholar article records, and examines the completed calendar years 2024-2025. Three scenarios are compared: strictly observed annual counts (A), hypothetical zeros for internal gaps only (B), and hypothetical zeros for all missing years within a valid publication interval (C). The number of publications with computable growth and acceleration indicators increases from 196 (A) to 257 (B) and 490 (C); the corresponding counts for a revival indicator are 131, 152, and 177. Although the ordering of publications eligible under both compared scenarios is unchanged (Spearman and Kendall correlations equal to 1.0), complete-ranking positions and Top-K membership may change markedly. In particular, acceleration exhibits a Jaccard overlap of 0.563 at K=50 between A and C, while revival exhibits 0.667 at K=10. These findings demonstrate that unchanged indicator values and perfect correlations on a common subset do not guarantee stable rankings when eligibility changes. The zero assignments are hypothetical sensitivity assumptions, not evidence of provider semantics. The results are descriptive and based on a single researcher profile. A reusable Google Scholar Tracker software workflow supports the audit and sensitivity analysis; version 1.8.5 is publicly available on GitHub and archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24170285).

Title: Two mathematical models of knowledge distillation
Author: Audrey Xie, Ludwig Schmidt, John Duchi
Text_Content: Many hypotheses compete to explain the successes of knowledge distillation. To help address this, we propose and analyze a mathematical model of distillation, which suggests that distillation's performance comes not from obtaining better models but from easier to optimize landscapes. For generalized linear models trained with stochastic gradient descent, we prove that distillation fits performant student models asymptotically more quickly than non-distilled models. In rank-1 matrix approximation, we characterize conditions on the target matrix under which gradient descent with distillation converges strictly faster than training on the supervised objective. The theory helps delineate the ways distillation provides benefits (i.e., in optimization speed, not in generalization), and experiments on real datasets corroborate the theoretical predictions.

Title: Peak Performance in Matched Filtering: Fused Correlation and Statistically Controlled Screening on CPUs and GPUs
Author: Alexander H. Nitz, Keisi Kacanja, Collin D. Capano
Text_Content: Batched matched filtering and cross-correlation over large template banks are a primary computational cost in gravitational-wave astronomy, seismology, and radio transient searches. Standard pipelines pair a general-purpose inverse Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) with separate multiplication and peak-finding kernels, writing intermediate spectra and full correlation series to memory for every template. We fuse the conjugate product into the first inverse-transform butterflies and the peak reduction into the last so only candidate peaks leave processor registers, and tile batches in 2D so $K^2$ correlations reuse $2K$ cached spectra. This shifts filtering from a DRAM-bandwidth-bound to an on-chip cache-bandwidth-bound regime. In some situations, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is concentrated toward lower frequencies while higher frequencies dominate the transform length. We develop a hierarchical screening method that exploits this via a sequence of short low-frequency transforms before evaluating the full band, deriving stage thresholds from the spectral power profile and matched-filter noise autocovariance to target a specified false-dismissal probability. We demonstrate these methods in the open-source matchedfilter library across eight CPU architectures and two integrated GPUs (AMD Radeon 8060S via Vulkan and Apple M2 via Metal). On an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 at $N=4096$, fused peak-only filtering is $1.4\times$ faster than a standalone AOCL-FFTW inverse transform on one CPU core and $6.2\times$ faster than rocFFT on its Radeon 8060S GPU ($3.1\times$ over MLX FFT on the M2 GPU). For a fiducial gravitational-wave search ($ρ_\mathrm{th}=5.5$, $10^{-2}$ false-dismissal target), hierarchical screening yields a $26\times$ speedup over AOCL-FFTW on CPU, $21\times$ over rocFFT on the 8060S GPU, and $19\times$ over MLX FFT on the M2 GPU.

Title: Linear Regression with Self-Selection Bias in Polynomial Time
Author: Felix Zhou
Text_Content: We revisit the problem of estimating $k$ linear regressors with self-selection bias in $n$ dimensions up to error $\varepsilon$ with the maximum self-selection criterion, as introduced by Cherapanamjeri, Daskalakis, Ilyas, and Zampetakis [CDIZ23, STOC]. Our main result is a $\mathrm{poly}(n,k,1/\varepsilon)$ time algorithm for the unknown-index variant of this problem, thereby improving upon the running times of the best known algorithms due to Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] and Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Zhou [KMZ26, COLT] with exponential dependence on $k$. Our algorithm succeeds in the presence of correlated noise between regressors, which captures the related setting of max-affine regression. Consequently, we also give the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem, improving on the prior works of Ghosh, Pananjady, Guntuboyina, and Ramchandran [GPGR22, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory] and Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] with exponential dependence on $k$. Prior works exhaustively search over a $k$-dimensional subspace spanned by the regressors, using conditional moments of the response to test candidates. In contrast, our algorithm is driven by an improved understanding of the moments of the covariates. We show that, restricting to observations with large response values, the degree-$(\log n)$ Hermite moment of the covariates approximately decomposes as a sum of tensor powers of the regressors. The first step of our algorithm can be viewed as a tensor decomposition algorithm for these implicitly represented high-order tensors, which outputs unit vectors parallel to the regressors. A secondary step based on a simple variant of ordinary least squares extracts estimates for the regressors given these unit vectors. We believe our analytic insight and algorithmic components may have applications to designing efficient algorithms for other latent-variable problems.

Title: Sheaf-Inspired Structured Scoring Extensions of LightGCN for Collaborative Filtering
Author: Ksenia Belkovskaya, Timur Lidzhiev, Maria Stebliy, Alexander Tarakanov
Text_Content: Graph-based collaborative filtering learns user and item representations by propagating embeddings over a user--item interaction graph. We investigate a modular, sheaf-inspired scoring extension placed on top of a three-layer LightGCN backbone. The motivation comes from cellular sheaves, where local vector spaces are related by linear restriction maps; here, this idea motivates structured, pair-dependent transformations of user and item embeddings rather than a change to graph propagation. We compare the identity inner-product scorer, diagonal, rank-one low-rank, and full matrix residual scorers, and a parameter-matched residual MLP baseline (\texttt{mlp\_full}) on Amazon-Book, Gowalla, MovieLens-1M, and Yelp2018. We report ranking quality and catalog coverage at cutoffs 10 and 20. The selected structured variants show modest, dataset-dependent changes in ranking quality and sometimes substantial changes in coverage. Our method is inspired by sheaf geometry but does not construct a cellular sheaf or implement sheaf-Laplacian diffusion; the experiments therefore do not establish a causal benefit from sheaf geometry itself.

Title: Data Archive for 2D and 3D Electrical Impedance Tomography with moderate conductivity contrast phantoms
Author: S. J. Hamilton, A. Hauptmann, A. Hänninen, V. Kolehmainen, J. Niskanen, T. Savolainen, J. Toivanen
Text_Content: This document describes open Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) measurement data that were collected from biomedical imaging inspired phantoms with moderate conductivity contrasts. The data were collected with the KIT4 and KIT5 EIT measurement devices at the University of Eastern Finland, and are intended for EIT image reconstruction algorithm development and testing. The data from thoracic imaging inspired cylindrical and chest-shaped phantoms are suitable for 2D algorithms, and the data from an intracerebral hemorrhage imaging inspired head-shaped phantom with resistive skull are suitable for 3D algorithms. In addition to the measurement data, computational meshes and example reconstruction codes are provided and sample reconstructions included.

Title: Combinatorial Bernoulli Factories with Polynomially Many Coins
Author: Renato Paes Leme, Rad Niazadeh
Text_Content: We provide an efficient implementation of combinatorial Bernoulli factories. Such a factory turns coins of unknown biases $x$ into a random vertex of a polytope $P$ whose mean is exactly $x$. For every affine slice of the cube (the class of polytopes that admit a factory), we give a single algorithm whose expected number of coin flips and running time at every interior $x$ are polynomial in the dimension and in $1/{δ_*}$, where ${δ_*}=\min_i\{x_i,1-x_i\}$ is never supplied to the algorithm. For perfect matchings this gives $O(n^{8}{δ_*}^{-2}\log(n/{δ_*}))$ flips, while the factory of Niazadeh, Paes Leme, and Schneider [STOC 2021] spends at least $n^{2n-1}$ flips in expectation at the uniform doubly stochastic matrix. For other polytopes, our method rounds exactly given a point deep inside $P$ and the promise that $x$ is far from the boundary of $P$.

Title: Scalable Conversational Assessment: Chat-Based Exams with a Two-Agent LLM Pipeline
Author: Geoffrey Challen, Craig Zilles
Text_Content: Oral exams are compelling because (1) students can be asked to provide their reasoning for an answer and (2) their interactive nature permits follow-up questions to resolve ambiguous answers. But oral exams scale poorly. In this paper, we present scalable conversational assessment, an LLM-based system that conducts interactive text-based conversations with students to assess their ability to make and support an argument. We use a two-agent architecture to separate concerns and reduce the likelihood that answers are leaked to the student: the interviewer interacts directly with the student, but only receives guidance about the next question to ask the student; the hidden evaluator knows the goals of the whole activity, tracks the student's progress using a rubric, and guides the interviewer on when to follow-up on the current question or proceed to the next question. The system was first tested using a collection of simulated students with LLM personas of a particular ability level or adversarial tactic (e.g., answer-extractors, prompt-injectors, confident fabricators). A novel element of this evaluation was that it required the use of a fictional assessment topic to prevent personas that shouldn't have information from using knowledge present in the LLM's pre-training. The system was also deployed in a small, elective AI literacy course in both formative and summative contexts. Through manual and post-facto AI review of the transcripts we identified opportunities to improve the follow-up question generation and ensure that grading only credited ideas that the student (and not the interviewer) contributed.

Title: Faster Deterministic All-Pairs Shortest Paths with Real Edge Weights
Author: Isaac Barouch Essayag, Aryeh Lev Zabokritskiy
Text_Content: For directed $n$-vertex graphs with arbitrary finite real edge weights and no negative cycles, we compute all-pairs distances deterministically in $O(n^{2.9929729})$ worst-case time using Uznański's half-width matrix multiplication bound. Using only the Le Gall--Urrutia rectangular multiplication bounds, our algorithm runs in $O(n^{2.99306273})$ time. This improves both the deterministic bound of $O(n^{2.9997})$ due to Chan, Itakura, Ma and Yu and the Las Vegas expected-time bound of $O(n^{2.993805})$ reported in the shreshth-s working note.

Title: Introducing Feedback Delays to Non-Delayed Adversarial MDPs: Optimal $\sqrt S$ and $\sqrt K$ Dependencies in Tabular and Linear AMDPs
Author: Aarush Kulkarni, Khang Nguyen, William Chang, Yan Dai
Text_Content: We study regret minimization in episodic Adversarial Markov Decision Processes (AMDPs) with unknown transitions and bandit feedback. In tabular AMDPs with $S$ states, $A$ actions, and horizon $H$, the best known $K$-episode regret is $\tilde O(HS\sqrt{AK})$, whose $\sqrt S$ gap to the $Ω(H\sqrt{SAK})$ lower bound has long remained open. In linear AMDPs with $d$-dimensional features, after a five-year line of improvements starting from $K^{14/15}$, computationally efficient algorithms without a simulator or exploratory assumptions still only attain $\tilde O(K^{3/4})$ regret. A common challenge in both settings is to estimate the Q-function of a changing policy: past data comes from earlier policies that differ from (and are correlated with) the current one, while freezing the policy for future episodes worsens the dependency on $K$. We instead propose a general technique called introduced feedback delays: we estimate the Q-function of the policy using future episodes while still updating the policy, as if the feedback were delayed. While feedback delays are usually an obstacle imposed by the environment, here they are introduced voluntarily and, perhaps surprisingly, come at no extra cost. We develop Geometric Resampling with Rejection (GRR) to account for policy changes during the delay, and threshold the visitation probabilities to avoid long delays on rarely visited state-action pairs. With this unified technique, our policy optimization algorithms achieve, with high probability, $\tilde O(\text{poly}(H)\sqrt{SAK})$ regret in tabular AMDPs, resolving the open problem; and $\tilde O(\text{poly}(d,H)\sqrt K)$ regret in linear AMDPs, giving the first efficient algorithm optimal in $K$. They also naturally extend to delayed AMDPs with a total feedback delay $\mathfrak D$, yielding the first bounds optimal in $S$ and $\mathfrak D$ (tabular) and in $K$ and $\mathfrak D$ (linear).

Title: Collaborative Task Allocation for Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Systems Through Iterative Clustering
Author: David R. Martin, Brooks A. Butler, Scott Nivison, Magnus Egerstedt, Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque, Pramod Khargonekar
Text_Content: Multi-robot systems face the challenge of efficiently allocating teams of heterogeneous robots to tasks. The task allocation problem is complicated by collaborative interactions between robots where teams of robots develop emergent capabilities that enable them to complete tasks that would be inefficient or impossible for individual robots. To address these challenges, we present an iterative clustering algorithm for collaborative task allocation in heterogeneous multi-robot systems. This approach partitions the computationally intractable global optimization problem into smaller, tractable subproblems by iteratively forming clusters of robots and tasks, then optimizing assignments within each cluster. By ensuring robots remain clustered with their currently assigned tasks, we guarantee monotonic improvement in overall utility with each iteration. We analyze the convergence of the algorithm and characterize how cluster size constraints determine which suboptimal assignments could trap the algorithm. In simulation, iterative clustering consistently outperforms simulated annealing, and a group-based auction in both computation time and solution quality, and outperforms a hedonic game approach in solution quality.

Title: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Sparse Convolution
Author: Keshvi Tuteja, Yu-Hsiang Tsai, Gregor Olenik, Markus Götz, Achim Streit, Hartwig Anzt, Charlotte Debus
Text_Content: Deep neural networks for image processing are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained edge devices such as drones, medical systems, and smartphones, where limited computational resources and memory bandwidth pose significant challenges for efficient inference. Pruning during training often produces highly sparse convolutional kernels, offering the potential to significantly reduce computation and memory requirements. However, exploiting this sparsity efficiently at runtime remains challenging due to irregular memory access patterns and workload imbalance across processing elements. In this work, we investigate the standard convolution with sparse weights and analyze its performance characteristics through roofline analysis, showing that a 3 x 3 sparse convolution achieves an arithmetic intensity of approximately 10 FLOP/byte compared to roughly 96 FLOP/byte for its dense counterpart. We propose techniques for an efficient sparse convolution at high sparsities. Preliminary results demonstrate that our approach achieves upto 1.65x speedup as compared to dense convolution on NVIDIA A100 and upto 1.52x on NVIDIA Jetson Nano (Tegra X1) , motivating further exploration of direct convolution as a practical path to efficient sparse inference on modern accelerators/edge devices.

Title: A Feasibility Study of Whole-Cerebrum Task-Based fMRI at 0.55 T: Motor and Visual Tasks Using Single-Shot EPI
Author: Parsa Razmara, Takfarinas Medani, Anand A. Joshi, Majid Abbasi Sisara, Ye Tian, Sophia X. Cui, Justin P. Haldar, Krishna S. Nayak, Richard M. Leahy
Text_Content: Purpose: To evaluate the feasibility of whole-cerebrum task-based fMRI on a modern 0.55T system, examining the effects of extended scan duration and within-session consistency on functional mapping outcomes and comparison to acquisition with matched tasks at 3.0T. Methods: Six healthy participants were scanned at 0.55T using a single-shot EPI sequence during bilateral finger-tapping and visual checkerboard tasks. Data were processed using an open-source pipeline. To investigate sensitivity improvements, two consecutive 5-minute runs were concatenated. Within-session consistency was also assessed. A representative 3T dataset provided additional reference context for temporal dynamics and statistical sensitivity. Results: Task-evoked activations were detected at 0.55T using Family-Wise Error (FWE) rate correction (p < 0.05) in both motor and visual cortices. While single 5-minute runs provided baseline detectability, extending the acquisition to 10 minutes increased t-statistic magnitudes and cluster extents while substantially reducing background noise (47% reduction in voxelwise dispersion). Run-to-run comparisons showed consistent peak locations and statistical significance across participants. Comparison with the 3T reference demonstrated that statistical significance increases with acquisition time so that a 0.55T scan approximately matches 3T significance levels at twice the scan duration across the range compared. Conclusion: Whole-cerebrum task fMRI is feasible at 0.55T using standard EPI and modern high-performance gradients. These results indicate that modest extensions in scan duration can compensate for reduced intrinsic BOLD sensitivity at lower field strengths.

Title: Crest factor optimization of multi-tone signals generated for low-temperature sensor readout
Author: L. H. Arnaldi
Text_Content: Microwave kinetic inductance detectors (MKID) are a growing technology of cryogenic detectors and have a great potential in radio-astronomy and cosmic microwave background (CMB) characterization. A review of the general readout performance requirements for experiments requiring the multiplexing of large arrays (~10.000 pixels) of such cryogenic detectors is presented. The focus is on the crest factor optimization process for proper excitation and readout of these large arrays of detectors. It is shown an algorithm to optimize the phase generation of the carriers to obtain a low crest factor, favoring the dynamic range usage of the electronic chain.

Title: PACER: GPU Excursion Management for ML Workloads
Author: Rutwik Jain, Nathaniel Morris, Yiwei Jiang, Shidhartha Das, Gary Kao, Indrani Paul, Shivaram Venkataraman, Srilatha Manne, Matthew D. Sinclair
Text_Content: Variability is an inherent characteristic of modern GPU systems, arising from a combination of process variation, dynamic environmental conditions, and power management decisions. Prior work has characterized inter-GPU variability and found consistent performance differences across GPUs. However, we observe that modern workloads, particularly large language models (LLMs), exhibit significant intra-GPU variability. Their short-running kernels interact poorly with the coarse granularity of dynamic power management mechanisms, leading to unpredictable performance. A key source of this intra-GPU transient variability is power excursions, also referred to as electrical design power peaks (EDP$_{p}$), where power temporarily exceeds the GPU's rated power limits. While power management mechanisms are designed to ensure reliable operation despite the presence of EDP$_{p}$ sustained power peaks cause throttling that detrimentally impacts overall application performance. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to characterize the magnitude and frequency of EDP$_{p}$, showing that frequent, significant power overshoots are especially common in ML workloads, which combine high power draw, short kernels, and rapidly changing compute demands. To address this, we design and leverage hardware and firmware mechanisms to provide consistent power management behavior that reduces intra-GPU variability due to EDP$_{p}$ and improves overall performance. We evaluate our techniques across a range of popular workloads. Our approach improves performance by 3-12% over state-of-the-art GPU power management and comes within 3% of an oracular solution.

Title: A Little Length Slack Goes a Long Way in Planar Length-Constrained Network Design
Author: D Ellis Hershkowitz, Richard Z Huang, Rhea Jain, Manas Korimilli
Text_Content: Problems in length-constrained network design ask for min-cost subgraphs connecting $k$ input vertex pairs by paths of length at most $h$. Algorithms that instead connect these pairs by paths of length at most $βh$ are said to have length slack $β$. Recent work has shown that poly-time polylogarithmic approximations with polylogarithmic length slack are possible for a broad class of both directed and multicommodity length-constrained network design problems on planar graphs. We give the first poly-time polylogarithmic approximations with $O(1)$ length slack for these problems on planar graphs. In particular, for the length-constrained setting, we give LP-competitive algorithms for planar graphs with length slack $1+ε$ and approximation ratios of $O(\log^2 k/ε)$ for directed Steiner tree and $O(\log^5 k/ε^2)$ for (undirected) Steiner forest. Similarly, for length-constrained directed Steiner forest, we give an $O(\log^6 k/ε)$ approximation on planar graphs with length slack $6+ε$. Our approach is based on a novel charging argument that charges the cost of our solution to the length of the LP and the length of our solution to the cost of the LP. We complement these algorithms with hardness results that separate planar and general graphs for both forest problems: under standard complexity assumptions, we rule out polylogarithmic approximations on general graphs with length slack below $3$.

Title: MALNISI-Infused Graph Construction and Weighted Contrastive Loss based GAT for Unsupervised Representation Learning in HSI
Author: Soumi Sarkar, Subhadip Boral, Sarbani Palit, Ashish Ghosh
Text_Content: Hyperspectral images (HSI) possess discriminating spectral characteristics with respect to land utilization due to high-dimensional information. Recently, unsupervised representation learning using graph neural networks has unveiled these utilization-specific complex spectral relations. This article has three main contributions. First, it proposes an index, the Mean Absolute Local Neighborhood Inverse Spectral Index (MALNISI), which measures the similarity between two pixels based on their neighborhood information. The index is used to construct a weighted adjacency matrix, giving the HSI a graph structure. Second, it proposes an upgraded Graph Attention Network that learns compact latent representations of hyperspectral data from the constructed graph. In this network, an enhanced multi-head attention mechanism incorporates the MALNISI weights as an auxiliary feature to emphasize learned attention between neighboring pixels. To alleviate over-smoothing and preserve fine-grained spectral details, the architecture integrates residual connections, skip projections, and feature normalization, which together enhance representation capability, stabilize learning, and accelerate convergence. Third, it proposes a weighted contrastive loss function that incorporates neighborhood-aware MALNISI between connected pixels, encouraging strongly connected pixels in the high-dimensional space to remain close in the latent space, and weakly connected pixels to stay apart. The resulting discriminative low-dimensional embeddings are then clustered using spectral clustering. Experimental analysis on six benchmark HSI datasets demonstrates the efficiency and necessity of the three aforementioned contributions, and the comparative study highlights superior performance over fourteen state-of-the-art approaches.

Title: Physically Interpretable Basin Selection in Discrete-Variable Origami Design
Author: Lucy Liu, Leon M. Kamp, Katia Bertoldi, L. Mahadevan
Text_Content: Automatic differentiation has enabled rapid progress on continuous-variable mechanical design problems, but gradient-based optimization still struggles with discrete variables. The standard approach is to optimize using a continuous relaxation of the choices, then commit to the nearest discrete design at the end. Why this procedure selects unfavorable basins is poorly understood. Here, we introduce a practical, interpretable design problem inspired by origami, in which automatic differentiation is used to design shapes with a target functional behavior. Each origami sheet has a fixed geometry, and a bilevel optimization framework tunes which one of four discrete hinge types to place at each fold. Baseline gradient-based design settles into basins with a large discretization gap: relaxed optimization solves 97% of runs, but the final, discrete solutions succeed only half the time. We find that the gap can be relieved with a surprisingly simple modification. An initialization prior uniformly biased toward the stiff, flat hinge option boosts the final solve fraction from 49% to 69%. Applying the prior adds no additional compute and leaves the optimization process unchanged. Compared to the baseline, sheets produced with the prior have greater geometric compatibility and mechanical stiffness. Directly penalizing frustration and floppiness in the outer loss function produces an even greater improvement than the prior does, raising the solve fraction to 78% and indicating that these properties help distinguish the unfavorable basins. Our results demonstrate that loss landscapes for mechanical design can have physically meaningful basins that are not robust to discretization and cause solves to fail. Targeting these basins' physical signatures, even with just an initialization bias, helps avoid them.

Title: eDMD: Endpoint Distribution Matching for Few-Step Diffusion Distillation
Author: Tong Zhao, Xianfang Zeng, Yucheng Han, Ruoyu Wang, Mingkun Lei, Gang Yu, Chi Zhang
Text_Content: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student's distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student's final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake model on intermediate states or across all denoising steps. Consequently, the student's update signal becomes entangled with intermediate distributions, which can distort the matching direction and remain nonzero even after the student's final outputs already match the teacher distribution. To resolve this mismatch, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student's final outputs and uses it to correct every denoising step. Our theoretical analysis proves that this endpoint reference guarantees that the distribution matching term vanishes if and only if the student's final output distribution matches the teacher's, regardless of intermediate distributions. Beyond the fake reference, we further strengthen teacher supervision through a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step guided predictions with short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, paired with a calibrated query density for intermediate steps. Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B), and Qwen-Image-2.1 demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching methods for 4-step generation.

Title: Maximizing Capacity Utilization of LoRA Adapters for Mitigating the Learning-Forgetting Trade-off
Author: Tomohiro Sawada, Kartik Goyal
Text_Content: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning-forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of $λ=0.01$ lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least $16$ relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most $0.02$ in all but one model-rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning-forgetting frontier. Our code is available at https://github.com/tomohiro-sawada/lora-capacity-utilization

Title: Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes
Author: Robert Fonod, Nikolas Geroliminis
Text_Content: Reference-frame stabilization registers every frame of a hovering-drone video onto one reference frame, keeping object positions comparable. The registration pipelines it relies on are selected on feature-matching benchmarks in which only the camera moves. Over a busy intersection, vehicles moving together supply mutually consistent correspondences that can draw the robust homography estimate toward their motion: consensus capture, which inlier statistics cannot flag. A two-part benchmark measures it and the object masking meant to prevent it. A static protocol scores ten pipelines under exactly known homographies on 4K aerial frames, tuned on a site-disjoint split at a matched resolution and feature budget. A dynamic protocol scores them at an offline and a real-time budget on hovers selected from the video alone to span the amount and coherence of moving foreground, plus a stationary control. It measures background alignment, object position error and the share of a moving group's displacement an estimate follows, against a pseudo-ground-truth reference audited with manually annotated ground control points, which also score every candidate. On static scenes, tuned AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK lead, retuning the matcher thresholds raises the mean average accuracy (mAA) by at most 0.0062, and masking costs less than 0.005. Unmasked ORB is captured on 28 of 304 real-time dynamic pairs and on 6 offline; its real-time captured estimates have a median corner error of 18.8 px yet typical inlier counts and ratios. Masking removes capture for every pipeline and leaves the leading pipelines unchanged. Code, data and results are released.

Title: The Gator low-background spectrometer: readout upgrade and photomultiplier tube radioassay for XLZD
Author: Laura Baudis, Sofia Calgaro, Jose Javier Cuenca-Garcia, Florian Joerg, Margherita Noia, Francesco Piastra, Aravind Remesan Sreekala
Text_Content: We report on a readout upgrade of Gator, a low-background high-purity germanium spectrometer operated at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso for material radioassay. The upgraded data acquisition records digitised waveforms, enabling noise rejection on an event-level basis, and offline energy reconstruction. Measurements before and after the upgrade show an improved energy resolution of 17% at the 2614.5 keV line of 208-Tl, with (2.14 +- 0.22) keV at FWHM, and suppression of electronic noise in the low-energy region. We assess the resulting sensitivity for a specified sample geometry, and present a new background measurement. The background rate in the (100-2700) keV range is (86.6 +- 0.5) counts/(kg day). We also show the radioassay results of sixteen Hamamatsu R17317 3-inch photomultiplier tubes with an improved stem design, which reduces the activities from the primordial 238-U and 232-Th chains by a factor of three, making them suitable candidate photosensors for the XLZD experiment.

Title: Cortex-FL: Agent-Mediated Collaboration for Federated Learning
Author: Rui Sun, Jinfeng Peng, Zehua Cheng, Jiahao Sun, Zhipeng Wang
Text_Content: Federated learning (FL) enables independent data owners to train models collaboratively without centralizing raw data. However, identifying collaborators, preparing training tasks, and coordinating execution and incentives hinder its practical adoption by organizations without specialized expertise. We present Cortex-FL, an agent-native FL system that enables users to express learning objectives in natural language and delegate the collaboration required to train a model. Agents translate these objectives into shared tasks, discover collaborators, and negotiate participation agreements, connecting collaboration formation with distributed training and incentive management. The architecture separates agent coordination from local execution authority, allowing owners to delegate coordination while retaining control over their data, computation, and financial commitments. We demonstrate the complete workflow on a four-node deployment, in which a model requested in natural language proceeds through collaboration formation, contract-governed training, verified model delivery, and x402 settlement on a blockchain testnet.

Title: Neural Render Proxies for Interactive and Differentiable Lighting
Author: Sergio Sancho, Alexander Rath, Marco Manzi, Pascal Chang, Amit H. Bermano, Derek Nowrouzezahrai, Markus Gross, Marios Papas
Text_Content: Within the CG animation production pipeline, the challenges artists tackle in Lighting can be immense. Even minor adjustments require re-rendering massive scenes with slow offline renderers; global illumination has to be sampled and complex shaders have to be evaluated, leading to iteration times of minutes to hours per frame. To accelerate this process, we introduce a novel neural render proxy (NRP) that enables differentiable relighting of static scenes with fixed camera and materials at interactive rates. Our main insight is the decoupling of traditional rendering into path sampling and emission computation. From a single, light-agnostic render pass, we collect light transport data in the form of path samples. This enables rapidly sampling lighting conditions on the fly, and training a scene-specific lightweight neural network that learns how light is transported from any scene location to any image pixel. This approach is compatible with non-differentiable production renderers, induces minimal memory requirements during inference, and scales only with resolution and the number of light sources and parameters, but independently of scene and appearance complexity. Our evaluation demonstrates interactive frame rates for relighting (~30-60 Hz) while closely approximating the visual fidelity of ground-truth path tracing. In addition, the differentiable NRP enables fast, gradient-based inverse workflows, allowing artists to efficiently solve for lighting parameters from intuitive image-space edits or generative targets.

Title: Omakase: Execution Congestion Control through Conflict-Graph Integration in Multi-Proposer Blockchain
Author: Dakai Kang, Ray Neiheiser, Alberto Sonnino, Eleftherios Kokoris Kogias, Mohammad Sadoghi
Text_Content: As multi-proposer protocols push consensus throughput, transaction execution has become the dominant bottleneck in blockchains. Layer-1 blockchains parallelize execution either pessimistically (Solana, Sui), requiring upfront state-access declarations and serializing contended transactions, or optimistically (Aptos, Sei, Monad), resolving dependencies at run time but suffering cascading aborts under contention. Both treat blocks in isolation, leaving inter-block parallelism unexploited and most cores idle. We introduce Omakase, a parallel execution framework that combines pre-execution, inter-block conflict-graph integration, and graph-aware Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC). Replicas use idle cores to pre-execute only the blocks they propose, spreading prediction work across concurrent proposers. After building per-block conflict graphs and identifying their hot resources, a greedy scheduler integrates graphs across the blocks committed in a round, keeping an integration only when a lightweight balance heuristic predicts a parallelism gain. A graph-aware OCC executor then runs the integrated graph, admitting transactions in dependency order, which eliminates aborts when the predicted graph is exact and reduces re-executions when it is not. On 15,000 Ethereum mainnet blocks (~2.4M transactions) and synthetic workloads with configurable contention, Omakase reaches a 2.47x speedup over sequential execution, well above single-block OCC and graph-aware baselines. Against the strongest alternative, which runs the whole round as one optimistic window, Omakase matches mean throughput but is markedly more stable under high contention, because integration bounds how much optimistic work is in flight: this is the congestion control of our title. Integration is not free, but overlapping it with execution across rounds hides 94% of its measured cost in the validator pipeline.

Title: New bounds on the boxicity of Kneser graphs
Author: L. Sunil Chandran, Suraj Kumar Sahoo
Text_Content: For a graph $G=(V,E)$, the boxicity $\operatorname{box}(G)$ is the least integer $d$ such that $G$ is the intersection graph of axis-parallel boxes in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The Kneser graph $K(n,k)$ is the graph whose vertex set corresponds to the family of $k$ sized subsets of an $n$ sized ground set, and a pair of vertices are adjacent if and only if the corresponding sets are disjoint. In this short paper, we provide new bounds for the boxicity of $K(n,k)$. We first show that for $k\ge 2$ and $n\ge 2k+1$, $\operatorname{box}(K(n,k))\ge n-2k$, thereby improving the lower bounds of Caoduro and Lichev [Discrete Mathematics 346(5):113333 (2023)] when $n\geq 3k+1$ and $k\ge 3$. The proof of this result uses the topological method and follows a strategy similar to Greene's proof of the Kneser's conjecture on the chromatic number of $K(n,k)$. We also show that for $k\ge 2$, $t\ge 1$ and $n=2k+t$, $\operatorname{box}(K(2k+t,k)) \leq O( t^3\log(2k+t) ).$ In particular, for every $t=t(k)\ge1$ with $t^3\log k=o(k)$, $\operatorname{box}(K(2k+t,k))=o(k)$. This is the first upper bound on the boxicity of $K(n,k)$ that is sublinear in $n$. We also show that for large enough $k$, $\operatorname{box}(K(2k+1,k))\le \frac{3\ln (2k+1)}{\ln\ln (2k+1)}$.

Title: Convolutional VocalTrax: Replacing Backpropagation Through Time with Convolution in Differentiable Articulatory Synthesis
Author: Yongyi Zang, Debasish Ray Mohapatra, Randal Leistikow, Perry R. Cook
Text_Content: VocalTrax recovers interpretable articulatory controls from a recording by gradient descent through a differentiable Pink Trombone synthesizer. Its vocal tract is a Kelly-Lochbaum waveguide updated twice per audio sample, so every gradient step backpropagates through a long recurrence, which is slow on GPUs. We propose Convolutional VocalTrax, which computes the exact frequency response of the same waveguide and applies it as a causal convolution. We assume that the tract is stationary within 5.8 ms blocks and that its lossy impulse response can be truncated after 93 ms. Gradients then pass through FFTs and a short recursion along the tract instead of through time. On 600 AudioMNIST recordings, the tract forward and backward pass runs 47 to 63 times faster on an A100 GPU, and a classifier trained only on real speech recognizes our reconstructions more often than those of VocalTrax (14.5% vs. 10.0%), although the log-mel distance to the target is 11% higher. Parameters fitted with our model keep this gain when rendered by the original VocalTrax (13.8%).

Title: Validation-Guided Prompt Selection for Differential Morphing Attack Detection
Author: Raghavendra Ramachandra, Hailin Li
Text_Content: Differential morphing attack detection (D-MAD) compares a trusted live capture with a document image that may contain a facial morph. We investigate whether labelled validation data can improve a frozen-parameter vision-language evaluator through prompt selection rather than model fine-tuning. Version~1 generates 50 candidate prompts and selects the top-ranked instruction using a security-oriented loss that prioritises missed morph attacks (MACER) while accounting for bona fide classification errors (BSCER), response failures, parse failures, and decision inconsistency. Version~2 recursively revises prompts using aggregate validation feedback. On a subject-disjoint test set of 160 pairs spanning LMA, MIPGAN-2, and PIPE, the selected Version~1 prompt achieves a (19.17\%) morph attack classification error rate (MACER), with (0.00\%) observed bona fide sample classification error rate (BSCER), compared with (70.00\%) MACER for a controlled manual prompt. The paired (50.83) percentage-point difference has a (95\%) subject-bootstrap interval of ([43.33,58.33]). Recursive revision does not surpass the best Generation~0 validation loss; the reported revised descendant obtains (31.67\%) test MACER. All 23 attacks missed by Version~1 are landmark-based (LMA) morphs. Overall, the results show that prompt formulation can substantially influence frozen-parameter VLM-based D-MAD performance, while also highlighting the challenge of recursive prompt refinement under a compact 10-subject validation setting.

Title: SpotDiff: A Plug-and-Play Framework for Zero-Shot Change Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery
Author: Anit Upadhyaya, Ata Akbari Asanjan, Chaitanya Jalluri, Subash Yeggina, Jeremy Kravitz
Text_Content: Remote sensing change detection usually relies on large collections of temporally aligned, pixel-level annotations, which limits its scalability across regions, imaging platforms and application domains. Recent zero-shot approaches reduce the need for supervision, but they often localize fine-grained changes poorly because their features are coarse or inconsistent across time. We present SpotDiff, a training-free, plug-and-play framework for zero-shot change detection built by composing complementary vision foundation models. SpotDiff uses DINOv3 for semantically robust features, AnyUp to reconstruct them at pixel resolution, and SAM 3 for text-guided region-of-interest proposals, which an inference-time multi-scale strategy (SWIMS) makes reliable on small objects. Change is then measured by comparing the reconstructed features of the two dates inside the proposed regions, with no learnable components, fine-tuning or change labels. To our knowledge, SpotDiff is the first change detection method to use a universal feature upsampler, which alone adds 13.8 F1 over bilinear upsampling of the same features. On LEVIR-CD, SpotDiff reaches 82.46 F1, 2.06 points above the strongest prior training-free method, and on the multi-class SECOND benchmark it improves building change detection by 10.3 IoU and the six-class average by 2.2 IoU. Qualitative results on PlanetScope (3 m) and Sentinel-2 (10 m) imagery show that the same pipeline transfers across resolutions without modification. Our results indicate that composing modern foundation models is an effective route to scalable, label-free change detection.

Title: Improving Algorithmic Trading for BESS on Intraday Electricity Markets through Distributional Price Forecasts
Author: Simon Hirsch, David Schaurecker, David Wozabal
Text_Content: Grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) are becoming increasingly important in short-term energy markets, where they help balance fluctuations in variable renewable generation. In many countries, the continuous intraday market is the most important wholesale market for BESS to monetize their flexibility. In this paper, we propose an extension to the myopic rolling intrinsic policy that incorporates intraday price forecasts tailored specifically to the BESS trading problem. While a large literature addresses intraday price forecasting, most existing work focuses on volume-weighted prices during the last hours of trading and consequently fails to capture the features most relevant to BESS trading. Our approach addresses this gap by introducing a novel target variable derived from the limit order book and its dynamics. The resulting forecasts are designed to inform the optimization about future profit opportunities while preserving computational efficiency and avoiding the burden of full stochastic optimization. In a realistic high-frequency simulation setting covering 2023 and 2024, our method improves profits by up to 42% over the naive rolling intrinsic formulation. We further analyze the relationship between forecast accuracy, stability, and financial performance, establishing a clear inverse relationship between accuracy and stability. Finally, we find evidence that BESS size and duration jointly influence both overall profitability and the marginal benefit of incorporating forecasts.

Title: Parsed, Plausible, Wrong: Output Format Controls Silent Errors in Small-Model Semantic Parsing
Author: Umar Ahmed, Maxim Dunaev, Mohammad Nour Al Awad, Sergey Ivanov, Ivan Khodnenko
Text_Content: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently: nothing downstream can tell. We ask whether the output format, a free design choice, controls how often this happens. On the PIZZA ordering benchmark we fine-tune two sub-billion models (Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M) with LoRA on six lossless encodings of the same target tree, from 44.3 down to 10.9 tokens per order, including two matched-length pairs that vary surface form at fixed length. Across 300 runs (5 training pool sizes, 5 seeds) with a hierarchical bootstrap and Holm correction fixed before the results were read, shortening alone never helps, but writing the target in ordinary words does. The word encoding is the most accurate format on both models (87.5% vs. 85.8% exact match for the native s-expression on Qwen) while emitting 4.1x fewer tokens, and it cuts the silent error rate by 2.3x on Qwen and 1.8x on LFM2, separating at every pool size. Error analysis locates much of the gain in negation. All runs also learn to refuse off-menu input (held out: 95.9-99.0% handled) and to apply in-utterance self-corrections. Strict refusal has a measured price: 2.1-10.1% of real, mostly polite, orders are refused.

Title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
Author: Haochen Liu, Qianhao Zhu, Zixuan Wang, Dingming Li, Tongbo Chen, Peng Qiu, Yingqi Qu, Weiming Lu, Jun Xiao, Yongliang Shen
Text_Content: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well. We compare three decision models and three general LLMs as actors and judges on ALFWorld, and use JEV as a teacher on ALFWorld and WebShop. As actors, all six models are pulled away from a subgoal that must come first by an easier one. As judges that see the whole trajectory, the same models credit the steps toward that subgoal, and asking whether each action helped, rather than whether the task will succeed, separates useful from useless actions. As a teacher, JEV raises a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy over GRPO from 72.8% to 82.9% success on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop. These results suggest that a poor actor can still teach well, because judging an action after the episode ends reveals the consequences that acting must anticipate. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/decision-agents.

Title: UAV-Flow++: A Unified Suite for Benchmarking and Learning Language-Guided UAV Flight
Author: Donglin Yang, Xiangyu Wang, Yantong Zhong, Wenhao Zheng, Zihan Ding, Yue Liao, Hongsheng Li, Ke Xu, Si Liu
Text_Content: Language-guided UAV navigation has largely focused on long-horizon route planning, leaving short-range, object-relative flight maneuvers underexplored. To address this gap, we formulate Flying-on-a-Word (Flow), a task requiring a UAV to convert concise natural-language instruction, egocentric visual observation, and current state dynamics into continuous flight actions. Flow encompasses both primitive motion commands and complex object-interactive behaviors, assessing motion intent comprehension and spatial context grounding. To enable policy learning and closed-loop evaluation, we introduce UAV-Flow, a comprehensive dataset comprising 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories across eight distinct motion categories, alongside 10,109 simulation trajectories in the UAV-Flow-Sim environment equipped with task-specific completion criteria. Furthermore, we develop FlowVLA, which undergoes imitation pretraining on mixed real-sim demonstrations and online post-training via Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). By leveraging group reward distributions, TGRPO effectively reinforces high-reward action sequences. Evaluated on 273 held-out UAV-Flow-Sim episodes, pretrained FlowVLA achieves a mean success rate of 75.58%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.72 percentage points, which TGRPO post-training further elevates to 93.16% with superior sample efficiency. Physical UAV experiments demonstrate robust execution of object-relative commands in both indoor and outdoor real-world scenes. Together, Flow establishes a novel benchmark and learning framework for language-conditioned flight maneuvers.

Title: Symmetry in Time: A Representation Theory of Linear Recurrent Memory
Author: Anif N. Shikder, Ramit Dey, Jan Minac, Lyle E. Muller
Text_Content: State space models (SSMs) are an emerging alternative to Transformers. SSMs offer linear-time inference and parallel training, but most implementations make the parallel scan efficient by making the recurrence diagonal: each channel of the hidden state is multiplied by an input-dependent real or complex number. These numbers commute, so the state records which inputs occurred but not their order. We formalize this with representation theory, which explains and fixes the state-tracking failures previously reported for SSMs. The state update defines a linear representation of the monoid of input sequences, and we show that an SSM tracks a group at every sequence length exactly when that group is a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices. Two consequences follow. Diagonal real- and complex-valued SSMs can track only commutative groups, while the transition matrices of any SSM that can track a group must split into independent blocks over the real, complex, and quaternion numbers. We then introduce HyperSSM, which adds quaternion channels while keeping linear-time inference and parallel training. Trained only on final answers, HyperSSM solves the group tasks of recent state-tracking benchmarks exactly with at most five state numbers. This includes $S_5$ with 32 generators, where previous SSMs are at chance, and HyperSSM generalizes to sequences 25 times longer than those seen in training. Because the theory says what the transitions must encode, the learned weights of the linear recurrence can be interpreted directly. We demonstrate this by recovering the calibration of a real gyroscope, the rotations of imperfect qubit gates and the geometry of protein backbones.

Title: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Author: Tanzeel Abbas, Tehseen Zia, David Windridge
Text_Content: Retrieval-augmented generation systems attach citations to attribute claims to their sources. These citations frequently misstate provenance, and standard verification cannot detect this. We measure provenance by counterfactual value substitution: a fact in the retrieved passages is replaced with a false variant and the model re-queried. We find that across five sizes of one model family and a second comparator family, 1.2% to 15.7% of citable claims derive from parametric memory rather than the retrieved context. At the most conservative substitution distance these figures are 4.6% and 8.5% on the two models we tested at it, with the rate rising with model size within a family. We further find that natural language inference verification, the standard approach, gives results indistinguishable from chance across models, even when restricted to the cited passage. We determine that the cause is structural: a model answering from memory selects a citation that agrees with its output. Comparing ten attribution methods on identical claims, the contrast between the model's distribution with and without context best separates provenance. Acting on that signal does not improve provenance honesty at these base rates. The resulting detector is hence still not accurate enough to act on: it measures what the model knew rather than what it used, and separating those remains the open problem.

Title: XBot-Omni: An Omni-Modal Model for Embodied Understanding and Interaction
Author: Kerui Gu, Xing Fu, Shuoyang Sun, Cheng Peng, Jingru Duan, Huayu Gu, Zhenyu Chen, Jiaxin Huang, Cheng Wen, Rui Zhen, Kairui Chen, Zhihui Peng, Shaoli Huang
Text_Content: Embodied interaction requires an agent to integrate multimodal perception with verbal and nonverbal behaviors to effectively communicate its intentions, including speech, body motion, and facial expressions. We present XBot-Omni, a Thinker--Talker--Actor architecture that extends the Omni paradigm to robotic modalities, including body motion and facial expressions, with ``X'' representing the extensibility to robotic-specific modalities. The Thinker processes text, images, audio, and video to formulate contextually appropriate responses, which are then realized by the Talker and Actor through speech and coordinated bodily expressions, respectively. In this report, we innovatively introduce the concept of ``Actor'' as a dedicated component for embodied agents: a coordinated, streaming module that leverages the native representations of the Thinker and Talker within an end-to-end pipeline, introducing only modest latency overhead. This unified architecture enables multimodal generation conditioned on omni-modal inputs directly to prevent information loss in staged designs. We comprehensively evaluate XBot-Omni across seven benchmarks, demonstrating strong multimodal understanding capabilities on both general-domain and robot-centric videos, as well as high-quality, natural, and well-coordinated motion generation. Furthermore, our results validate its capability to generate embodied multimodal responses directly from omni inputs, meeting the diverse requirements of embodied interaction. XBot-Omni enables robots not only to perceive the omni world but also to express themselves through speech and bodily behaviors, extending Omni models from conversational interaction to embodied communication in physical environments.

Title: Inner Product Regularization for Imitation Learning
Author: Benjamin A. Christie, Tianyu Qiu, Amy H. Choi, David Fridovich-Keil, Dylan P. Losey
Text_Content: Robots that learn from demonstrations should extrapolate their policy despite state perturbations such as sensor noise, scene variation, and compounding errors. One approach to this robustness is regularization. Prior regularizers consider each state on its own and limit how sensitive the policy is to any perturbation at that state. By contrast, we explore how the policy's output shifts when given the same perturbation at different states. Our insight is that, locally, the robot should respond to state perturbations in a consistent manner: e.g., if changing an irrelevant object position does not impact the policy at one state, that same change should not shift the policy output at a nearby state. Applying this insight, we develop inner product regularization (InneR). We show that the inner product on action space induces an inner product on state space through the policy Jacobian (the Fisher information for stochastic policies), and that the null space of this inner product governs which state perturbations have a first-order effect on the policy. By clustering states whose inner products are aligned, averaging the inner products within each cluster, and minimizing the smallest eigenvalues of that average, InneR shapes the learned policy so that nearby states share a common null space. InneR enforces consistent responses to perturbations without limiting policy expressiveness, and can be appended to existing imitation learning pipelines for deterministic or stochastic policies. In simulated experiments, InneR makes learned policies more robust to irrelevant state dimensions and shifts between training and test distributions, whereas norm penalties often perform worse than behavior cloning. On a real robot arm performing three manipulation tasks, InneR raises the average success rate of a diffusion policy from 18% to 57% without additional data.

Title: A hierarchical graph neural network for efficient particle-resolved prediction of granular flow dynamics
Author: Kuang Shi, Qingqi Zhao, Teng Man, Sergio Andres Galindo-Torres, Yimin Lu
Text_Content: Graph neural surrogates for granular flow can resolve the motion of individual grains, but propagating information across a large amount of grains requires repeated, costly updates on the full particle graph. This study introduce a Hierarchical Coarse-Grained Graph Neural Network (HCG-GNN) that couples direct interactions between neighboring grains with information exchange on two coarser graphs of occupied spatial cells. In discrete element method (DEM) benchmarks of granular flows down incline planes, HCG-GNN captured key flow characteristics, including front propagation, lateral spreading, deposition morphology, free surface evolution, internal shear behavior, and energy conversion. Results also show that preserving grain-specific features as coarse information returned to the particle graph and integrating predicted accelerations to advance particle motion both improved multi-step accuracy. With 5 of its 7 message-passing steps performed on coarse graphs, HCG-GNN achieved accuracy comparable to a conventional particle-level GNN with a 6.47-fold training speedup and 46.2% lower GPU memory use. A model trained on up to 5000 grains predicted a 2 s release of 10000 grains in 31 s, compared with 2000 s for DEM under the benchmark conditions. This combination of speed and grain-scale resolution supports particle-resolved inverse design, with prescribed runout or discharge targets guiding the search for suitable geometries and grain dynamics revealing the basis for differences in performance.

Title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics
Author: Peter Sharpe, Carmelo Gonzales, Corey Adams, Mehdi Ataei, Sanjay Choudhry
Text_Content: Neural surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are trained and ranked on datasets that each vary one design family in one flow domain. Such datasets cannot test the least that an aerodynamic foundation model must do: predict CFD-quality incompressible flow in seconds for new shapes in new enclosures. On DrivAerML, larger models and longer training barely lower Transolver's error; doubling the training cases cuts it by about 12% up to 400 cases, exhausting the dataset. We introduce AeroZoo, a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 time-mean solutions to the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations with a transition model, across seven geometry families, eight enclosure configurations and Reynolds numbers from $10^3$ to $10^8$. Each sample poses a well-posed PDE problem in the form a solver receives it: the boundary meshes grouped by condition type, the prescribed values and the fluid properties. The 2,816 samples with a stable time mean form the canonical benchmark: two tasks, engineering metrics and 22 frozen splits, disjoint in geometry, that hold out geometry families, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts and Reynolds ranges. On the random split, boundary-condition tokens cut GeoTransolver's median velocity error from 76.9% to 8.4% of the inlet speed in single-seed runs (uniform inlet flow: 11.0%). ISLA, a transformer for boundary-driven PDEs, reaches 5.3% over four seeds, about 4 times the change from a finer mesh. On the same test samples, a held-out geometry family barely changes ISLA's error relative to uniform flow, and a held-out enclosure or boundary-condition layout raises it 2.4 to 9.2 times. The data and the scoring code will be released.

Title: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes
Author: Mark Lovett Feng Fu
Text_Content: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game. Within this new framework players' strategies are represented as positions within a trait space. Players then receive a share of a portion of a resource based on their relative influence at that resource's points traits. For the influencer's game, we show that there is a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium that exists under strict log-concavity of the influence kernel. Using the unique equilibrium we show that the stability of the system depends on the influence kernel's parameters, number of players, and the resource distribution shape. For any dimension we demonstrate a stability threshold that depends on both the scatter and curvature of the players. When this threshold is crossed, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes and gives way to a variety of bifurcation types; including, specialist clusters, limit cycles, and sub-games that reproduce the larger game's structure. We ground these results using real-world data for resources as a demonstration of the game's application. Finally we extend the game dynamics to use multi-agent reinforcement learning and further show that the predicted bifurcation structure persists under partial observability and discretized strategy spaces. In all, the influencer's game provides a novel framework for predicting when competitive pressure drives convergence versus fragmentation with possible applications across domains.

Title: HiVE-VQA: Hierarchical Interaction via Volumetric Embedding for Video Quality Assessment
Author: Robbie Hamilton, Fan Zhang, David Bull
Text_Content: The proliferation of user-generated video content has made accurate and robust no-reference video quality assessment (NR-VQA) a highly important challenge. Existing research increasingly relies on architecturally complex multi-branch pipelines or computationally intensive fine-tuning of single-branch backbones. In this paper, we investigate whether a single frozen video foundation model can serve as an effective NR-VQA backbone, and propose HiVE-VQA, the first framework (to our knowledge) to apply a JEPA-based video encoder to this task. HiVE-VQA extracts token grids from multiple depths of a pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder and stacks them into a hierarchical spatio-temporal volume, which a compact 3D convolutional head fuses across its layer, spatial, and temporal axes, combining low-level distortion cues from shallow layers with the semantic and temporal context captured at greater depths. The encoder remains frozen throughout, so only the head is trained: 5.2M parameters (5.7\% of the total), with no auxiliary multi-modal models and an inference cost that is invariant to video resolution. Trained solely on LSVQ and evaluated without any fine-tuning, HiVE-VQA outperforms 17 state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in SROCC and PLCC on both intra-dataset (LSVQ-test, LSVQ-1080p) and cross-dataset (KoNViD-1k, LIVE-VQC) benchmarks. These results indicate that hierarchical, depth-wise fusion of features from a single frozen video foundation model provides a more effective and efficient basis for NR-VQA than task-specific multi-network fusion. Code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/RobHam99/HiVE-VQA.

Title: Enhancing Preference Detection using Eye Movement Cascade and Multilayer Combinatorial Fusion
Author: Yuanhong Wu, Mary Tsaryk, Sam Watson, Tahsin Ahmed, Christina Schweikert, D. Frank Hsu
Text_Content: Understanding how visual attention influences human preference formation is a fundamental problem in consumer behavior and cognitive science. In this work, we investigate how eye movement patterns can be used to predict preference decisions when subjects compare two alternatives. To address this problem, we analyze an eye-tracking dataset, where subjects view pairs of face images and their gaze behavior is recorded throughout the decision process. We model this problem using multiple machine learning classifiers and apply the Multi-layer Combinatorial Fusion (MCF) framework to iteratively combine diverse models. The MCF framework expands models to a large pool of model fusions and then reduces them based on cognitive diversity, repeating this process across layers until diversity diminishes. Experimental results show that MCF significantly improves performance over individual models. The best single model achieves a Pre@k of 0.90, which is improved to 0.9143 after the first layer of MCF, and further increased to 0.9286 in the second layer. This progression demonstrates that the second layer not only surpasses the performance of the first layer but also outperforms the best individual model, highlighting the effectiveness of leveraging diversity through multi-layer fusion.

Title: A Convex-Analytic Reformulation for Poisoning Attacks on Logistic Regression
Author: Carina Moreira Costa, Maria Eduarda Pinheiro, Martin Schmidt
Text_Content: We study data poisoning attacks on logistic regression with $\ell_2$-regularization, where an attacker chooses the features of a fixed number of injected observations with prescribed labels to maximize the logistic loss on the clean training data. Strong convexity of the defender's problem yields an exact reformulation through its first-order optimality conditions. Using convex conjugacy of the softplus function, we replace the sigmoid relations by a single convex optimality-gap inequality and express the attacker's objective as a concave function. A change of variables makes the stationarity condition affine, leaving bounded bilinear equalities as the only nonconvex constraints. We derive finite bounds on all variables involved in these equalities, including a global bound on the coefficient norm and tighter bounds obtained by preprocessing based on convex optimization. Experiments on eight binary classification datasets evaluate attack effectiveness and compare the two reformulations when solved with \textsf{SCIP}. Attacks obtained by local optimization degrade predictive performance on most datasets, while the convex-analytic formulation produces substantially stronger reported dual bounds within a fixed time limit.

Title: FORGE: Force-Aware Multi-Granularity Control for Efficient Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Author: Liangjun Xing, Ke Fan, Kailin Li, Bin Wang, Xiaojie Niu, Qingwei Ben, Jiafei Cao, Wei Yao, Yebin Liu, Jingbo Wang, Weinan Zhang
Text_Content: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated locomotion, balance regulation, and manipulation under frequent contacts, making teleoperated demonstration collection difficult: a practical controller must simultaneously provide precision, stability, and contact awareness. We propose FORGE, a force-aware multi-granularity control system with a coarse-to-fine command space spanning velocity navigation, planar foot placement, wrist-pose tracking, and optional force-conditioning inputs. Policy training requires no full-body human motion trajectories or joint-angle references; deployment consumes only sparse bilateral wrist poses relative to the pelvis, coarse motion commands, and optional desired wrist-load inputs. For sustained contact, FORGE combines a momentum observer with a learned correction trained using simulator contact-force supervision. At deployment, it estimates low-frequency, wrist-equivalent interaction forces from proprioception and reconstructed low-level arm PD torques, without wrist force/torque sensors. A quasi-static virtual-target loop uses this estimate and an optional desired applied-force input to adapt the wrist target. A frozen locomotion prior and asymmetric residual actions stabilize manipulation-induced whole-body corrections. Experiments evaluate unified-control stability, task-space tracking, quasi-static wrist-equivalent force estimation, squeezing forces during sustained contact with a rigid box, and downstream diffusion-policy execution of a squat-and-lift task across payload conditions. Website: https://bb0928.github.io/forge/.

Title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs
Author: Peter Sharpe
Text_Content: A foundational principle of physics is that all coordinate systems are equally valid: the behavior of a PDE-governed system does not depend on the origin or orientation of the frame, nor on the units or mesh used to write it down, and neither should a surrogate model. Yet the neural surrogates with the lowest errors on today's aerodynamics benchmarks lack these invariances and fail under simple transformations of the same problem: for models trained on PDEs of cars in one pose (i.e., translation and rotation) and from one mesher, rotating the full PDE raises the surface-pressure error from 4% to more than 100%, and re-sampling its boundary raises it to about 30%. We introduce ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention), a slice-attention transformer for steady, boundary-driven PDEs in which no learned operation receives a coordinate and every sum over the boundary is a quadrature. Positions enter only as distances and relative angles to learned slice anchors, lengths are measured in a unit computed from the boundary, and interior points query the boundary through a tree-accelerated learned kernel without influencing one another. With every boundary cell a token and an exact boundary read, ISLA is equivariant to rigid motions and reflections, invariant to the units of its declared data, and consistent under mesh refinement, while at every setting each query is independent of all other queries. On AeroZoo, 2,816 flows that vary in shape, size, speed, and boundary conditions, its mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are at least 3.1 and 3.3 times lower than any baseline's. On AirfRANS its errors are second only to those of a boundary-integral model (GLOBE) and at least 1.6 times lower than those of Transolver and GeoTransolver.

Title: Support-Constrained Offline Policy Improvement for Pediatric ECMO from Limited Clinical Data
Author: Fateme Golivand Darvishvand, Saurabh Mathur, Nikhilesh Prabhakar, Michael A. Skinner, Ameet Soni, Neel Shah, Ethan L Sanford, Lakshmi Raman, Sriraam Natarajan
Text_Content: Managing children on ECMO (Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation) requires balancing short-term physiological stability with the long-term goal of preventing neurological injury. Standard reinforcement learning can propose risky, out-of-distribution actions, while imitation learning is limited to reproducing clinician behavior. We introduce Support-Constrained Fitted Q-Iteration (FQI-SC), an offline reinforcement learning framework that cautiously improves upon expert behavior by restricting optimization to empirically supported state-action pairs and defaulting to the clinician baseline in low-data regions. On 78 pediatric trajectories totaling over 6,000 hours of clinical data, we evaluate our framework using Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE) and a behavioral disagreement. Additionally, we formalize the performance-safety trade-off by introducing a unified Balance Score ($S(π)$). Our empirical evaluation shows that support-constrained policy improves the Balance Score by 38\% relative to FQI, improves estimated value by 1.28 FQE units over imitation learning, and reduces disagreement with clinician actions by 71\% relative to FQI.

Title: Library of peptides: Analysis of a complex reactive mixture with the use of statistical physics and inference
Author: Laura Messio, Taleen Peker, Roba Moumné, Hélène Berthoumieux
Text_Content: Self-assembled mixtures enable the exploration of vast chemical diversity, yet characterizing the hundreds of coexisting species they contain remains a major challenge. Standard analytical techniques such as chromatography and spectroscopy produce overlapping signals that cannot be resolved by conventional deconvolution methods, which neglect the concentration correlations imposed by the reactive network.
