Across the evaluated Video-LLM backbones, BiScopeNet improves action, hand-role, and object recognition over the corresponding supervised baselines, achieving the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated configurations on BiScopeCap.

Title: Wayfinder: Adaptive Resource Routing from Agent Citations
Author: Miguel Romero, George Karypis
Text_Content: To act effectively, agents must gather contextual information across resources such as chats, issue trackers, email and knowledge bases, to answer questions like "what was decided in the last project meeting?" or "where is the FAQ for our internal tooling?" Where this information lives in a user's environment is unknown to the agent, so it re-explores the same resources across consecutive interactions. Common routing approaches represent each resource as a tool and rely on high-level descriptions to generalize to unseen environments. Such descriptions often fail to separate similar or overlapping resources and cannot improve from the agent's subsequent interactions. We introduce Wayfinder, an adaptive router that uses the documents cited by the downstream agent as feedback about where relevant information resides. These citations update Wayfinder's internal resource representations, which subsequent interactions use to prioritize the resources likely to contain relevant information. We also introduce resource augmentation during offline reinforcement learning, which anonymizes and permutes resource identities to discourage training-time overfitting of which resource holds which topic; our ablations suggest it helps most when few training environments are available. Because no openly available professional environments pair realistic queries with resource-access patterns, we construct and release three controlled testbeds derived from existing datasets: NFCorpus, FEVER and Tech Startup. Compared with supervised, tool-retrieval and contextual bandit baselines under a shared closed-loop protocol, Wayfinder gives the best routing when resources contain semantically overlapping content that static descriptions cannot distinguish, while description-based tool retrieval suffices when resources are drawn from distinct corpora.

Title: Human-Likeness and Conversational Preference Diverge for Synthesized Agent Speech in Customer-Service Calls
Author: Jeffrey M. Girard, Antony D'Avirro, Jason Z. Zheng, Jacqueline R. Vertino, Benjamin Peloquin
Text_Content: Listeners can judge an agent's speech on how human it sounds (human-likeness) and on how much they would want to talk to it (conversational preference). Listening tests rarely ask about conversational preference, so the relation between the two judgments is unclear. We compared them in paired-choice tests on 120 turns that actors improvised as customer-service representatives. On each trial, two agents spoke the same turn. In Study 1, both agents came from six commercial text-to-speech systems, each with eight voices. In Study 2, one was the actor's original recording and the other a system. Some systems ranked higher on human-likeness, and others on conversational preference. Listeners chose systems over actors in 19% of human-likeness trials but 36% of conversational preference trials (and 49% for the most preferred system). On both judgments, variation among a system's voices was about three-quarters of that between systems. Of three automatic naturalness scores, two predicted lower human-likeness, and none predicted conversational preference. In this setting, listeners tended to favor faster speech and fewer pauses between clauses on both judgments, and more pitch variation for conversational preference. Thus, measuring only human-likeness or testing one voice per system can misjudge which agents listeners would rather talk to.

Title: Your PID Is Already a Neural Network: Learning Its Gains with Only Three Weights and No Teacher
Author: Felipe de Jesús Félix-Arredondo, Nezih Nieto-Gutiérrez, Carlos Astengo-Noguez, Alejandro Ucan-Puc
Text_Content: A discrete PID controller is exactly a recurrent neural network, a classical state-space fact: a fixed linear memory of the running integral and the last error, read out by three trainable weights that map one-to-one to the PID gains. Networks with bounded hidden states, such as LSTMs of any width, only approximate it. Trained only on a one-step physical cost (the expected cost of one transition from a fixed state distribution), with no demonstrations, teacher controller, or known gains, the network solves a strongly convex least-squares problem, so gradient descent converges from any initialization to the unique one-step optimal PID gains; the limit network is that PID, with the same action on every error sequence. Partitioned regression then shows what extra capacity buys. Orthogonal residual features keep these gains and improve on the PID if and only if they correlate with the part of the optimal action outside the PID span. On a nonlinear second-order example the gap is 5.88% of the optimal PID cost, and 4.00% against PID with a bias; no controller can improve on PID by more on this objective. A residual started at a tuned PID begins exactly at that PID; at the one-step optimal PID, a fixed-feature residual's first gradient step lowers the cost if and only if its features can improve on the PID. Experiments confirm the realization, recovery, and gap results to numerical precision. On held-out plants of three families, under a protocol frozen before the test data existed, a residual warm-started at a heavily tuned PID and trained with it lowers the long-horizon cost by 3.5%, 3.5%, and 1.9%, with family-wise 95% bounds excluding zero, also under distribution shift; a post hoc comparison with the PID tuned alone suggests that most of it comes from the recurrent part in two families. The primary endpoint, a gain of at least 5% from a generic PID start, is not met in any family.

Title: Privacy Leakage from Recurrent State in LLM Inference
Author: Weimin Fu, Shikun Liu, Qiying Li, Yuntao Liu, Pan Li, Xiaolong Guo
Text_Content: Personalized LLM services place private facts and application instructions into a prompt, then retain representations of that context for later inference. Latent-state LLMs compress part of this history into fixed-size recurrent state. The information preserved by its learned updates is implicit, and later computation can expose it even when an observer receives neither the private text nor the responses. We investigate privacy leakage from recurrent state through partial-state probing and physical observation of its use. Our methodology separates recoverable information, persistence through public dialogue, causal influence on later decisions, and leakage through power. Experiments with released hybrid implementations show that a small state observation supports multiple predictions about private facts and response rules, and that personal attributes generalize to unseen authors. The information remains inferable after public dialogue and changes later decision margins. Complete-read power recovers private facts under a fixed execution schedule. On a partitioned GPU, an unprivileged account infers age from whole-device power during public requests; a separate state-isolation experiment establishes the recurrent contribution to this channel. These findings extend context confidentiality to the lifetime and execution of retained state. They identify access-control responsibilities for serving systems, telemetry restrictions for GPU operators, and data-dependent power leakage for accelerator designers.

Title: Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation as an Optimization Constraint for Continual Learning
Author: Davide Wiest
Text_Content: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is a widely used regularization-based technique for continual learning, protecting performance on old tasks with a quadratic penalty whose empirical Fisher is usually justified through probabilistic curvature. We instead introduce Continual Learning as an Optimization Constraint (CLOC): new training must preserve chosen functionals of learned behavior. EWC's empirical Fisher is exactly the first-order form of this constraint when the preserved functional is each sample's loss. This derivation exposes a flaw: EWC implicitly weights each sample by the scale of its loss gradient, so well-fitted samples lose importance. EWC-DR observed this failure in classification; CLOC identifies its general cause. Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation (IEWC) penalizes output changes according to the first-order approximation of each old sample's loss level set, removing the weighting for any differentiable loss and output geometry, and prevents corrupt samples from dominating the importance matrix. Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC variants match or improve on EWC and outperform EWC-DR. In a held-out evaluation with validation-selected hyperparameters, uniform IEWC improves ImageNet-R accuracy over matched EWC by 2.00 percentage points (95% CI 0.93-3.07).

Title: Continual Event Recognition for Autonomous Optical Network Monitoring
Author: Khouloud Abdelli
Text_Content: Autonomous optical networks require monitoring systems capable of adapting to evolving disturbances without repeated retraining or service interruption. We propose a continual event recognition framework for state-of-polarization (SOP)-based optical monitoring based on prototype representations, open-set recognition, and few-shot prototype registration. The framework supports recognition of known disturbances, detection and integration of novel events, and investigates whether overlapping disturbances can be inferred through compositional reasoning from existing prototypes. Experimental validation on a 2600-km ROADM-based optical testbed demonstrates 99.82% closed-set recognition accuracy, successful adaptation to novel disturbances without encoder retraining, and reveals that overlapping optical disturbances exhibit varying degrees of latent compositionality. While some overlaps can be recognized in a zero-shot manner through prototype composition, others require explicit few-shot registration. These results establish continual event recognition as a promising paradigm for future autonomous optical network monitoring systems.

Title: Plurality Consensus for $h$-Majority via First-Repetition Rules
Author: Niccolò D'Archivio, George Giakkoupis, Frédéric Giroire, Emanuele Natale
Text_Content: In the h-Majority dynamics, each of n agents holds one of k opinions and, in every synchronous round, observes the opinions of h agents chosen independently and uniformly at random and adopts a most frequent one among them, breaking ties uniformly at random. Let M_0 be the initial number of agents holding the most frequent opinion, and Delta_0 its bias, its lead over the second most frequent opinion. We show that, for every sample size h >= 3, if Delta_0 >= L sqrt(M_0 log n) max{1, n/(h^2 M_0)} for a sufficiently large constant L, then h-Majority reaches consensus on the initially most frequent opinion within O((1 + n/(h^2 M_0)) log n) rounds with high probability. This is the time bound proved for the DejaVu dynamics with h samples (arXiv:2604.03648); our bias condition is that of DejaVu when h >= sqrt(n/M_0), and larger by a factor sqrt(n/(h^2 M_0)) otherwise. Our main contribution, the analysis of one round, rests on a comparison principle: among all rules that read the same observations and treat opinions symmetrically, plurality maximizes the difference between the probability of outputting the most frequent opinion and that of outputting any fixed competitor. We apply it to the rule that adopts the first opinion repeated among h-1 observations, and otherwise the h-th observation: its output law is the law of the new opinion of a random agent after one round of DejaVu with h-1 samples. Hence, in expectation, one round of h-Majority widens the gap between the most frequent opinion and each competitor at least as much as that round of DejaVu, whose analysis we use as a black box. Independently and concurrently, d'Amore, Rybicki, Shimizu, Shiraga and Vacus (arXiv:2610.40562) obtained, among other results, the same time bound under the weaker bias condition of DejaVu, with a different analysis of one round and a martingale analysis over many rounds.

Title: Robustness Within a Fairness Budget: Parity Frontiers and Equal-Opportunity Reversal
Author: Pablo Rivas, Jeremy Frank
Text_Content: Adversarial training protects predictive performance under attack but does not determine how decisions are distributed across protected groups. We formulate binary classification as projected gradient descent (PGD) adversarial-risk minimization under a squared soft demographic-parity (DP) budget, optimized with projected multiplier and one-sided penalty updates. On Adult Income, using the binary sex field supplied by the benchmark for group auditing but excluding it from prediction, we test logistic regression and a one-hidden-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) across three paired seeds, four PGD strengths, and five budgets. At $\varepsilon=0.3$, PGD training improves balanced accuracy over empirical-risk minimization (ERM) by $7.77$ and $11.45$ percentage points and removes $85.7\%$ and $89.5\%$ of attack-induced growth in hard demographic-parity difference (DPD). At the representative interior value $τ=0.015$, constrained training cuts DPD relative to PGD training by $52.2\%$ and $49.2\%$, while remaining $3.18$ and $8.34$ balanced-accuracy points above ERM. Across all eight seed-averaged model-attack paths, the sampled budget path strictly orders DPD and accuracy and reverses mean signed equal-opportunity difference (EOpp). A rate theorem gives the exact true-positive-rate shift required for reversal, and the measured group rates satisfy it. Within this controlled feature-space study, robustness and parity admit useful joint operating points, but one fairness metric cannot replace a full group-rate audit.

Title: Scaling public input on AI policy with pluralistic agents
Author: Jacy Reese Anthis, Ken Burke, David Madras, Crystal Qian, Meredith Ringel Morris, Logan Cross, Caroline Pantofaru, Utsav Prabhu
Text_Content: AI is being deployed across a vast range of application domains, cultural environments, and human stakeholders. Safe and responsible AI development requires continuously accounting for diverse perspectives. We develop and test pluralistic agents, AI agent representatives that deliberate on behalf of individuals to align AI systems with diverse human perspectives. Pluralistic agents could help people contribute to many more discussions than they could directly participate in, on technical topics that would require training, and on policy choices that rely on private information that corporations and governments cannot readily share. Our experiments identify opportunities, risks, and perceptions of pluralistic agents. Agents were able to reliably shift policies in the direction of their represented persona's preferences, but the extent of each agent's influence was sensitive to the instructions from its persona, such as having more influence when instructed to be more verbose or less cooperative. This suggests that influence in AI-assisted deliberation could vary based on how participants prompt their agents and how the system is designed. In a preregistered study, 746 humans participated in the pluralistic agents process. Participants viewed pluralistic agents as useful and fair, preferring agents over the baseline of providing input to a single AI reasoning model. Most participants preferred participating themselves over either pluralistic agents or the baseline, but pluralistic agents recovered 68% of the baseline-direct gap in reported satisfaction and 82% in fairness. Because pluralistic agents can be used in many real-world contexts where direct discussion is not, they could be a promising tool to scale AI safety policy development. We encourage cautious exploration of this method, playing to its strengths as an amplifier of human input rather than a replacement.

Title: A Unified Interpretable Semantic Framework for Multi-Modal Fiber Sensing Under Data Scarcity
Author: Khouloud Abdelli
Text_Content: We propose a unified interpretable semantic framework for multi-modal fiber sensing under data scarcity. The framework maps heterogeneous measurements from state of-polarization (SOP) monitoring, distributed acoustic sensing (DAS), and optical time-domain reflectometry (OTDR) into a shared set of physics-grounded semantic descriptors capturing impulsiveness, persistence, structural characteristics, and energy concentration. Inference is performed through reasoning over semantic class profiles, optionally assisted by retrieval of semantically similar examples to resolve ambiguity and support adaptation without model retraining. Experimental validation on real SOP, DAS, and OTDR datasets demonstrates robust performance across sensing modalities, achieving accuracies of 95.0%, 91.1%, and 94.6%, respectively, while providing transparent and physically interpretable decisions. The proposed framework establishes a unified and data efficient approach for optical fiber sensing in evolving and data scarce deployment environments.

Title: SimpleClock: a satellite-disciplined oscillator for astronomical instrumentation
Author: Albert Wai Kit Lau, Bruno Pollarolo, Juan Mena-Parra
Text_Content: SimpleClock is a low-cost, high-stability timing reference designed for astronomical experiments that combines a global navigation satellite system (GNSS) timing receiver, a digitally tunable 10 MHz microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) oven-controlled oscillator, external thermal regulation and autonomous control. It provides 10 MHz and pulse-per-second references at an estimated prototype hardware cost of US\$500. Independently enabled frequency and phase feedback support precise point positioning (PPP) with Galileo's High Accuracy Service (HAS), satellite-based augmentation system (SBAS) solutions and standalone operation. Three-unit phase comparisons separate component noise and characterize disciplined-output stability over 200\,000 s recordings. Across five configurations, each analysed over 200\,000 s, equivalent single-unit differential Allan deviation and time deviation at 1000 s span $3.5\times10^{-13}$--$1.0\times10^{-12}$ and 115--447 ps, respectively. The maximum equivalent time deviation over averaging times from 1 to 50\,000 s spans 143--1090 ps. These results support applications in astronomical timing, including low-frequency very long baseline interferometry (VLBI).

Title: Closed-Form Gaussian Information Projection for Embedded Hypercubes and Beta--Gaussian Mixtures
Author: Ali Darijani, Emadedin Soufian, Jürgen Beyerer
Text_Content: We derive closed-form Gaussian information projections of Beta--Gaussian distributions whose tangential components are supported on affine embedded hypercubes and whose normal components are Gaussian. The optimal Gaussian is uniquely characterized by moment matching, and the corresponding minimum Kullback--Leibler divergence admits an explicit expression depending only on the intrinsic Beta parameters, independently of the embedding geometry, ambient dimension, and normal Gaussian parameters. In the uniform case, this divergence reduces to a linear function of the intrinsic dimension. We further extend this construction to finite, pure embedded cubical complexes by considering mixtures of the componentwise Gaussian projections. Using the joint convexity of the Kullback--Leibler divergence, we establish an explicit upper bound on the approximation error of the resulting Gaussian Mixture. For uniform tangential distributions and volume-based mixture weights, the bound is linear in the intrinsic dimension and independent of the geometry of the complex, its embedding, and the normal Gaussian parameters.

Title: Imitating the Imperfect: Offline-to-Online Robust Imitation Learning from Heterogeneous Demonstrators
Author: Cheng Pan, Nan Lu, Kai Arulkumaran, Josie Hughes
Text_Content: Imitation learning (IL) typically relies on large-scale offline demonstrations collected from multiple human or algorithmic demonstrators. However, most existing approaches assume these demonstrators are homogeneous or near-optimal experts, a convenient but unrealistic assumption in real-world applications. In practice, demonstrations are often collected from heterogeneous demonstrators with unknown and varying levels of expertise, resulting in highly mixed-quality data. In this work, we study a challenging yet practical setting of imitation learning from such heterogeneous imperfect demonstrators. We propose Latent Expertise and Optimality Scoring based Imitation Learning (LEOS-IL), a principled framework that jointly learns (i) a state-action optimality scoring model and (ii) latent expertise levels for each demonstrator from unlabeled suboptimal offline demonstrations. The learned scoring model is then integrated into an online policy optimization procedure, where the agent is trained to maximize estimated optimality scores while its online rollouts are iteratively leveraged to refine the scoring model, thereby mitigating distributional shift during online adaptation. We further provide theoretical guarantees for optimality score identification and conditional optimal occupancy and policy recovery under explicit sufficient conditions. Experiments on continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms existing baselines across highly heterogeneous and low-quality demonstration regimes.

Title: Protocol-Aware Auditing of Domain-Blind Feature Attribution in Network Intrusion Detection
Author: Emmanuelli El-Mahmoud, Abanisenioluwa Kolawole Orojo, Pablo Rivas, Erika Leal
Text_Content: Feature-attribution methods can query rule-violating network states through perturbations, coalitions, references, paths, and ablations, making explanations and their evaluation sensitive to model behavior outside the operational domain. We formalize this failure mode as domain blindness and prove valid-query invariance: when models agree on the required oracle information within a declared rule-valid set, a procedure confined to that set returns the same attribution. We instantiate one protocol-aware query-control principle in LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, and DeepLIFT and audit paired configurations across four NIDS datasets and three classifier families. In six settings where standard LIME reports perfect top-feature repeatability, PA-LIME reveals substantial variability, with a mean of 0.575. Under FGSM followed by protocol repair, PA-DeepLIFT and PA-IG achieve the largest attribution-similarity curve areas, 0.452 and 0.413, while mean within-PA rank agreement rises to 0.366 from 0.217. PA-XAI therefore turns structured domain assumptions into explicit, testable controls for explanation auditing; support modeling, raw-flow reconstruction, and adaptive explanation attacks provide complementary validation layers.

Title: Runtime Analysis of Cartesian Genetic Programming on Max: A Proven Exponential Speedup
Author: Duc-Cuong Dang, Roman Kalkreuth, Andre Opris
Text_Content: Genetic Programming (GP) is a search paradigm inspired from natural evolution for the automated discovery of expressions, functions, and computer programs. Cartesian GP (CGP) is a flavor of GP that uses a graph-based model to encode candidate programs, as contrasted to the conventional Tree-based GP (TGP). Since its inception two decades ago, CGP has predominantly been analyzed empirically, thus little is known regarding its theoretical performance guarantees. This paper analyzes CGP for the Max problem, which has been only rigorously studied for TGP with a proven expected runtime superlinear in the optimal program length $n$. We prove that the expected time for the ($1$+$1$)~CGP employing common mutation operators to evolve an equivalent optimal of the same output is polylogarithmic in $n$, specifically at most $O(\log^9{n})$. This is remarkable, as it shows an exponential speedup by switching to CGP. Our results shed light on the benefit and the compactness of the graph-based representation for programs, and on how CGP can navigate its search and fitness spaces efficiently. This is a first proven performance guarantee for CGP on an established benchmark problem. Experiments complement our theoretical findings.

Title: Topology-Aware 4D Gaussian Splatting for Egocentric Videos
Author: Leonardo Vanni, Stefano Gasperini, Federico Tombari, Chiara Plizzari
Text_Content: Reconstructing dynamic scenes and objects from monocular egocentric video is crucial for embodied AI, yet existing 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) approaches struggle with everyday interactions involving topological changes, such as cutting, assembly, opening, or closing. Since 4DGS methods rely on deforming a fixed representation, events that split, merge, or reveal surfaces cause severe visual artifacts. To address this challenge, we introduce TopoEgo, the first benchmark dedicated to topological changes in egocentric video (covering fission, fusion, open, and close), alongside Topo-4DGS, a topology-aware reconstruction method. Topo4DGS jointly models part-level motion and time-varying surface support by assigning independent rigid transformations to interacting parts and dynamically activating or deactivating Gaussians as surfaces appear, disappear, or separate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Topo-4DGS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 4DGS approaches across topological changes, especially on post-event frames. Code and data will be made publicly available.

Title: Iris-Z: Scaling One Generative Model Past Specialist Geometry Models
Author: Alejandro Cañada, Chema Garabito
Text_Content: Language moved from many task-specific models to one unified model: a single generative model with a single generative training task that handles all of them within the same backbone, and keeps improving with data, parameters and compute. We believe the bitter lesson applies just as much to computer vision, 3D and spatial understanding, in the end to visual intelligence: the effort should go into general architectures that solve all these tasks in a unified way, and into scaling them, rather than into task-specific designs. We test this on monocular geometry, a task that has belonged to specialised architectures for years. Iris-Z is a general image generator that produces appearance and geometry together. A single backbone denoises, reasons about and understands the image and its depth at the same time, and one set of weights generates images with their depth, estimates depth from photographs and paints images onto a given depth. At enough scale it surpasses state-of-the-art specialists on established depth benchmarks while keeping the generative abilities of the backbone it started from without specialized layers. We release two models for the community.

Title: JustRUA: A Controlled Study of GPT-6 Robot-Use Agents
Author: Zefan Wang, Yufan Dang, Xuanwei Shi, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yin, SikYuen Tam, Hanyu Liu, Yasheng Wang, Yaxi Lu, Songyang Zhang, Xin Cong, Yuan Yao
Text_Content: GPT-6 Astra can drive a robot arm directly through a fixed harness, and scores of such robot-use agents on RoboDojo have risen quickly since. Reported systems differ in harness and test subset and often change several designs at once, so it is hard to tell which choices produce the gains. We take these designs apart and test them in one framework, along the harness around the model, the action interface, the reuse of experience and the scene geometry given to the model. A lean harness that keeps the full episode history and stops each motion early goes a long way. Reusing experience changes how the model acts but is not a free lunch, and scene geometry helps most, even when depth is predicted from RGB alone. JustRUA starts from the official L3 harness and keeps only what matters most. Even with no learned policy, self-improvement loop or task-specific tuning, this simple harness raises the score on the RoboDojo simulation benchmark substantially, from 29.7 to 50.3.

Title: Fit-LRP: Fitting Linear Relaxations to Polytopes for Neural Network Verification over Non-Convex Regions
Author: Brian Yarbrough, Jesse Wayment, Jingbo Wang, Philip E. Paré, Shreyas Sundaram
Text_Content: State-of-the-art neural network verifiers evaluate linear relaxations over axis-aligned bounding boxes. However, verification domains in cyber-physical systems are rarely boxes. Reachability specifications, obstacle-avoidance constraints, and neural Lyapunov certificates typically yield oblique or non-convex polyhedral regions, over which box-based bounds become extremely loose. This paper proposes Fit-LRP (Fitting Linear Relaxations to Polytopes), a framework the implements exact optimization of affine bounds over non-convex domains (represented by unions of polytopes) by solving a sequence of small, low-dimensional linear programs. Our approach seamlessly enhances the final optimization step of LiRPA and $α,\! β$-CROWN branch-and-bound (BaB) algorithms. In BaB verification, approximating oblique constraints with axis-aligned splits causes severe combinatorial blowup and risks non-termination. By optimizing the final affine bound of a nonlinear function over the exact polyhedral state-space constraints our method eliminates box-induced over-approximations, enabling earlier search-tree pruning. On ARCH-COMP and neural Lyapunov benchmarks, Fit-LRP reduces branching on the hardest region by $47\times$, cuts worst-case verification time by $15\times$, and with region-wise partitioning, verifies on a single CPU $6.1\times$ faster than $α,\! β$-CROWN on a GPU.

Title: A Proper Random Walk Spline Model for Bayesian Smoothing
Author: Eman Kabbas, Janet van Niekerk, Håvard Rue
Text_Content: We introduce the Proper Random Walk (PRW) family of spline models with a particular focus on the Second-Order Proper Random Walk (PRW2), a proper stationary alternative to the standard random walk of order 2 (RW2) spline. The PRW2 retains the computational strengths and spline-like smoothing of the RW2 while providing uniform marginal variance and stable uncertainty behavior. The PRW2 model is governed by a range parameter that controls correlation decay: in the infinite-range limit, it recovers RW2. In addition to its discrete representation, we show that the PRW2 model admits a continuous-time formulation as the critically damped Matérn model with smoothness $ν=3/2$, which provides an interpretable parameterization and enables construction through a Galerkin finite-element approximation on general grids. To mitigate edge distortions on bounded domains, we propose a local boundary correction that enforces the stationary joint law while preserving sparsity and $O(n)$ factorization. Finally, we develop penalized complexity priors for the model hyperparameters, enabling principled shrinkage toward the RW2 limit. The model is applied to simulated and real data to illustrate its properties and advantages.

Title: Predicting the Needle in a Petabyte Scale Haystack: Open-Vocabulary Event Anticipation in Satellite Imagery
Author: Shreelekha Revankar, Mikhail Klassen, Creon Levit, Ash Hoover, Kavita Bala, Bharath Hariharan
Text_Content: Satellite constellations now image the Earth daily, capturing the lifecycle of events from deforestation to urban construction. Anticipating these events before completion enables timely intervention, yet existing systems cannot jointly identify where a change occurs, what it will become, and when it will finish across an open vocabulary. Building such a model requires diverse event data, but events are like needles in a haystack, making manual annotation at global scale infeasible. We address this problem by representing change as the vector difference between vision-language model embeddings at distinct time points. This arithmetic approach allows us to search for semantic transformations directly in the latent space, enabling (1) an automated data engine for global event discovery without manual annotation and (2) the largest global satellite event dataset to our knowledge, comprising 21,000+ locations across 64+ event types with ~2M images from PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 spanning six continents, to train (3) a novel global-scale event anticipation model. Our model detects change with a 93.5% max F1 score, outperforms baselines 3.6x on predicted event retrieval, and forecasts completion dates with a 3-day median error, even nine months before completion. Code: https://github.com/ShreelekhaR/predicting-the-needle

Title: What Can Next Generation Ultrafast Light Sources Tell Us About Quantum Materials?
Author: Allan S. Johnson
Text_Content: Ultrafast spectroscopy of quantum materials has emerged as a principle application of modern ultrafast optical sources. Measurements made with ultrashort pulses allow the normally strongly coupled internal degrees of freedom inside these systems to be de-coupled in the time-domain, revealing the key interactions for the different orders that lead to dramatic emergent phenomena. This has naturally motivated a wide range of experiments, and quantum materials have now been studied with ultrafast sources spanning from the hard X-ray to the THz, with fields intense enough to create non-equilibrium states, and using pulses down to the attosecond duration. As the optical spectroscopist's toolbox becomes increasingly complete, it is worth pausing and reflecting on what are the capabilities that we currently lack for examining quantum materials, and what are the problems that require the next generation of ultrafast sources now coming on-line or being designed. Here I will offer an overview of the remaining missing capabilities in ultrafast optical sources as required for studying quantum materials, and identify some outstanding problems where I believe these new sources can provide decisive impact in our understanding of quantum and strongly-correlated materials.

Title: The multiplicative complexity of the three-bit low-half multiplier
Author: Bshara Alhodali, Gregory Morse
Text_Content: We prove that the multiplicative complexity of the three-bit low-half multiplier is six, giving a structural, enumeration-free lower-bound proof valid against unrestricted nonlinear reuse in Boolean XOR-AND circuits. The value was previously established by SAT searches of the second author. An explicit six-AND circuit supplies the upper bound. The lower bound combines derivatives, quadratic products, complementary minors, and extraction modulo a Boolean ideal. Independent finite checks accompany the arguments. $\mathrm{MC}(M_3)=6$ is fully formalized in Lean 4. The kernel-checked proof uses only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

Title: Adaptive Distance Detection and Adaptive Instance Segmentation
Author: Kai Yi Ji
Text_Content: This paper is about object detection model and semantic segmentation model in an FPS game Counter Strike: Condition Zero to detect enemies. Semantic segmentation is pixel-wise detection algorithm. We customized the architecture for semantic segmentation. We used YOLOv5s to train object detection model. After training, the inference time of semantic segmentation was compared to object detection. It was observed that object detection was slightly faster and semantic segmentation is slower but better at detecting the exact shape of the object. However, we found out that this slight difference of inference can grow exponentially if the both models get more complex. To solve this, we propose a novel approach called Adaptive distance detection which combines both algorithms. We will also introduce Adaptive instance segmentation to combine semantic segmentation and panoptic segmentation.

Title: Characterizing the Edge of Stability in Variational Training Without Priors
Author: Juraj Marusic, Jonathan Wenger, Beau Coker, John P. Cunningham
Text_Content: Variational approaches in deep learning promise to deliver improved uncertainty quantification and out-of-distribution generalization by inferring a distribution over weights, regularized by a divergence to a chosen prior. However, prior elicitation presents a significant challenge in deep learning, resulting in the common practice of significantly downweighting the regularization term in the variational objective. Recently, it was proposed to train solely via the expected loss by relying on implicit regularization from the optimizer, rather than explicit regularization from the divergence to the prior. While this approach largely sidesteps the issue of prior elicitation, current theory lacks an understanding of how key optimization hyperparameters impact the implicit regularization. Here, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that larger learning rates and fewer parameter samples lead to flatter minima of the loss landscape, which are known to generalize better. We show that training on the expected loss operates at a modified edge of stability, characterized by the signal-to-noise ratio of the gradient estimates and the number of Monte Carlo samples. Experiments on out-of-distribution benchmark datasets confirm the practical significance of the theoretical results.

Title: What Roles Do System Prompts Really Assign? Validating and Steering Occupational Role Vectors in LLMs
Author: Jose L. Sampedro Mazon, Ilmi Yoon, Nadim Saad
Text_Content: Applications built on large language models assign the model a role through its system prompt, intending to shape how it responds for their use case. We introduce a validation framework for extracting and injecting occupational role vectors, activation-level directions that capture how someone in a given occupational role would distinctively respond to a task or question. We validate these vectors through two complementary lenses, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The interpretability lens asks whether each vector is a stable, separable, domain-consistent representation of its role: extracted vectors are highly reproducible across repeated runs and sampling temperatures, remain separable even for very similar roles, and agree more with themselves across in-domain and out-of-domain questions than with other roles' signal. The control lens asks whether injecting a role vector during generation makes the model express the role, and sustain it over a conversation, as well as a role prompt does. On Qwen, injecting the vector alone makes the model express the intended role substantially more often than unsteered, but at best matches a role prompt; on both models, adding the vector to the prompt strengthens the role in single answers but did not slow the role's decline over 30 turns. Together, the two lenses show why both are needed: out of domain the role is expressed only subtly, yet the activations still encode it; and a vector that is stable and separable can still barely steer the model's behavior.

Title: Three-body streaming forces lower the axial binding threshold of a held transverse three-sphere chain
Author: Julian Olszewski, Zijian Liu, Erfan Eskandari, Yang Lin, Yuan Gao, Jie Xu
Text_Content: Particles in oscillatory liquids can form chains perpendicular to the drive. We ask whether the forces between isolated pairs predict when three spheres can bind at a finite spacing. We first hold the spheres fixed during small-amplitude oscillation and calculate the cycle-averaged force on an end sphere. The three-body contribution lowers the critical Stokes number from 4.283 for the pair-additive model to 3.534 for the full chain, a reduction of 17.5 percent. An independent finite-element calculation reproduces the shift. The three-body attraction also draws the spheres close enough for the nearest-neighbour pair forces to become repulsive. This compression accounts for most of the tendency to bend out of the plane containing the drive and the chain. For freely translating and rotating spheres at a particle-to-liquid density ratio of 2.2, the multipole calculation predicts initial growth of this bend at five sampled equilibria. A point-singularity calculation confirms the sign at two of those spacings.

Title: TRACE: Trajectory Synchronization for Training-Free Resolution Extension in Video Generation
Author: Libo Zhu, Fan Li, Zhixin Wang, Binglu Wang, Weisheng Dong, Yulun Zhang
Text_Content: More text-to-video models are available, but many remain limited to low resolutions. Training them for higher resolutions is costly, while existing training-free methods still struggle with fine detail, scene structure, and efficiency. We propose TRACE, a training-free method that synchronizes low- and high-resolution generation trajectories. During early denoising, TRACE aligns predicted scene content at corresponding noise levels. It computes high-resolution updates from low-resolution predictions and the current high-resolution state, without high-resolution model inference. The high-resolution trajectory retains fine-grained variation for generating new details. Local window attention then refines fine details in a shared high-resolution latent state. TRACE checks suspected duplicate subjects against the corresponding low-resolution layout and corrects selected regions and their solver history while preserving detail elsewhere. Experiments across all kinds of video generation backbones and resolutions show improved perceptual quality and text-video alignment over FreeSwim, a state-of-the-art training-free method, with 2.0-2.9x end-to-end speedups. Our code and models will be released at https://github.com/libozhu03/TRACE.

Title: DexRemo: A Force-Sensing Hand Platform and Task Suite for Contact-Rich Removal Manipulation
Author: Liman Wang, Hanyang Zhong, Sun Zhaole, Wenting Cao, Babar Jamil, Andy Tyrrell, Shan Luo, Jihong Zhu
Text_Content: Many manipulation tasks require separating adhered, embedded, contaminated, or mechanically constrained targets. We study this setting as removal manipulation, where progress depends on evolving contact states that are only partially observable from vision and kinematics. We introduce DexRemo, a three-finger robotic hand with high-force actuation, modular fingertips, and three-axis fingertip force sensing, together with a nine-scenario real-robot task suite spanning adhesive detachment, surface cleaning and self-cleaning, and occluded retrieval. To make multi-finger force observations easier to fuse, we express fingertip forces in a shared wrist-centered frame, giving force components consistent geometric meaning across fingers and time. Using an Action Chunking Transformer backbone, policies fuse multi-view vision, proprioception, fingertip pose, and force observations to predict closed-loop action chunks from demonstrations. Evaluation uses six core benchmark tasks for controlled fingertip-input and force-frame ablations, plus three extension scenarios for additional held-out coverage. Across these evaluations, the learned policies achieve consistent removal performance, and ablations show that wrist-frame forces, especially with fingertip pose, improve stability and generalization over local-frame force inputs and no-force baselines. Project website: https://dexremo.github.io

Title: Data-driven Correction Reduced-Order Stochastic Collocation Method for the Time-Dependent Navier-Stokes Equations
Author: Md. Abdul Aziz, Muhammad Mohebujjaman, Xuping Xie
Text_Content: We develop two hybrid data-driven Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) Reduced-Order Models (ROMs) for the non-stationary incompressible Navier--Stokes Equations (NSEs) with random viscosity. The proposed framework combines Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) ROMs, spatial filtering, data-driven closure modeling, and the Stochastic Collocation Method (SCM). A key feature is the approximation of the realization-dependent closure term by the closure associated with the expected viscosity. Consequently, a single data-driven closure model constructed from the full-order solution corresponding to the expected viscosity can be reused across all realizations, thereby avoiding the expensive construction of realization-specific closure models. This leads to the Data-Driven Correction UQ ROM (DDC-UQ-ROM) and its physically constrained variant, the Constrained DDC-UQ-ROM (CDDC-UQ-ROM), in which physical constraints are imposed on the data-driven correction model. The proposed methods are evaluated for a two-dimensional (2D) flow past a circular cylinder problem with a 5D random viscosity field, considering mean Reynolds numbers $Re=100$ and $Re=500$, different correlation lengths, and both in-sample and out-of-sample parameter settings. Numerical results show that the DDC-UQ-ROM generally improves upon the standard Galerkin ROM (G-ROM), while the CDDC-UQ-ROM exhibits the most accurate and robust approximation of the benchmark energy evolution across the cases considered. The robustness and accuracy of the CDDC-UQ-ROM are further assessed through statistical error analyses of the first- and second-order energy moments, reduced-training-data experiments, and an indicative comparison of wall-clock computational costs with the full-order UQ calculations.

Title: Tests of Covariate Effects and Model Selection in Finite Mixture Regression Model
Author: Chong Gan, Jacqueline May, Zeny Feng
Text_Content: Finite mixture regression models are widely used to capture the heterogeneous effects of covariates on a response variable. Our study, motivated by the analysis of Chiroptera, explores the dynamic effects of various environmental, biological, and human-related covariates on the evolutionary development of bat forearm using finite Gaussian mixture regression (GMR) models. In this paper, we address two key questions: (1) which covariates are associated with the variation in forearm length; and (2) whether the associated covariates have the same effect across all subpopulations. To answer these questions, we propose two stepwise procedures within the finite GMR framework based on the weighted significance test (WEST): (1) a stepwise variable selection procedure to identify relevant influential covariates, and (2) a stepwise effect-type determination procedure to determine each relevant covariate as having either a homogeneous or heterogeneous effect across subpopulations. Based on these procedures, we introduce a stepwise model selection procedure for finite mixture regression, illustrated through finite GMR models. Simulation studies are conducted to assess the performances of our proposed procedures. The proposed procedure will be applied to the Chiroptera dataset.

Title: Towards Unified File Management for Data Lakehouse Systems
Author: Keonwoo Oh, Akshay Mehra, Joshua Kimball, Amol Deshpande
Text_Content: Data lakehouse systems have garnered widespread adoption, yet their metadata management systems face a fundamental architectural dilemma. File-based OTFs (Open Table Formats) scale well, but suffer from metadata bloat, high commit latencies, the absence of multi-table transactions, and unsafe garbage collection. On the other hand, catalogs relying entirely on a transactional database incur severe scalability bottlenecks due to analytic file-level metadata. To reconcile this tension, we present Raven, an operational catalog that stores transactional metadata within a database while offloading analytical metadata to underlying OTF structures. Based on this hybrid architecture, Raven introduces an extended Merge-on-Read (MoR) mechanism to reduce commit latency and mitigate metadata bloat, alongside multi-table transactions under snapshot isolation. Furthermore, Raven unifies core data lakehouse semantics including versioning and reference tracking under an extensible ER (Entity-Relationship) metadata model, enabling safe global garbage collection across diverse types of assets. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that Raven substantially reduces commit latency and metadata bloat when integrated with Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake, maintains a catalog storage footprint orders of magnitude smaller than database-only systems like DuckLake, and achieves scalable garbage collection with minimal disruption.

Title: Video-Action Models for Data-Efficient Industrial Manipulation
Author: Eugenio Chisari, Stefanos Charalambous, Oliver Sanchez, Thomas Umbach, Michael Gentner, Fabio Quattrini, Norica Bacuieti, Sabin Grube Doiz, Valentin Bertle, Sigmund Hennum Hoeg, Alain Ryser, German Rodriguez, Mario Arduini, Dang Nguyen, Florian Aumann, Felix Hegg, Manuel Meier, Philipp Wand, Julian Lotzer, Alessio Desogus, Benedek Forrai, Michael Bloesch, Stephan-Daniel Gravert, Stefan Weirich, Patrick Lanners, Elvis Nava
Text_Content: Industrial manipulation requires precise alignment and controlled handling of rigid, deformable, and flexible components. Yet, the benefits of pretrained visuomotor policies remain underexplored in settings where limited access to specialized hardware, components, and fixtures constrains demonstration collection and evaluation. Understanding task-specific data requirements is important for assessing their scalability across diverse processes on the factory floor. We investigate whether video pretraining can support reliable industrial manipulation with limited action data. We propose FLUX-mimic, a video-action model, motivated by the potential of video pretraining to capture motion and interaction patterns that enable sample-efficient training. FLUX-mimic is built on a backbone pretrained on large-scale web and industrial task data, and an action expert to generate robot trajectories. We train our policy by joint video-action training. Across four automotive manufacturing benchmark tasks and two bimanual robot platforms, FLUX-mimic outperforms all considered baselines on the dexterous robot platform and matches pi_{0.5}'s average success rate on the gripper-based robot platform. On a deformable part kitting task, FLUX-mimic reaches 77.5% success with as little as two hours of task-specific action-labeled demonstrations.

Title: Better Boundary Prediction Does Not Guarantee Better Structural Representation
Author: Michael Zhou, Markus Frohmann, Junghyun Min, En-Shiun Annie Lee
Text_Content: Punctuation marks often mark phrase boundaries, carrying linguistic information. Therefore, punctuation marks' abundance and feasibility as proxies of linguistic structure has led to suggestions that using punctuation marks to optimise on phrasal structure may help language models (LMs) improve their representations of argument, semantic, and syntactic structures. In this paper, we test the above claim in English across three primary LM architectures: decoder-only, encoder-only, and encoder-decoder LMs, by complementing traditional token prediction with punctuation restoration (PR). Our evidence, collected at the <1B parameter scale, suggests that optimising for boundary prediction does not necessarily guarantee higher-quality structural representation in decoder-only, encoder-decoder, and encoder-only LMs, failing to improve performance on downstream tasks that require understanding structure in linguistic input.

Title: DuoJEPA: Cross-Modal Translation Between Unaligned Self-Supervised Embedding Spaces
Author: Mahmut S. Gokmen, Mitchell A. Klusty, Evan W. Damron, Caroline N. Leach, Samuel E. Armstrong, V. K. Cody Bumgardner
Text_Content: Learning from paired modalities is commonly equated with aligning them: two encoders are trained until the embeddings of a pair coincide in a shared space. We study whether cross-modal retrieval and classification can instead be obtained while the two encoders' own embedding spaces remain directly unaligned. DuoJEPA trains one encoder per modality with the self-supervised LeJEPA objective and appends to each encoder a single transformer layer that translates its embedding into the other encoder's space, supervised by a contrastive objective computed entirely within that target space. No loss term compares the two own spaces directly, although the encoders are optimised jointly through the translation objective. In our experiments, the translator's residual connections determine where the cross-modal pressure is absorbed: with a residual translator the two encoders become directly aligned, whereas with a skipless (residual-free) translator a paired-cosine test detects no alignment in the final models, and at most a weak one in the ablations, at comparable cross-modal performance. The learned class-token translation is well approximated by a single scaled rotation of the source space. We evaluate DuoJEPA on two modality pairs that differ in nearly every respect. On chest radiographs and reports from CheXpert Plus, it attains a zero-shot AUC of 86.6 and a cross-modal retrieval score of 78.5, compared with 60.0 and 64.2 for our reimplementation of LeVLJEPA with the same encoders and data. On Sentinel-2 optical and Sentinel-1 radar imagery, the frozen encoders fall within the range of published Sentinel foundation models under our reproduction of the Copernicus-Bench linear-probe protocol, the translator retrieves the paired image of the other sensor among 4,000 candidates in 77-79% of cases, and a patch-level extension transfers the within-image similarity structure of the scene.

Title: Comprehensive quantum electrodynamics of fast electrons interacting with dissipative nanostructures and quantum light
Author: Alessandro Ciattoni
Text_Content: Theoretical descriptions of the quantum electrodynamical interaction between fast electrons and nanostructures conventionally rely on standard macroscopic quantum electrodynamics (MQED), which, when applied to bounded objects in vacuum, formally requires an asymptotic limiting procedure to account for free-space radiation modes. To explicitly incorporate these modes from the outset, we employ the modified Langevin noise formalism (MLNF), which independently quantizes both the asymptotic scattering modes and the electromagnetic field generated by dissipative material sources. Utilizing an exact second-order Magnus expansion, we derive a closed-form, nonperturbative master formula for the transverse-momentum-resolved energy exchange probability. In the unilluminated regime, we demonstrate that at finite nanostructure temperatures, the vacuum scattering and thermal material fluctuations do not mathematically recombine into the total imaginary part of the dyadic Green's function. This breakdown does not violate the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem, because the explicit zero-temperature scattering field acts as an independent dynamical system that maintains the configuration out of global thermodynamic equilibrium. This fundamental separation reveals an intrinsic Stokes--Anti-Stokes asymmetry, yielding distinct transverse diffraction patterns for energy loss and thermal energy gain, and establishing a generalized detailed-balance relation that governs the radiative reduction of the apparent temperature in nanoscale electron thermometry. In the illuminated regime, our framework rigorously incorporates quantum-optical states into macroscopic dissipative electrodynamics, demonstrating that...

Title: Subject-Held-Out Evaluation of Deep Ground Reaction Force Estimators Across Two Laboratories: Leakage and Cross-Laboratory Transfer
Author: Hernan David Santos, Yinong Chen, Yu Ding, Xudong Zhang, Jian Tao
Text_Content: Deep networks that estimate ground reaction forces and centers of pressure from motion-capture markers are validated within one laboratory, in a seldom-stated coordinate frame, and sometimes with trial-level splits that put the same person in the training and the test set. We measured what each practice costs, and whether such models transfer between laboratories. Three sequence models (convolutional, convolutional-recurrent, and convolutional-transformer) were evaluated on two independent datasets, locomotion (6 subjects) and occupational patient handling (10 subjects), under one pipeline, one tuning procedure, three seeds, and four protocols: trial-level split, leave-one-subject-out, pooled two-laboratory training with matched held-out subjects, and cross-laboratory transfer. At a fixed configuration, trial-level splits overstated the subject-held-out coefficient of determination by +0.040 to +0.194; on occupational data the overstatement exceeded every difference between architectures. With subjects held out, the three models reached values between 0.583 and 0.804; the leader differed between datasets, and gaps lay within subject-to-subject variability. Pooling the laboratories changed neither dataset on matched subjects. Transfer between laboratories was below chance in both directions, including the vertical force, which no in-plane rotation can affect. Leaving force targets in the plate frame while inputs were heading-aligned cost 0.57 of locomotion anteroposterior-force explained variance, enough to make that force look hardest; a Newton's-law correlation detected the mismatch before training. Split protocol and target frame changed reported accuracy more than architecture did. Learned force estimators should be validated with subjects held out, checked for frame consistency before training, and tested across laboratories before deployment claims are made.

Title: PhysICL: In-Context Learning of Physical Fields on Unstructured Meshes from Procedural Priors
Author: Fabien Casenave
Text_Content: Engineering design studies produce a few tens to a few hundred simulations of one problem, each on its own mesh, and their surrogates are retrained for every study. Tabular foundation models instead infer a new task from its examples in one forward pass, after pretraining on synthetic tasks. We demonstrate the feasibility of in-context learning for physical field prediction on unstructured meshes. A single model, PhysICL, pretrained solely on procedural tasks, predicts fields, with quantiles, directly on each query mesh from labeled simulations, without updating its weights. The same checkpoint accepts variable numbers of context examples, scalar inputs and input fields, and any number of output fields, while mesh size and connectivity can vary within a task. Its procedural prior draws generic laws and boundary-element physical models on morphed 2D and 3D template meshes, evaluated only at the points the model samples, fast enough that tasks generated on the fly by CPU workers keep the GPUs busy throughout pretraining. On five PLAID datasets never seen in pretraining, its field error decreases as the context grows and, from $K = 32$, is below that of the nearest context simulation on every dataset and context draw. It is on par with per-dataset reduced-order models on two of them, behind them where the fields are low-rank. On AhmedML surfaces with a median of 1.1 million nodes, twenty times the largest pretraining mesh, its fixed spatial budgets keep the peak GPU memory at $K = 64$ at 4.27 GiB, against 4.07 GiB on the 6,000-node meshes of 2D\_MSHE. Finally, on 2D\_MSHE, far from the prior, fine-tuning on procedural tasks that reproduce its geometry and loads, without any of its outputs, at a tenth of the pretraining cost, divides the stress error by 2.7.

Title: COMBS: Concealed Object Multi-modal Bayesian Search
Author: Taylor Bergeron, Kevin Leahy
Text_Content: This work addresses the problem of finding a concealed object in an environment by unifying formalisms for partially observable environments with multi-modal priors drawn from a mix of ontologies, semantic networks, LLMs, and VLMs. We propose a concealment-adaptive mixed-observability MDP (CA-MOMDP), a Bayes-adaptive setting where uncertainty is over both object locations and which nodes can conceal them, held as a hypothesis with a bounded ontology prior and resolved only by interaction. We define a hierarchical transition system (HTS) to abstract the environment into room and object nodes that can be planned over via our CA-MOMDP. We further propose a COMBS-score: a multi-modal fusion of a human informed semantic network, LLM, and VLM, to initialize the belief over object locations, which grounds our abstractions and reduces reliance on a single model. Belief is maintained via Bayes' rule, which never lets a look rule out a closed container. We prove a present target is found in a bounded number of searches under exact perception and that its location is never ruled out given missed detection under noisy perception. We ablate each component to demonstrate their significance. Across five simulator configurations, from a gridworld to Matterport3D with a real detector, COMBS finds 92-100% of in-distribution and 92-100% of out-of-distribution targets, matches or beats the baselines in processing speed, significantly outperforms a per-step LLM policy at lower cost on the larger scenes, recovers more out-of-distribution placements than a TidyBot ranking, and matches an LLM-only prior at a fraction of its per-decision latency. COMBS is the only standalone method that can declare a target absent at a stated error level, and the per-step LLM policy offered a termination action abandons 12-22% of targets that were present, against 1.6-3.2% for COMBS on the same episodes.

Title: WELP : Weighted Ensemble in the LooP for committor learning
Author: Jacky Chen, Rishal Aggarwal, David Ryan Koes
Text_Content: Understanding how complex molecular systems transition between metastable states is a central challenge in computational chemistry and biophysics. A key tool for characterizing these transitions is the committor function: the probability that a trajectory initiated from a given configuration reaches one state before another. Because the committor encodes both the progress and the mechanism of a transition, it is an ideal collective variable (CV). Learning it, however, requires sampling the rare transitions it describes. We address this circular dependency with a ``WE-in-the-loop'' framework that couples committor learning with weighted ensemble (WE), an enhanced sampling method that uses a CV to drive transition dynamics. Our framework alternates between the two: WE simulation generates transition data for training a neural network committor with a self-consistent loss, and the learned committor then serves as an improved CV for subsequent WE simulation. Across a two-channel 2D system, alanine dipeptide, and chignolin, our framework consistently outperforms greedy baselines, highlighting the importance of principled exploration. We also curate a public benchmark of empirically determined committor values for alanine dipeptide. Together, the framework and benchmark provide a new method for studying rare transitions in high-dimensional molecular systems and a standard for evaluating committor learning methods.

Title: Is Spoken Hungarian Low-resource?: A Quantitative Survey of Hungarian Speech Data Sets
Author: Péter Mihajlik, Katalin Mády, Anna Kohári, Fruzsina Sára Vargha, Gábor Kiss, Tekla Etelka Gráczi, A. Seza Doğruöz
Text_Content: Even though various speech data sets are available in Hungarian, there is a lack of a general overview about their types and sizes. To fill in this gap, we provide a survey of available data sets in spoken Hungarian in five categories (e.g., monolingual, Hungarian part of multilingual, pathological, child-related and dialectal collections). In total, the estimated size of available data is about 2800 hours (across 7500 speakers) and it represents a rich spoken language diversity. However, the distribution of the data and its alignment to real-life (e.g. speech recognition) tasks is far from optimal indicating the need for additional larger-scale natural language speech data sets. Our survey presents an overview of available data sets for Hungarian explaining their strengths and weaknesses which is useful for researchers working on Hungarian across disciplines. In addition, our survey serves as a starting point towards a unified foundational speech model specific to Hungarian.

Title: DUFT: Device-Unique Feedback Traversal for Entropy-Estimated Response Extraction and Mutual Authentication using SRAM PUFs
Author: Syed Talha Imam, Amna Zafar, Arslan Munir
Text_Content: Static Random Access Memory (SRAM) Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) are a promising technology in the realm of random number generation for key generation, but for PUF-based authentication, they have been sidelined due to their limited challenge space as a reservoir of Challenge-Response Pairs (CRPs). In this paper, we develop a seed-based, round-iterated feedback mechanism, which we name Device-Unique Feedback Traversal (DUFT). The feedback chain is driven by the device's unstable and stable bit positions in its stability mask against the address to create a unique traversal. Additionally, a device-key hashed from the unique SRAM-PUF array is also included in calculating the next round of the chain to keep it secret. By estimating the physical SRAM source's entropy and error rate empirically, or by having a source with established metrics in both, DUFT estimates the number of rounds of feedback in the traversal to be performed to achieve a certain amount of min-entropy. We reach 128 bits of estimated min-entropy on our reference hardware under stated assumptions and experimental estimates. The number of rounds in the traversal scales directly with measured source-entropy, allowing security to be increased for weaker sources at the cost of running time. Using this feedback-traversal wrapper over SRAM-PUFs to obtain a measured-response, we propose an extremely lightweight authentication and key-encapsulation protocol for resource-constrained embedded devices. We realize and evaluate DUFT end-to-end on physical IoT/embedded hardware: a discrete-SRAM node pair running the complete mechanism and end-to-end protocol, and an embedded-SRAM microcontroller for the mechanism alone.

Title: Riordan Arrays as Structured Operators for Artificial Intelligence
Author: Dennis Davenport, Dewayne A. Dixon, Moussa Doumbia
Text_Content: Riordan arrays have traditionally been studied as infinite lower-triangular matrices that encode generating-function transformations and combinatorial relationships. This note proposes a complementary direction: using Riordan arrays as structured operators in artificial intelligence and data analysis. For a data sequence with generating function $A(z)$, a Riordan array $(g(z),f(z))$ produces the transformation \[ A(z)\longmapsto g(z)A(f(z)). \] This yields a parameterized family of causal linear operators that combine convolution, substitution, and multiscale mixing. The resulting structure may support parameter-efficient neural-network layers, variable-length sequence models, interpretable recurrent systems, invertible architectures, and models for hierarchical or recursively generated data. We explain what the infinite-dimensional viewpoint does and does not provide, outline several possible architectures, identify theoretical and numerical challenges, and propose an initial experimental program. The aim is not to claim that Riordan arrays are appropriate for all data, but to identify settings in which their algebraic structure supplies a useful inductive bias.

Title: Quasi-Cyclic Qudit Lifted Product Codes with Almost Linear Minimum Distance
Author: Shantom K. Borah, Abhinav Vaishya, V. Lalitha, Asit Kumar Pradhan, Bane Vasic, Narayanan Rengaswamy
Text_Content: Quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes are a promising route to fault-tolerant quantum computation with low overhead, and qudits offer advantages over qubits including more efficient information representation, improved magic state distillation, and richer algebraic structure for code design. Asymptotically good QLDPC codes arise from the lifted product (LP) construction with non-abelian lifts, but cyclic lifts remain attractive in practice because the resulting quasi-cyclic codes have circulant structure that hardware decoders exploit, which matters especially for non-binary decoders with costly check node operations. We introduce a qudit generalization of the LP construction over cyclic group algebras, which extends hypergraph product and LP codes to arbitrary prime-power dimensions and yields quasi-cyclic qudit CSS codes for every stacking order. We bound encoding rates via a connection to additive codes, and show that in the fully stacked case, qudit LP codes built from lifted Tanner codes on expander graphs form families with $Θ(\log N)$ logical qudits and almost linear minimum distance $Θ(N/\log N)$, via a distance bound that holds for a general class of LP factors. We also study an additive decoder for general qudit codes and a linear merged-syndrome decoder for fully stacked codes. Monte Carlo simulations under a depolarizing channel with equal symbol error probability show that qudit codes achieve lower frame error rates than comparable qubit codes, and that the linear decoder gives further gains for fully stacked codes.

Title: Starscream: Reimagining LLM Sharding on AMD Instinct GPUs with GPU Partitioning
Author: Sumanth Gudaparthi, Smeet Chheda, Ganesh Dasika
Text_Content: As GPU accelerators grow larger to meet rising compute demands, they exhibit increasingly pronounced non-uniform memory access (NUMA) characteristics that challenge existing LLM frameworks. Chiplet-based architectures provide a practical path to larger GPUs while mitigating manufacturing yield constraints. Modern GPUs such as AMD Instinct MI300X employs such a multi-die design, and further offer GPU partitioning capabilities, partitioning a single physical GPU into multiple logical devices with NUMA-aware memory domains, promising faster kernel launches, and reduced memory access latencies with improved locality. However, current parallelization strategies, designed for homogeneous GPU topologies, when applied under partitioning, extend its unidimensional sharding causing significant performance degradation. Three bottlenecks emerge: (1) memory redundancy; (2) arithmetic intensity collapse; (3) communication overhead from flat collectives. We present Starscream, a rethinking of LLM sharding for the chiplet era. Rather than stretching inter-GPU sharding thinner, Starscream adds intra-GPU sharding along an orthogonal dimension, grounded in three foundational principles: kernel shape preservation, memory redundancy elimination, and communication overhead minimization. These principles form the basis for extending any sharding strategy into the partitioning regime. We demonstrate their effectiveness using tensor parallelism as a case study. On AMD MI300X and MI355X, exploiting partitioning capabilities yields up to 4x speedup for attention and 1.43x for fused GEMMs compared to chiplet-oblivious baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of chiplet-aware designs. Starscream's principles generalize across sharding strategies and future architectures.

Title: Modeling the Travel Time-Pollution Exposure Trade-off in Urban Route Choice
Author: Cafer Avci, Zhaoyao Bao, Maximilian Dittgen, Danni Lu, Alireza Yazdiani, Mohammad Tayarani, H. Oliver Gao
Text_Content: Traffic-related air pollution is a major contributor to respiratory and cardiovascular disease, and travel time disproportionately drives daily exposure. Conventional routing algorithms minimize time or distance, ignoring street-level pollutant variability and leaving travelers exposed to avoidable risk. We develop a bi-objective routing framework that couples a high-resolution AERMOD-based PM2.5 dispersion surface with a shortest-path algorithm. The algorithm uses a deterministic, gradient-based weight-update scheme to enumerate Pareto-optimal paths along the time-exposure frontier. We apply the framework to 790,000 origin-destination pairs on New York City's road network, covering 1.48 million daily commuters. Link-level concentrations differed by a factor of two or more between adjacent parallel streets. Exposure-aware routes reduced cumulative exposure by about 38% at a median travel time increase of about 28%. The algorithm ran in 30 milliseconds per query and recovered more frontier paths than uniform weight sampling (4.5 vs. 2.4). These results show that exposure-aware routing is computationally practical at metropolitan scale and suitable for real-time navigation and infrastructure planning.

Title: Efficient Influence Minimization via Source-Integrated Sampling
Author: Jingbang Chen, Junyao Wang
Text_Content: Influence minimization by node blocking is a fundamental problem in graph data management that seeks a small set of vertices whose removal minimizes the expected spread from a fixed source set. It supports decisions about where to intervene in large interaction networks to control harmful propagation, such as the spread of rumors and infectious diseases. Under the Independent Cascade (IC) model, selecting blockers requires comparing a large number of candidate sets, and estimating their effects on propagation can be costly. We propose SIG (Source-Integrated Greedy), a sampling framework for efficiently finding high-quality approximate solutions. Our key idea is to group the possible sets of neighbors directly activated by the sources according to their effects on blocker selection. SIG represents these groups in a compact weighted tree and computes their probabilities directly, allowing each sample to account for all source outcomes without enumerating them. We prove that SIG produces unbiased estimates of the lower-bound objective without increasing variance for fixed blocking plans, and establish a high-probability quality guarantee through independent validation. Extensive experiments on real-world networks show that SIG has the lowest mean total running time in all main comparisons, with speedups of up to 583x over the fastest baseline. SIG produces solutions competitive with those of prior methods and achieves the highest influence reduction in multiple settings, including on many of the largest networks, where several baselines exceed the runtime limit. Additional experiments show that SIG maintains consistently low running times as graph size and the blocking budget increase, while delivering stronger blocking solutions at larger budgets.

Title: Introducing and Repealing an EV Subsidy: Evidence from New Zealand's Clean Car Discount
Author: Fabian Dunker, Jyotsna Garg
Text_Content: New Zealand's Clean Car Discount (CCD) was a feebate scheme that offered rebates for low-emission vehicles from July 2021, added fees for high-emission vehicles from April 2022, and was abolished at the end of December 2023. Shortly afterwards, road user charges were introduced for electric vehicles (EVs). We study how EV adoption responded to the introduction and the abrupt repeal of the scheme, using monthly vehicle registration data from 2014 to 2024. A structural break analysis following Bai and Perron, combined with a regression discontinuity in time, shows that breaks in the registrations of battery electric, plug-in hybrid and conventional vehicles coincide with the policy dates. To estimate causal effects, we apply a difference-in-differences approach with Queensland, Australia, as a comparison region and Newey-West standard errors. Because the New Zealand market was about four times larger, the analysis uses log-transformed registrations, so that parallel trends refer to equal growth rates. The results are asymmetric. After the introduction of the rebates, EV registrations in New Zealand rose strongly, but by a similar proportion as in Queensland, and the average effect relative to Queensland is not statistically significant. A specification allowing for a change in slope suggests a gradual acceleration of EV uptake. After the repeal, EV registrations fell by about 72% relative to Queensland, and the decline persisted in 2025. Both policy dates were preceded by a rush of purchases. The average CO2 emissions of newly registered vehicles fell markedly during the scheme and rebounded after its end. The results suggest that an abrupt end of EV purchase incentives can cause a large and lasting drop in EV uptake, and that a gradual, pre-announced phase-out may be preferable.

Title: Reinforcement Learning for Inventory Control under Regime-Switching Demand: A Controlled Comparison of LSTM, MLP, and (s,S) Policies
Author: Alex Haines, Nathanael L. Baisa
Text_Content: Classical inventory policies such as (s,S) are provably optimal under stationary demand but cannot adapt when demand switches between hidden regimes, and memoryless deep reinforcement learning policies, confined to a fixed observation window, cannot maintain a belief over latent demand structure. We ask whether a recurrent policy offers a measurable advantage over both a memoryless policy and a classical baseline under regime-switching demand, and how that advantage scales with supply-chain lead time. We build a custom Gymnasium environment in which daily demand is generated by a two-state hidden Markov process with Poisson emissions, so that the regime is known at evaluation time but hidden from the agent. An optimised (s,S) heuristic, an MLP PPO agent, and an LSTM Recurrent PPO agent are trained under matched compute and evaluated at lead times of 0, 3, 6, and 10 days over 30 deterministic episodes each. The recurrent policy outperforms both alternatives at every lead time, and its margin over the MLP widens monotonically with lead time, from parity at lead time 0 to 2.17$\times$ at lead time 10. Principal component analysis of the LSTM hidden state explains the widening gap: the representation shifts from encoding a binary regime indicator at short lead times to encoding multi-step pipeline state at long lead times. Recurrent memory becomes the decisive architectural factor as the credit-assignment horizon lengthens.

Title: Flow Structure in Idealized Rotating Detonation Combustor with Supersonic Inflow
Author: Ruben A. Fernandez, Venkat Raman
Text_Content: The work presented investigates the flow structure and stability of an airbreathing rotating detonation engine (RDE) in an idealized combustor. The presented derivation of a modified pressure cutoff injection scheme allows for supersonic injection in an idealized two-dimensional RDE as a function of a specified design Mach number and the pressure ratio across the injection surface. Numerical simulations are conducted using a compressible reacting flow solver with finite-rate chemistry built on an Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) framework. The fuel mixture is set to a stoichiometric hydrogen-air mixture for all simulations. Stable operation occurs for a wide range of inflow conditions with inflow Mach numbers up to 4. The increased total temperature associated with increasing Mach numbers causes burning at the injection surface during the injector recovery process, resulting in unstable operation. Meanwhile, increasing total pressure facilitates sustained supersonic injection. Analysis of the steady flow structure shows a familiar structure with significant changes to the detonation structure when compared with a rocket RDE. With supersonic inflow, an oblique detonation wave (ODW) forms along the injection surface connected to the moving detonation through a slip line. Changes in the oblique detonation wave and normal detonation angle occur with changes in the inflow Mach number, however the overall detonation structure remains similar when supersonic injection occurs.

Title: Lang-SVG: Hierarchical Image Vectorization with Language Priors
Author: Xi Liu, Chaoyi Zhou, Run Wang, Jiaang Li, Feng Luo, Junxiang Huang, Siyu Huang
