Text_Content: Training large language models to generate efficient CUDA kernels requires supervision spanning diverse computational requirements and iterative code optimization. Constructing this supervision is challenging because of heterogeneous specifications, and useful implementations emerge through iterative complicated testing and refinement. We introduce KernelMosaic, an open dataset pairing diverse CUDA tasks with verified solutions and trajectories. Human-guided review and diversity-aware selection curate tasks expressed as natural-language descriptions, reference programs, mathematical specifications, and their intersections. To build the solutions and trajectories, our agentic framework guides a strong LLM through implementation, correctness repair, and performance optimization with reusable CUDA guidance and execution feedback. Supervised fine-tuning of a small open-source model on KernelMosaic raises correctness from 4%, 0%, and 0% to 88%, 82%, and 16% on KernelBench L1, L2, and L3, respectively, while increasing the fraction of tasks with kernels faster than PyTorch eager at every level. Further training experiments show that supervision from the curated trajectories substantially outperforms direct responses and promotes sustained testing and revision. These results demonstrate that KernelMosaic enables a general-purpose model to achieve substantial gains in CUDA kernel generation.

Title: A Margin Perspective on LoRA: Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting and Adapter Merging (MaLoRA)
Author: Ziqing Xu, Hancheng Min, Lachlan Ewen MacDonald, Salma Tarmoun, Enrique Mallada, Weijie Su, Rene Vidal
Text_Content: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks, achieving strong task adaptation with minimal trainable parameters and low optimization cost. Beyond this efficiency, practitioners have observed two striking properties: \textit{robustness to catastrophic forgetting} and the ability to \textit{merge independently trained adapters} into a single model that performs competitively across multiple tasks. These properties are central to continual and multi-task learning, yet remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a theoretical explanation through a unified \textit{margin-based perspective}. We analyze LoRA in multiclass linear classification under a near-orthogonal task regime with $\ell_2$-regularization, and characterize the optimal LoRA adapter across regularization regimes. Our analysis shows that, in an intermediate regime of regularization parameters, the optimal adapter aligns with the \emph{max-margin solution} on the fine-tuning data. Building on this characterization, we derive two key consequences. First, we obtain closed-form expressions for the margins on pre-training and fine-tuning data, revealing a precise margin trade-off: the regularization parameter controls the balance between retention and adaptation. Second, we analyze adapter merging, proving that merged models achieve positive margin on each task and deriving optimal mixing coefficients that balance margins across tasks and maximize the margin over their union. These results lead to a simple, training-free merging rule, which we term \textit{margin-based LoRA merging} (MaLoRA). Experiments on modern architectures and real datasets validate our theoretical predictions, showing that MaLoRA matches or outperforms several adapter-merging baselines across a range of vision and language classification tasks.

Title: Improved Myelin Water Fraction Estimation and Uncertainty Mapping in Multicomponent T2 Relaxometry via NNLS Bootstrap Aggregation
Author: Erick J Canales-Rodríguez, Thomas Yu, Juan Manuel Górriz, Santiago Galdo-Álvarez, Tobias Kober, Tom Hilbert, Gian Franco Piredda, Miguel Ángel Rivas-Fernández
Text_Content: Estimating the myelin water fraction (MWF) from multicomponent T2 relaxometry requires solving an ill-conditioned inverse problem, making estimates sensitive to noise. Regularization can improve stability but may introduce bias. Conventional NNLS-based methods also provide point estimates without directly quantifying voxelwise variability. To address these limitations, we propose the non-negative least squares Bootstrap Barycenter (NNLS-BB), combining residual resampling with repeated NNLS reconstruction. We average spectra and derived parameters across bootstrap replicates and use their standard deviations to characterize sensitivity to signal perturbations. The method requires neither an explicit spectral regularization penalty nor a training dataset. NNLS-BB was evaluated on 40,000 simulated voxels with signal-to-noise ratios of 50-1000, against conventional NNLS, two regularized NNLS methods, and a model-informed machine-learning (MIML) method. Scan-rescan repeatability was assessed across 20 white-matter regions in two independent cohorts comprising 13 healthy participants. NNLS-BB achieved the lowest MWF mean absolute error and root mean squared error in all simulated noise regimes. Mean absolute error decreased by 36-41% relative to conventional NNLS, alongside lower error dispersion. Compared with Bayes-Reg-$D^{-1}$ and MIML, NNLS-BB achieved comparable dispersion but substantially lower bias, although MIML reconstructed the full spectrum more accurately. In vivo, NNLS-BB yielded the lowest regional scan-rescan dispersion and highest mean correlation in both cohorts. Bootstrap standard-deviation maps provided complementary information about parameter variability. These results support residual-bootstrap aggregation for improving MWF estimation while providing voxelwise variability maps from a single acquisition.

Title: Evaluating Tactile Encoding Strategies for Communicating 3-D Shape
Author: MacKenzie C. Harnett, Rebecca F. Friesen
Text_Content: Two-dimensional haptic displays, such as programmable pin arrays and vibrotactile or friction-modulating touchscreens, enable tactile communication of complex shapes in a low-profile form factor. However, many shapes of interest, including CAD models, three-dimensional graphs, and map topographies, are inherently three-dimensional. This work investigates two methods for encoding 3-D information using a 2-D tactile display: (1) a single tactile height map providing coarse but quantifiable depth cues, and (2) a series of binary layers communicating sequential slices of a 3-D model, supporting more complex geometries such as overhangs and cavities. We further compare performance across two display types--a friction-modulating display and a pin array--to examine how the level of haptic abstraction affects users' ability to decode discrete 3-D information. A user study demonstrates that participants were able to effectively complete a 3-D assembly task using both strategies, achieving high accuracy across all display types. While the pin array supported faster task completion and higher-rated--though not statistically significant--user experience than the friction-modulating display for the binary-layer task, these differences did not translate to significant differences in overall usability (i.e., reassembly accuracy success). Together, these results identify design trade-offs and inform development of future surface haptic displays that support the communication and interpretation of discrete 3-D information in tactile graphics.

Title: The two-component picture of soft hadron production: Regge exchange, duality, and resonance cascades
Author: Ondrej Chvala
Text_Content: The fragmentation regions of soft hadronic collisions approach energy-independent limits. Benecke, Chou, Yang, and Yen stated this hypothesis of limiting fragmentation in 1969. Feynman gave it a parton-model formulation the same year. Measurements from the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings (ISR) to the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) still show this approach. Fischer and co-workers interpret the NA49 spectra from the CERN Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS) as the sum of a target and a projectile component, each the decay of an excited hadronic system. This review traces the theory behind that two-component picture. It examines the hypothesis that the hadronic tools that predate quantum chromodynamics (QCD) suffice for the soft, non-perturbative domain of QCD. Regge exchange organizes the fragmentation region in triple-Regge form. It supplies the diffractive mass law of the excited systems, with the shrinkage of the Pomeron in its transfer dependence. Finite-energy sum rules and the two-component duality of Harari and Freund equate averaged towers of resonances with that exchange. Duality therefore motivates describing the excited systems in hadronic degrees of freedom. The review follows the cascade description through its predecessors, namely the fireballs of Niu, the novas of Jacob and Slansky, the clusters of Hwa, Good-Walker diffraction, and the two-stage dissociation of Hama. HEART (Hadronic Excitations And Resonance Transitions) assembles these pieces into an event-level cascade of two-body hadronic transitions. A companion paper (arXiv:2611.11570) defines it and tests it against the NA49 data. The review closes with the fragmentation-region measurements that would separate a resonance cascade from a string, namely the isospin of forward baryons, the local balance of strangeness in associated production, and forward resonance signals with their mass tails.

Title: Blurring the Block Boundaries: Overlapping Block Denoising for Efficient Diffusion Language Models
Author: Amir Mann, Jonathan Fhima, Shaked Brody, Or Avitan, Asif Zamir, Shahar Tsiper, Niv Nayman
Text_Content: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as effective alternatives to autoregressive models for latency-critical tasks, enabling faster token generation. Recent advances employ block diffusion with self-editing capabilities, where each block refines tokens iteratively before advancing to the next one. Yet each block is only as fast as its slowest token, and the next block cannot start before it. We suggest Blurring the Block Boundaries (B3), a novel method with which two blocks are refined in parallel within a shared forward pass. B3 calibrates itself on the fly, opening the next block only once the model is ready to start generating it. It is a training-free and hyperparameter-free acceleration method which seamlessly integrates within any self-editing block diffusion model. Evaluated on state-of-the-art DLMs across 10 diverse datasets spanning varied tasks and difficulty levels, B3 results in on par generation quality and 11.5-14.5% speedup compared to the base model, pushing the Pareto frontier for latency-quality trade-offs in DLM inference.

Title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning
Author: Bo Dai, Yilun Du
Text_Content: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, $p_θ(x)\propto\exp(-E_θ(x))$, and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time.

Title: Cognitive Mapping of Learning by Thinking Mechanisms in Large Language Models
Author: Dong Han, Jin Zhang, Kunyue Yang
Text_Content: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly exhibit capabilities that resemble human Learning by Thinking (LbT), the acquisition of new insight through internal processes such as explanation and reasoning, without new external input. A systematic account of the cognitive mechanisms behind these capabilities, and of their limits, remains underdeveloped. This paper proposes a Cognitive LbT Framework that maps four mechanisms (Reflective Reasoning, Synthetic Memory Formation, Internal Simulation, and Conceptual Self-Organization) onto computational processes in LLMs. Drawing on representative methods, including chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, self-reflection, Tree-of-Thoughts search, Self-Instruct, and self-taught reasoning, the analysis argues that selected methods can functionally approximate aspects of these mechanisms and can improve performance on some tasks without additional labeled examples, although this does not always constitute durable learning in model parameters. For example, Self-Instruct generated approximately 52,000 instructions from 175 seed tasks and reported a 33% absolute improvement on Super-NaturalInstructions (Y. Wang et al., 2023). The same mechanisms also produce characteristic failures, including hallucination diffusion, model collapse, concept drift, and high computational cost. These failures are not isolated technical defects but follow from four structural asymmetries between LLMs and human cognition: the identity of generator and monitor, closed learning loops without external grounding, symbolic rather than sensorimotor simulation, and the cost of inference-time computation. The framework yields testable propositions about when LbT in LLMs should succeed or fail and offers a structured basis for designing more reliable autonomous learning systems.

Title: Optimization principles, revisited
Author: William Bialek
Text_Content: The brain solves a wide range of problems, and some of these solutions are very good indeed. It is an old idea that, in some cases, these solutions may be as good as possible given the relevant constraints. If this is true we can promote this notion of optimization to a principle from which aspects of function and mechanism can be derived, ideally with no free parameters. Optimization principles are powerful and have had many successes, but they remain controversial. We start with a reminder of a classic example---diffraction limited optics in insect eyes---and then a summary of why you should worry about optimization as a more general principle. Next we turn to recent progress on the theory of optimal motion estimation in fly vision, and finally summarize recent results on the landscape for optimization, arguing that (contrary to widely held intuitions) optimal performance need not require the underlying mechanisms to have finely tuned parameters. I hope to convince you that this is a moment to take optimization seriously as the basis for theories of neural coding and computation. This is based on a rather informal lecture at the summer school LASCON X in Sao Paulo, and I have tried to preserve that tone here; pointers are given to more detailed and technical discussions.

Title: What Factors Matter for Collection-Level Counting with Human-AI Collaboration?
Author: Seoyun Jeong, Logan Lawrence, Owen L. Martin, Benjamin Koger, Daniel Sheldon, Subhransu Maji
Text_Content: Many scientific and policy decisions require estimating the total number of target objects across a large image collection. Exhaustive human labeling is often infeasible, while raw model predictions can be biased, especially under domain shift. Recent human-AI estimation methods combine imperfect model predictions with limited human verification to obtain reliable collection-level estimates. However, existing work provides little guidance on how practitioners should choose among models, estimators, and adaptation strategies for a new deployment. We study these choices within a common human-in-the-loop counting framework across 12 tasks spanning biomedical microscopy, ground-level and aerial wildlife surveys, and overhead imagery of urban structures. Our results show that modern multimodal models provide a strong, training-free starting point for many tasks, while fine-tuned detectors become more advantageous at larger labeling budgets and across repeated deployments. Estimation efficiency improves further when model predictions are used to prioritize which units humans label, rather than sampling uniformly. We also find that each model's ranking quality can be estimated with a small pilot set, yielding practical guidance for selecting strategies on new counting tasks. In a field deployment on aerial pronghorn surveys, a task-specific adaptation of these methods meets the survey's $\pm 5\%$ tolerance after reviewing a median of only $3.2\%$ of collected images.

Title: Complexity of Deciding Existence of Maltsev Polymorphisms of Finite Relational Structures
Author: Dejan Delic, Ali Syed
Text_Content: In this article, we show that the problem of deciding whether a finite relational structure $\mathbf{A}$ admits a Maltsev polymorphism is a computational problem, which can be solved in polynomial time. We provide a proof of this result by reducing the problem to deciding whether a binary relational structure, associated with $\mathbf{A}$ admits such a polymorphism. In our construction of such an algorithm, we make an extensive use of a property of binary relations, which is implied by the existence of a Maltsev polymorphism, the so-called rectangularity property.

Title: Stochastic Discrete Variable Representation: Tensor Network Eigenstates on General Potential Energy Surfaces
Author: Hannes Hoppe
Text_Content: Tensor network states such as tree tensor network states (TTNS) or matrix product states (MPS) allow very compact representations of high-dimensional wave functions. Using them efficiently relies on a compact representation of the Hamiltonian, and many methods are limited to the sum-of-products (SOP) form. General potential energy surfaces (PESs) do not have this form. To overcome this issue, a stochastic discrete variable representation (SDVR) is presented. The matrix elements of the potential operator in the node-local basis are estimated stochastically by importance sampling of grid configurations. The estimator of the matrix elements is unbiased, and the PES is only evaluated pointwise. The variance is reduced by representing parts of the potential with a 2-mode representation and only sampling the remainder. Sampling noise biases the eigenvalues. A noise-control scheme mitigates this bias. Final energies are obtained from an unbiased variational Monte Carlo estimator. The method is demonstrated by calculating vibrational states of CH3 (6D) and acetonitrile (12D), as well as the zero-point vibrational energy of uracil (30D). For all three systems, the energies agree with the exact references to sub-wavenumber accuracy.

Title: Operational limits of reference renewal for retained quantum-service results
Author: Roberto Fernández-Barrios, Iker Pastor-López, Amaia Pikatza-Huerga, Pablo García Bringas
Text_Content: We implement reference renewal to reconsider retained physical quantum-service results under a prespecified protocol. Twelve transitions retained six results each; ten completed renewal, eight met the prespecified endpoint, and five succeeded using retained results alone. The exact one-sided p=0.0546875 does not establish the recovery hypothesis. Incomplete references, binding failures and sequential waits expose operational limits. Offline reconstruction recovers decisions from preserved counts. Retrospective binding-plus-oracle checking accepts all 60 usable-transition results without renewal. With the exact oracle also supplying calibration scores, the study does not demonstrate incremental numerical-correctness utility of renewal.

Title: Uncertainty-Aware Hybrid Offline Reinforcement Learning with Online Action Selection Enabled by Sparse Gaussian-Process Critics
Author: Marco Chan, Christos Evripidou, Liqiu Dong, Benoit Chachuat, Mehmet Mercangöz
Text_Content: Start-ups and grade changes remain largely operator-driven, while developing and maintaining dynamic models for model-based control requires substantial engineering effort. Hybrid Offline Learning and Online Optimisation (HOFLON) uses one-step offline reinforcement learning to select actions from historical transition data. In its original implementation, the online objective combines the predicted return from a tree-ensemble critic with an adversarial-autoencoder (AAE) penalty for unfamiliar state-action pairs. We examine the effect of this penalty and replace the critic and AAE with a sparse variational Gaussian-process (sGP) critic. Actions maximise $μ- κσ$, an uncertainty-adjusted estimate of the return from one action followed by the historical operating practice. On the HOFLON polymerisation-reactor benchmark, removing the AAE from HOFLON led to 4 failed start-ups in 15 runs over five critics. At its published weight, the variation in the AAE penalty is four orders of magnitude smaller than the variation in the tree-ensemble critic. Nevertheless, it changes actions when the predicted returns of competing candidates are nearly equal, and paired runs with and without the penalty diverged from the first move. With a Matérn-5/2 sGP critic, $κ= 0$ led to failure in 13 of 15 runs, whereas with $κ= 3$ none of 15 runs (five critics, three noise realisations) failed. The median and lowest returns were 13,464 and 13,398 (HOFLON: 13,393 and 12,411). A squared-exponential sGP critic with learned inducing inputs needed $κ\geq 3$ to remain within the empirical data support in steady state, and then settled with a temperature offset of 2.0 K.

Title: Gaussian Process-Augmented Model Predictive Contouring Control for 6-DoF Trajectory Tracking with a Holonomic AUV
Author: David Dörner, Giancarlo Troni, Ignacio Torroba, Ivan Stenius
Text_Content: Small, holonomic Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) enable close-range inspection of underwater structures from arbitrary viewpoints, requiring accurate position and attitude tracking under state and input constraints. Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) naturally handles these requirements, but relies on an accurate dynamics model, which is difficult to obtain underwater. In this paper, we present a nonlinear MPCC in all six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) for a holonomic AUV and alleviate the inaccuracies in the dynamics by augmenting the nominal model employed with residual dynamics learned via Gaussian Process (GP) regression. The learned residual is embedded in the optimal control problem through a zero-order robust optimization scheme, which keeps the controller real-time capable at 25 Hz. A simulation ablation shows that residual selection is essential when designing the controller, and simulation and in-water experiments with the Multimodality, Observing, Low-cost, Agile (MOLA) AUV validate the resulting controllers against a nominal MPCC and a field proven Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller.

Title: A fast two-phase model for PEM fuel cell impedance
Author: Andrei Kulikovsky
Text_Content: We report a physics-based matrix model for PEM fuel cell impedance that takes into account liquid water transients in the cathode catalyst layer (CCL). This model is an extension of our previous single-phase matrix model for functionally graded CCLs. The solution to the boundary-value problem for the perturbation amplitudes is constructed from basic solutions to the respective Cauchy problem with constant coefficients on numerical cells. The single-phase model employed analytical solutions to this problem. Here, for a larger system of ODEs, the analytical solution does not exist and we used spectral decomposition of the ODE system matrix to obtain the basic solutions numerically. Our impedance model is two orders of magnitude faster than a model based on a standard, general-purpose boundary-value solver. Fitting the matrix model to an experimental spectrum takes about a minute on a laptop. The developed matrix method can be used to numerically solve high-order linear boundary-value problems with variable coefficients.

Title: Reliable and explainable analysis of AVS/RS by Statistical Model Checking and Process Mining
Author: Emanuele Guerrazzi, Andrea Vandin
Text_Content: Automated Vehicle Storage and Retrieval Systems (AVS/RS) are increasingly adopted to boost warehouse throughput while containing operational costs. We present a tool-supported analysis workflow that combines discrete-event simulation, Statistical Model Checking (SMC), and Process Mining (PM) techniques to quantify and explain AVS/RS performance. SMC, implemented through the MultiVeStA tool, delivers statistically reliable estimates of key indicators, such as cycle times and inventory consolidation, across alternative stocking and picking policies with user-specified confidence levels. MultiVeStA orchestrates multiple independent simulations in a black-box manner, enabling automated verification. PM ingests the resulting event logs to uncover the behavioural patterns and bottlenecks that drive those indicators, closing the interpretability gap typical of simulation studies. We instantiate the framework on a new open-source AVS/RS simulator configured according to recent industrial guidelines and evaluate multiple control strategies and different scenarios. Results show that the coordinated use of SMC and PM supports both predictive what-if analyses and post-hoc diagnostics. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of a combined SMC-PM workflow to AVS/RS operations, complemented by a reusable open-source simulation and analysis toolchain.

Title: A Bayesian approach for checking and estimating block designs in agricultural experiments
Author: Josefina Lacasa, Ignacio A. Ciampitti, Trevor J. Hefley
Text_Content: Spatial blocking is a common technique used in designed agricultural experiments. Spatial blocking, however, requires important assumptions about the spatial dependence patterns in the field. Statistical models of blocked agricultural experiments often show spatial structure in the residuals, suggesting that the original model may benefit from additional assumptions regarding the spatial dependence patterns present in the field. We propose a Bayesian model for checking block membership and estimating spatial patterns missing in the original block design. Our model is particularly motivated by cases with mis-specified blocks. To accomplish this, we embed a regression tree within a Bayesian statistical model to estimate spatial effects with a block-like spatial structure. We illustrate the benefits of our model using simulated data mimicking four typical scenarios we have encountered in our applied experience in agricultural research and using two datasets generated from designed agricultural experiments. We found that our model may serve two purposes: validating the originally designed block layout, or mis-specified block-like spatial structures. Thus, our model provides researchers with a novel tool for analyzing data from designed agricultural experiments.

Title: From Video Frames to Robot Meta-Frames: A Unified Latent Interface for World Action Models
Author: Guoqiang Liang, Yiqi Lin, Yanzhe Chen, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Mike Zheng Shou
Text_Content: Pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) offer a powerful foundation for World Action Models (WAMs), which jointly predict robot actions and future observations. Building such models requires injecting low-dimensional robot signals (e.g. proprioception, actions, and values) into a latent space shaped by natural videos, and a key design choice is the interface through which these signals enter: existing schemes treat it as a formatting detail, spending a separate latent frame on each signal or bolting on dedicated encoders and decoders. We argue that signal injection is instead a distribution-alignment problem: how well a representation matches the prior of the pretrained VDMs during denoising. Using the relative reconstruction error of a frozen VDM denoiser as a probe, we find that conventional spatial encodings sit far off this prior, whereas frequency-domain packing yields latents that the denoiser corrects far less. Motivated by this diagnostic result, we propose MetaWAM, which folds all robot signals into a single unified meta-frame: each signal is assigned to a disjoint frequency-domain channel band and lifted to the spatial latent by an inverse DCT, yielding a decodable interface aligned with the pretrained VDM prior without any added module or architectural change. A fixed band layout together with slot-aware routing lets the same meta-frame support policy, world-model, and value prediction over a shared set of robot variables. On RoboCasa, MetaWAM reaches 68.9% success while collapsing the per-signal frames into one and cutting inference latency by 39%, and attains 85.0% success on three real-world Franka tasks. Code and models are available at https://github.com/showlab/MetaWAM

Title: ARE-bench: Benchmarking Agents' Research Ability in Real-World Researcher Sessions and Workspaces
Author: Jiahang Lin, Wanying Ren, Wanghan Xu, Huayu Sha, Yang Shu, Zhonghang Lu, Chengjun Pan, Yi Dong, Shichun Liu, Yuyang Hu, Shihan Dou, Honglin Guo, Huijie Lv, Pujun Zheng, Zhe Sun, Yuankai Ying, Yiding Wang, Jiahao Chen, Zhixiong Yang, Dingbo Yuan, Yicheng Zou, Zhecan Wang, Guoxiu He, Xiaoyu Xing, Qi Zhang, Tao Gui, Xuanjing Huang
Text_Content: Research agents achieve increasingly strong benchmark scores, yet these scores do not necessarily translate into reliable delivery in ongoing research projects. Many research-agent benchmarks emphasize standalone tasks and relatively self-contained workflows in clean or curated workspaces. However, researchers ask agents to complete one step within an ongoing project, where requests depend on earlier session decisions and workspaces contain unfinished files, outdated versions, and failed attempts. We introduce ARE-bench to evaluate whether research agents advance ongoing projects while respecting prior decisions and existing workspace state, grounded in real session context and in-progress workspaces. ARE-bench includes 75 tasks built on agent sessions and full workspaces from recruited researchers' own projects, spanning seven research stages, 33 requirements, and 150 sub-requirements, with 1,173 binary checklist items in total. Each task is anchored at a real user request, preserves its requirements, and summarizes the earlier requests still in effect as background. The complete workspace is replayed to that boundary without cleanup, preserving artifacts from earlier turns. Each checklist is compiled from an intent-aligned rubric and credits any valid solution. Across seven frontier models, the strongest passes every checklist item on only 66.2% of tasks, and Design and Execution rank among the hardest stages for every model. Three models pass about 69% of tasks when only delivery contracts and general norms are checked, but just 28.4% to 40.0% once historical and material or workspace requirements are also checked. Evaluating delivery without these contextual requirements can therefore overestimate research agents and mask differences between them.

Title: How Well Do SAST Tools Work Across Languages? An Empirical Study Using OCPP Implementations
Author: Zachary Wadhams, Emma Sheppard, Dalton Arford, Clemente Izurieta, Ann Marie Reinhold
Text_Content: As electric vehicle (EV) adoption accelerates globally, securing electric vehicle charging station (EVCS) software becomes increasingly critical. The Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP), widely adopted for EVCS management, places significant responsibility on developers to securely implement specifications that are subject to multiple interpretations. The variety of OCPP implementations across different programming languages provides a unique opportunity to evaluate security tooling in a real-world, multi-language context where implementation variability may introduce vulnerabilities. This study provides the first empirical evaluation of Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tool performance across multiple programming languages using OCPP implementations as a real-world test corpus. We applied both comprehensive multi-language tools (SonarQube and Semgrep) and language-specific analyzers to twelve OCPP 1.6 implementations--each written in a distinct programming language--to examine how detection patterns vary across language ecosystems. Total issues ranged from just two in Rust to 1,689 in Java. Mature programming languages like Java yielded substantially more findings than newer languages like Rust, likely because established languages have more developed SAST tool ecosystems rather than inherently worse code quality. These results suggest that developers should consider available SAST tooling when selecting implementation languages for security critical systems.

Title: An Eyring-Kramers Formula for Singular Wells
Author: Yingli Wang, Lingjiong Zhu
Text_Content: Understanding the persistence of learned behaviors in AI safety motivates an investigation of the dynamical counterpart to the equilibrium geometry studied in singular learning theory. We analyze this persistence through transitions between singular wells. We establish an Eyring-Kramers formula for a low temperature Langevin diffusion between two compact connected zero components of a real-analytic potential. The wells may be singular and nonisolated, and the unique minimizing gate is a nondegenerate index-one saddle, with gates understood as inclusion-minimal sets meeting every minimizing path. A boundary-gate construction shows that uniqueness of this inclusion-minimal gate is equivalent to every minimizing path passing through the saddle and one such path meeting the communication level only there. Compact semianalytic topology provides a separating function away from a fixed saddle neighborhood; analytic Morse coordinates give matching capacity bounds by first sending the temperature to zero and then shrinking that neighborhood. An anchored energy estimate and a small-ball potential-theoretic identity give uniformity for deterministic starting points. The leading constant is expressed in terms of the sublevel-volume coefficient, a Gamma factor, and the saddle Hessian.

Title: The Unused Input: The Initial State as a Conditioning Interface for Recurrent TSFMs
Author: Bernhard Voggenberger, Christian Ganhör, Levente Zólyomi, Sebastian Böck, Sepp Hochreiter
Text_Content: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast unseen series without task-specific training. Increasingly they are built on recurrent backbones, whose constant per-step cost makes long-context inference cheap, and which, unlike transformers, carry a state. A recurrent backbone computes its prediction from two inputs: the observed context window and the initial recurrent state. In practice only the first is utilised and the initial state is unused by convention. We ask whether the initial state can be utilised in recurrent TSFMs. Using the xLSTM-based zero-shot forecaster TiRex as a case study, we freeze the backbone and train only a small head that writes a context vector into the initial state, so that any change in accuracy is attributable to the injected state rather than to adapted weights. A spectral summary of the input window, learned once and applied unchanged to every series, lowers mean GiftEval MASE by 0.175%, with every seed improving, which neither a parameter-matched LoRA adapter nor a learnable static state reproduces. An embedding of text attached to each series, evaluated on six MoTime datasets, reveals two roles for the state. As a per-dataset adaptation surface, a static state lowers MASE by 0.04-6.96% of the zero-shot baseline (8-70% of the gain of full fine-tuning). As a channel for exogenous information, the text-conditioned state lowers it by a further 0.15-0.41% of the zero-shot baseline on four of six datasets and, combined with a LoRA adapter, exceeds full fine-tuning, which has no access to the text, on one of them. In TiRex, the effect concentrates in the mLSTM blocks and is strongest at short context. The results are preliminary and the improvements small, but they point to the initial state as a direction for further research.

Title: EngineAgent: Agentizing On-Device LLM Inference Engines with Inference Stack Hierarchy Awareness and Hardware Abilities
Author: Zhengxiang Huang, Yujie Sun, Shengheng Chen, Zhaode Wang, Chaoyue Niu, Zeyu Zhao, Chengfei Lv, Fan Wu, Guihai Chen
Text_Content: Rapidly evolving LLM architectures and heterogeneous mobile hardware make supporting new models in on-device inference engines a recurring and costly system challenge. Each model may require coordinated changes across conversion, graph construction, operators, and hardware backends. Existing coding agents often miss these cross-layer dependencies and struggle to diagnose failures across host--device execution paths. We present EngineAgent, an agentic system for automating on-device LLM model enablement. Its key insight is to separate reusable engine and hardware knowledge from model-specific implementation. Before enablement, EngineAgent constructs a hierarchy-aware engine index that captures engine abstraction layers and cross-layer dependencies, and pre-validates backend-specific build, execution, and debugging workflows using already supported models. For each new model, a builder uses this knowledge to coordinate cross-layer changes, while an auditor checks implementation completeness and drives iterative debugging through device-side validation. Across 12 tasks spanning three mobile LLMs and four engine--backend pairs on CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, EngineAgent achieves 75% end-to-end success with either of two underlying LLMs, versus 33.3% for the strongest coding-agent baseline. Success requires compilation, on-device execution, and output-logit agreement with reference implementations. EngineAgent also reduces average per-task time and model-API cost relative to baselines using the same underlying LLMs.

Title: CLADE: Category-Level Answering from Deficient Evidence in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
Author: S M Rayeed, Charles V. Stewart, Yao Ma
Text_Content: Retrieval-augmented systems often retrieve passages that are accurate and relevant but state the answer at a coarser level of granularity than the question requires. For example, a question may ask which specific disease a drug treats (familial hyperlipidemia), while the retrieved passage mentions the broader disease family (hyperlipidemia). Prior work on context sufficiency treats such coarse passages simply as insufficient. We argue that they form a distinct case, which we call resolvable insufficiency: text alone cannot settle the fine-grained answer, but the broader category it mentions maps to a short list of candidate answers in a domain ontology. When language models read these coarse, family-only passages, they exhibit a phenomenon we call Clade (Category-Level Answering from Deficient Evidence): they answer instead of abstaining or searching further. On biomedical questions from PrimeKG, family-only passages reduce abstention by 13.8 points compared to uninformative passages, and the resulting guesses are wrong about half the time. A counterfactual test confirms the cause: replacing an exact disease name with its broader family name lowers abstention by 17.4 points compared to deleting the sentence. Simple fixes like confidence filtering, scaling to a larger model, and explicitly instructing the model to abstain cannot resolve Clade, and this replicates on ecological species interactions in GloBI. Finally, we test whether an ontology can turn coarse passages into exact answers. Given the correct family, an ontology list includes the true answer in 98.5% of cases, but string matching finds that family on the page for only 19.8%. Letting the model choose the family raises this to 30.0% and end-to-end recovery from 10.0% to 26.8%. Overall, our results show when language models should stop guessing and consult an ontology, and highlight which steps of that process remain unsolved.

Title: A Conservative Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes Formulation for Digital Rock Flow Simulation with Embedded Second-Brinkman Effects
Author: Gospel E. Stewart, Hannah P. Menke, David Egya, Jacqueline Mifsud, Julien Maes
Text_Content: Accurate pore-scale direct numerical simulation (DNS) typically requires boundary-conforming meshes on fully resolved geometries, which is memory-intensive and often becomes impractical when modelling complex rock geometries. In contrast, the Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes (DBS) framework enables simulations to be performed directly on voxelized micro-CT images. However, the commonly used simplified DBS formulation (DBS1) neglects the second Brinkman term (SBT) and the porosity-gradient viscous-diffusion term, leading to errors in flow-field characterisation and permeability prediction. Although it is well established that the SBT is essential for capturing viscous boundary effects, it is often assumed that its inclusion requires separate discretisation. In this work, we show that no separate discretisation of the SBT is necessary: writing the DBS equation in its conservative form and applying a standard central differencing scheme in a finite-volume discretisation naturally retains the full DBS formulation. We refer to this formulation as DBS2, and validate its implementation in the GeoChemFoam framework (our open-source computational fluid dynamics simulator based on OpenFOAM) using three benchmark cases: (i) microchannel flow, (ii) a 2D heterogeneous micromodel, and (iii) a 3D micro-CT image of Bentheimer sandstone. Simulation results show that the DBS2 formulation reproduces the DNS velocity field exactly in the microchannel and matches DNS permeability to within 1.5-3.8% in the micromodel and Bentheimer cases at matched spatial resolution. In contrast, DBS1 systematically overpredicts permeability (14.1 to 37.9% in our cases) under the same discretization. Notably, the conservative treatment of the viscous stress preserves the computational efficiency of DBS1 while achieving DNS-level accuracy.

Title: Smoothed Least-Absolute Conditional Multidimensional Scaling via Iteratively Reweighted Majorization
Author: Xiao Ling
Text_Content: Conditional multidimensional scaling combines latent coordinates with observed covariates to fit pairwise dissimilarities. We develop a smoothed l1 formulation using the shifted Charbonnier loss. We prove residualwise sharpness of the quadratic loss majorizer, monotonicity, compact containment, and stationarity of noncollapsed accumulation points. A uniform additive bound quantifies approximation to exact least-absolute conditional stress. The experiments use paired contamination, separately calibrated loss parameters, combined-configuration recovery, and direct checks of the theorem's inequalities.

Title: Directed Singular-Value Sparsifiers with $O(n \log n/ε^2)$ Arcs
Author: Emile Anand
Text_Content: Given an unweighted directed graph, a sparsifier is a nonnegative reweighting of original arcs that preserves every in-degree and out-degree exactly. In this work, we study singular-value sparsifiers, which are generalizations of spectral sparsifiers. Singular-value sparsifiers find a number of applications in theoretical computer science, such as maintaining directed cuts and flows, speeding up directed Laplacian solvers, and sparsifying dense weight matrices in neural networks. Strong singular-value (SV) approximation supports sparse representations of directed random walks with guarantees that remain stable under products, and controls bilinear error in the left and right Schur-complement metrics. We prove that every unweighted directed graph on $n$ vertices admits an $\varepsilon$-SV sparsifier with $O(n\log(2n)/\varepsilon^2)$ arcs, improving the $O(n\log^5 n/\varepsilon^2)$ support bound of Lau, Wang, and Zhou. The sparsifier is a nonnegative reweighting of original arcs and preserves every in-degree and out-degree exactly. We also give a randomized construction with $\tilde{O}(m+n)$ real-arithmetic running time, where $m$ is the input support size, and the output has the same support bound and rational weights of polynomial bit length.

Title: Constraining electron heat flux from reduced measurements
Author: Victor Edmonds
Text_Content: Coronal heating estimates depend partly on electron heat transport. Different electron velocity distributions can match the same observations yet carry different heat fluxes. We ask which measurements are enough to determine heat flux without finding how electrons are distributed across all speeds and directions. The solar wind carries electrons outward from the corona and allows their velocities to be measured directly. Using one Wind measurement, we keep density, mean flow, temperature and angular summaries for each energy channel. In the fixed-bin model, electron distributions that match these quantities have heat fluxes from 3.58 to 19.85 $μ$W m$^{-2}$. Keeping the correlation between electron motion along and across the magnetic field fixes the heat flux at 11.73 $μ$W m$^{-2}$, matching the original bin calculation. This recovers heat flux without reconstructing the full shape of the electron velocity distribution. When the measured counts vary, retaining the required correlations leaves the same heat-flux range as direct calculation from those counts. We propose testing coronal observations in the same way to find which features of electron motion they constrain well enough to determine heat transport. Those constraints could help establish the heating requirements used to assess coronal heating mechanisms.

Title: An Information-Theoretic Perspective on Regulatory T Cell Localization as an IL-2 Interference Filter
Author: Alexander Wietfeld, Kristina A. Ganzinger, Wolfgang Kellerer, Andrew W. Eckford
Text_Content: Diffusible signals enable communication between immune cells but can also create interference between nearby activation sites. In lymph nodes, effector T cells (Teff) concentrate around antigen-presenting cells (APCs), release interleukin-2 (IL-2) following antigen recognition, and sense IL-2 through cell-surface receptors. Experiments show high-uptake regulatory T cells (Treg) clustered around IL-2-producing cells. However, it is unclear how strongly responses at neighboring activation sites are coupled through diffusible IL-2, and how this coupling is influenced by the spatial organization of Treg acting as IL-2 sinks. We interpret two neighboring sites as a molecular communication system and study the effect of clustering using a three-dimensional IL-2 field coupled to T cell population dynamics. Across a broad parameter sweep, clustering Treg produces a larger mean reduction in neighboring-site interference than adding dispersed Treg. Compared with no Treg, clustered Treg suppress interference while largely preserving the strong local response with corresponding consequences for population expansion and survival. Information-theoretic analysis shows improved discrimination between weak and strong local sources at short separation, whereas at larger separation clustering primarily reduces the remaining estimated neighboring-source information. These findings support a spatial-filtering role for Treg clustering in maintaining locally informative immune responses.

Title: $\mathsf{SVP}_\infty$ Is NP-Hard for Power-of-two Cyclotomic Ideals
Author: Yansong Feng, Jiaqi Liu, Hengyi Luo, Yanbin Pan
Text_Content: We prove that exact decision-$\mathsf{SVP}$ in the coefficient $\ell_\infty$-norm is $\mathsf{NP}$-complete for principal ideals and free modules of rank two over the cyclotomic rings $R_n=\mathbb{Z}[X]/(X^n+1)$, where $n$ ranges over powers of two. For each case, we give a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from the Subset Sum problem. For an instance with $s$ positive input integers, the output lattice has dimension $O(s)$. A solution to the original Subset Sum instance can be recovered in polynomial time from any nonzero output lattice vector of norm at most the specified bound. We also transfer these reductions from $R_n$ to the power-of-two cyclic rings $S_{2n}=\mathbb{Z}[X]/(X^{2n}-1)$. This gives $\mathsf{NP}$-completeness of decision-$\mathsf{SVP}$ in the coefficient $\ell_\infty$-norm for principal ideals and free modules of any fixed positive rank over these rings.

Title: AI Isn't Getting Dumber, We're Getting Pickier: Rising Standards in Human Evaluation of Large Language Models
Author: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu
Text_Content: Users often complain that AI assistants such as ChatGPT are getting worse. Some versions do change, but human evaluation leaves a second possibility untested: the people judging may change. We separate the two on Chatbot Arena, a public platform where people compare answers from two anonymous large language models (LLMs) and pick the better one or say both are bad. We study 1,260,967 blind votes cast from May 2023 to August 2024 on pairs of models whose versions are fixed: dated vendor snapshots and models with fixed open weights. For the same pair of unchanged models, the share of votes saying "both are bad" rises by 1.71 percentage points a month on a mean of 17.1%, and by 1.91 points a month in 2024. In fourteen pairs observed often in both 2023 and 2024, it rose in every one, from 15.5% to 23.3%. The ranking does not trend: in 2024, the stronger model's share of decisive votes is flat. The rise holds within the same voter and on the same pair, and across arrival cohorts from their first recorded vote. It holds with prompt controls, in every major language, for dated vendor snapshots, open-weight models and models with stable answer length, and between interface changes. The drift is shared across models: month effects estimated from other models' pairs remove it from each model's own pairs. Platform-wide, the average model would be expected to score 78% against the 2023 average, yet the share of "both are bad" votes ended near where it began. The pattern fits a standard that follows the category's progress, so a product that stands still is judged as declining. Absolute verdicts on AI drifted while relative comparisons held steady, an evaluation drift that matters for LLM leaderboards and for the human feedback used to train models.

Title: Forward-Value Discretization: Faster Stochastic Diffusion Sampling Without High-Order Approximation
Author: Yuchen Jiao, Na Li, Changxiao Cai, Yuting Wei, Gen Li
Text_Content: Stochastic diffusion samplers often require substantially more neural function evaluations (NFEs) than deterministic samplers to achieve comparable sample quality. Although higher-order discretization accelerates deterministic sampling, its benefits for stochastic sampling remains unclear. We establish matching upper and worst-case lower bounds showing that stochastic samplers with higher-order approximations remain first-order convergent, even with exact score functions. Thus, increasing the approximation order does not generally improve the convergence order. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce forward-value discretization, a training-free framework that evaluates the data/noise prediction model at a lookahead estimate constructed from previous predictions. For deterministic sampling, the resulting Forward DPMSolver (F-DPMSolver), improves sample quality at low NFE budgets through its DDIM-based variant, despite remaining first-order convergent. For stochastic sampling, we develop Forward DDPM (F-DDPM), which evaluates the model at a cleaner lookahead point adjusted for subsequent noise injection. This estimate reuses both the previous model prediction and the previously injected noise. Both variants admit first-order convergence guarantees with one model evaluation per iteration. Across CIFAR-10, ImageNet, FFHQ, and LSUN, F-DDPM consistently achieves lower FID than the evaluated stochastic baselines at matched NFE budgets. With 1.5 times as many NFEs as deterministic baselines, it achieves competitive sample quality, narrowing the practical efficiency gap between stochastic and deterministic sampling. Code is available at https://github.com/Na-Li66/F-DDPM.

Title: Characterizing Fixed-Treewidth Planar Graphs
Author: Laura Merker, Samuel Schneider, Torsten Ueckerdt
Text_Content: We give the first inductive characterization of planar graphs of treewidth $k$ for each $k \geq 3$. Our definition generalizes the well-known inductive definition of planar $3$-trees and the recent definition of so-called planar quasi-$4$-trees [Förster, 2024]. As a key step, which may be of independent interest, we show that every planar triangulation $G$ of treewidth $k$ admits a tree decomposition of width $k$ where each adhesion set induces a cycle in $G$. As an application of planar quasi-$4$-trees, we show that planar graphs of treewidth at most $4$ have vertex arboricity at most $2$. That is, the vertex-set of every planar graph of treewidth at most $4$ can be partitioned into two sets that each induce a forest.

Title: When Should Agents Remember? Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution for LLM Agents
Author: Runxuan Tang, Haoyu Gao, Yuyan Ding, Junyi Yao, Zihao Zheng, Zecheng Sheng, Liwei Hou
Text_Content: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. FGSE applies the hypothesis only in a temporary state, tests it on target-transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects it according to measured gain and risk. Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks, FGSE achieves strong task performance, including 39.8 WebArena success rate, 78.8 AppWorld average completion, and 0.724/0.487 Pass$^1$ on $τ$-Retail/$τ$-Airline, while reducing falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%. These results suggest that testing memory updates as hypotheses supports more reliable long-term adaptation.

Title: Point-in-Time Encoders for Earnings Calls
Author: Alessio Brini
Text_Content: Text encoders turn earnings calls into vectors for search, for language models that answer from retrieved passages, and for forecasting models. A live retriever can use an encoder trained once on all available text, as finance retrievers are, but a backtest needs an encoder that read no text written after the date of each vector. To address this look-ahead bias, from 412,248 calls we train vintages under four pretraining recipes, with yearly cutoffs from 2010 to 2024, and each vintage reads only text dated on or before its cutoff. We then fine-tune each vintage on the question-answer pairs of the calls themselves. The vintages we train on calls alone, with 33.8M parameters, retrieve answers on held-out calls better than the general retrievers we tested in every test quarter. Their vectors also raise by about half the rank correlation between next-day returns and forecasts built from past returns and firm size. When each vintage continues the previous one, a later vintage retrieves better on earlier quarters than the vintage available at the time, and a point-in-time language model that answers from the passages the later vintage retrieves inherits the gain. The 2024 vintage of our families also forecasts earnings surprises better, although the interval of this gain includes zero on calls that no vintage read. It forecasts returns no better, so point-in-time vintages matter most for retrieval and little for forecasts of returns.

Title: Auditing the Judge: Internal Signals for LLM Reasoning Assurance
Author: Mayank Gulati, Gerhard Wunder
Text_Content: Language-model systems use self-judgment to decide which answers to release, review, or recompute. Because intervention is costly, an assurance score must rank errors well at the available budget, not merely over the full ranking. We compare the judge's continuous verdict-token score with a supervised correctness probe trained on attention-head activations from the same prompt. Exact identities link fixed-budget error recall to residual risk and show that AUROC averages recall over all budgets. Across three open 7-12B models on GSM8K and MATH, the probe finds 1.3-22.5 additional percentage points of errors at 5% review in all six model-dataset settings (median 7.4 points). At 10% routing, probe-guided allocation improves accuracy over equal-cost random allocation in both GSM8K experiments, but beats judge-guided routing only for the weaker judge. Cross-dataset transfer lowers probe AUROC for every model in both directions relative to target-domain training. Because dataset, weight precision, and generation budget change together, this measures a joint protocol shift rather than a dataset-only effect. Internal signals can improve supervised, in-domain budget allocation, but are not domain-general confidence estimators.

Title: Bounding and Approximating Kostka Numbers
Author: Jonathan Leake, Zirou Zhang
Text_Content: Kostka numbers, the coefficients of Schur polynomials, count semistandard Young tableaux of prescribed shape and weight. We give a deterministic algorithm for approximating Kostka numbers within a simply exponential factor in the number of variables and the size of the partition. Our approach combines Gurvits capacity bounds for log-concave polynomials with an algorithm for approximating the Gurvits capacity of a Schur polynomial. For a Schur polynomial in $n$ variables indexed by $λ$, we show that the logarithm of the capacity associated with any nonzero coefficient can be approximated to additive error $ε$ in time polynomial in $n$, $|λ|$, and $\log(1/ε)$. The analysis establishes an explicit bounded optimization region and efficient approximate first-order oracles, and handles boundary weights through a factorization into smaller Schur polynomials.

Title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
Author: Yukyeong Lee, Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, Sung Ju Hwang
Text_Content: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace

Title: A New Computational Model for the Spin-Free Sum-of-Squares Energy Bounds of Electronic Hamiltonian
Author: Yuming Bao, Yancheng Wu, Dongdong Ge, Yinyu Ye
Text_Content: Optimizing spin-free sum-of-squares (SOS) energy bounds for electronic Hamiltonians leads to semidefinite programs whose expanded size grows rapidly with the orbital dimension. We derive an exact reformulation of an established spin-free SOS model as a convex quadratic problem over a single symmetric matrix constrained between zero and the identity. Explicit recovery maps connect feasible quadratic-program iterates to certificates in the original SOS formulation, and identify the Frank--Wolfe gap with the separation between recovered primal and dual objectives. We implement the quadratic action through GPU-accelerated Coulomb contractions and solve the reformulated problem using a cached implementation of fully corrective Frank--Wolfe, referred to here as the dimension-reduced simplicial method (DRSM) that caches operator products and optimizes convex-combination weights in a small corrective quadratic program. Numerical experiments cover 65 FCIDUMP models, molecular geometries, and regular hydrogen rings, including original-coordinate recovery checks on nine instances and comparisons with FISTA and a boundary-point SDP solver. On eight H100 GPUs, a cold-start calculation for C$_{720}$ with 10,080 spatial orbitals reaches a freshly recomputed Frank--Wolfe gap of $8.82\times10^{-9}$ hartree in 5.02 hours. Full-space hydrogen-ring calculations reach 10,000 orbitals, with cyclic reduction providing further computational savings. These results show how exact reformulation, data structure exploitation and reuse of Coulomb actions make optimization of the selected large-scale SOS relaxation practical.

Title: MammothDP: Private Boosted Decision Trees Ready for Trusted Hardware and Leakage-free Hyperparameters
Author: Moritz Kirschte, Thorsten Peinemann, Kari Kostiainen, Jan Wichelmann, Thomas Eisenbarth, Esfandiar Mohammadi
Text_Content: Data spaces like the European Health Data Space (EHDS) require the protection of sensitive data in studies during the data's processing and the study's release alike. In this work, we investigate how to implement this mandate using established trusted execution environments (TEEs) and timing side-channel hardening to protect the processing even under a compromised server, and the state-of-the-art differential privacy (DP) notion to protect the release of studies on tabular data. This combined setup could seem to complete the picture, but in fact raises unexpected security challenges that we mitigate by introducing MammothDP: a significant milestone towards a holistic machine learning system based on the recent gradient boosted decision tree learner S-BDT that is provably DP if used within a privacy filter, timing side-channel hardened, and deployed on a TEE. To achieve a strong privacy-utility tradeoff, we introduce two novel components: an early stopping criterion that adaptively selects the number of trees without any privacy overhead, and an improved rollback protection that is no longer vulnerable under timing side-channel attacks.

Title: PSL-RGHA: Parallel Split Learning with Reference Gradient Half-Space Alignment for Mitigating Gradient Divergence
Author: Han Li, Zheng Lin, Miao Yang, Zehang Lin, Jing Yang, Zihan Fang, Qiyang Zhang, Zhaolu Kang, Jianmin Li, Lin Li, Mingwei Hong, Shunzhi Zhu
Text_Content: The escalating complexity of deep neural networks hinders the deployment of federated learning (FL) on resource-constrained devices, especially for multimedia applications such as on-device image classification and speech recognition. Parallel split learning (PSL) has emerged as a promising solution by offloading a substantial portion of the computational workload to the server through layer-wise model partitioning, making it particularly suitable for resource-limited visual and speech intelligence scenarios. However, the absence of client-side aggregation renders PSL sus ceptible to severe training divergence and potential convergence failure under heterogeneous data distributions. To address this challenge, we propose PSL-RGHA, a gradient-aligned PSL framework that employs reference gradient half-space alignment mechanism to mitigate training divergence among client devices. PSL-RGHA comprises two novel components: reference gradient progressive construction (RGPC) and gradient half-space alignment (GHA). Specifically, RGPC evaluates the directional consistency of client gradients and progressively synthesizes a robust reference gradient via Weiszfeld updates, effectively approximating the global descent direction. Then, GHA constrains client gradients within the reference half-space defined by RGPC to mitigate gradient conflicts and rectify local updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our PSL-RGHA framework outperforms existing baselines in various settings.

Title: Multimodal Abstention That Preserves Acquired Correct Answers
Author: Jinyuan Zhang
Text_Content: Adding abstention to a task-adapted multimodal model can discard correct answers, including capabilities acquired during adaptation. We formulate abstention repair as maximizing correct abstention on unanswerable questions under a budget on newly lost correct answers. We propose ReFrain (Regression-Free Abstention), which combines a linear probe on first-token logits, threshold calibration on held-out image clusters, and a deterministic veto that replaces rejected outputs with the displayed "none of the above" option while preserving all other responses. "Regression-free" denotes zero loss on the calibration set at the zero-budget target. All abstention methods in our main comparison start from the same answering-SFT checkpoint; we separately track lost correct answers, repaired errors, and retained SFT gains. On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, ReFrain at zero budget retains all 57 SFT-gained answers with no losses and improves correct abstention by 7.30 percentage points. At a 0.5% calibration budget, it reaches 74.05% correct abstention with 8 losses and retains 55 gains; CLIP-UP EmbLoRA reaches 64.65% with 62 losses, 41 repairs, and 40 retained gains. The same probe at its default threshold loses 298 correct answers. With models and thresholds frozen, confirmation on 228 independent question clusters yields 66.05% correct abstention and no losses at the 0.5% point, exceeding EmbLoRA by 32.72 percentage points. Ordinary refusal SFT achieves higher correct abstention at greater regression cost. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/ModeLiberaL/ReFrain.

Title: MMDM: Measuring Massive Multitask Decision Making
Author: Junhao Shen, Qing Zong, Yue Guo, Zhanqiu Zhang, Yiwen Guo, Hong Cheng
Text_Content: System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. For example, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 reaches 78.75% Hard Single-select Accuracy on world knowledge, but only 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning, while the best Hard Multi-select Accuracy across all models is 36.81%. These results highlight joint reasoning, constraint-aware selection, and complete multi-select recovery as key priorities for decision model development, with MMDM providing a testbed for measuring this progress.

Title: TaoMate-R1: Temporal Role Specialization for Streaming Multi-Reference Video Generation
Author: Qijun Gan, Chenwei Zhang, Xinyang Li, Meiguang Jin, Junfeng Ma
Text_Content: Streaming multi-reference video generation establishes a scene from specified people and objects, then continues it under changing instructions. We introduce TaoMate-R1, a streaming multi-reference generator that organizes adaptation parameters through temporal role specialization. It assigns separate low-rank adapters to scene establishment and continuation on a frozen backbone. Each adapter performs both denoising and context writing for its role; Self Gradient Forcing jointly trains the roles through the history they construct. This allocation contrasts with operation-based specialization, which separates denoising from context writing across all chunks. A fixed-replay gradient analysis characterizes the update directions admitted by the two sharing schemes. On 32 multi-reference cases, we compare the schemes at the same two-adapter budget. Across ten approximately two-minute streams with changing instructions and shared teacher-audio conditioning, TaoMate-R1 reduces the mean boundary luminance jump from 1.96 to 0.613, with higher boundary feature similarity. It also achieves higher mean CLIP and DINO temporal similarity across short interactions, long streams, and public reference compositions. These results support grouping adaptation parameters by scene establishment and continuation for streaming multi-reference generation. Our code and model are released at https://github.com/TaoLiveAIGC/TaoMate-H3.

Title: Experimental Investigation of Heat Transfer in Axisymmetric Open Cavities at Hypersonic Speeds
Author: T. V. Krishna, J. Cohen, S. K. Karthick, Soumya R. Nanda
Text_Content: An experimental investigation was conducted to characterize the heat-transfer behavior of an axisymmetric cavity mounted on a cone with a semi-apex angle of $(48^ \circ)$ under Mach 6 freestream conditions in a Ludwieg tunnel. The effects of cavity geometry, represented by the length-to-depth ratio $(L/D = 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0,$ and $6.0)$, rear-wall height-to-depth ratio $(h/D = -0.25, 0,$ and $0.5)$, and Reynolds number ($Re_D = 23000 - 74000$) were systematically investigated. Flow-field characteristics and surface heat-transfer behavior were examined using schlieren and planar laser Rayleigh scattering visualization techniques, together with surface pressure and heat-transfer measurements. The results indicate that increasing the cavity length-to-depth ratio leads to a reduction in the downstream Stanton number $(St_d)$. For the longest cavity $L/D = 6$, however, the downstream Stanton number was found to exceed the upstream value $(St_u)$ indicating enhanced heat transfer in the region downstream of the cavity.

Title: Tidal potential measured with distant optical clocks
Author: Lei Hou, Xiang Zhang, Qiang Zhu, Xiang-Pei Liu, Fa-Xi Chen, Wen-Xuan Song, Zhuan-Xian Xiong, Jian-Yu Guan, Yu-Chen Zhang, De-Quan Kong, Jia-Hao Zhang, Long-Fei Liao, Shao-Mao Wang, Bing Wang, De-Zhi Xiong, Xing-Yang Cui, Ping Xu, Peng Liu, Jie Li, Xiao Jiang, Hua-Qing Zhang, Ling-Xiang He, Li-Bo Li, Qi Shen, Youchao Xie, Lei Wang, Sheng-Kai Liao, Juan Yin, Cheng-Zhi Peng, Wen-Bin Shen, Baolong Lyu, Han-Ning Dai, Qiang Zhang, Yu-Ao Chen, Hai-Feng Jiang, Jian-Wei Pan
Text_Content: Fibre-linked optical clocks sense tidal changes of the gravitational potential, but separating overlapping tidal components and quantifying their precision remain challenging. Using strontium and ytterbium clocks 692 km apart, we measure over 353 days a response of 0.95 (0.11) to the combined solid-Earth and ocean-loading tide and 1.01 (0.13) for the lunar semidiurnal group, and separate the lunar and solar-frequency semidiurnal contributions. A signal-to-noise model based on the actual sampling accounts for the lunar precision and guides future clock-network observations.

Title: Nanostructuring Semiconductor Surfaces Using Self-Assembled Metal Nanoparticles for Optoelectronic Applications
Author: S. Catalán-Gomez, M. Ibáñez, P. Guo, V. Braza, B. Vázquez, R. Sun, F. Li, P. Ibáñez, Y. K. Ryu, M. Vila, J. Bartolomé, D. F. Reyes, J. Martínez, D. González, H. Wang, J. M. Ulloa, A. Hierro
Text_Content: Semiconductor nanostructures are key light-management elements because their geometry can strengthen light-matter interaction, suppress reflection, and enhance optical coupling. Yet their adoption across material platforms is constrained by lithography, multistep pattern transfer, persistent masks, and material-specific etching. Here, we introduce a lithography-free two-step strategy in which thermally evaporated self-assembled Ga nanoparticles act as self-consuming masks during Ar inductively coupled plasma reactive-ion etching. Correlated transmission electron microscopy on GaAs reveals the formation mechanism. Comparable erosion of the Ga nanoparticles and exposed substrate progressively converts Ga-capped pedestals into pure semiconductor nanocones while preserving crystalline order. Nanocone dimensions extend from tens to hundreds of nanometres, and surface coverage is tunable through Ga deposition and plasma power. The same process produces nanocones on GaP and Si and dense nanostructures on polycrystalline hybrid metal-halide perovskite without detectable PbI2 formation. During nanostructuring, the sun-weighted reflectance reaches minima of 11-15% on the monocrystalline substrates, whereas the perovskite achieves 0.5% after complete mask consumption. The approach therefore combines a self-assembled mask, its consumption, and pattern transfer in a single physical etching step, providing a simple route to light-coupling surfaces for III-V, Si, and perovskite optoelectronics.

Title: Nonreciprocal Josephson Dynamics of a $\mathcal{PT}$-Symmetric Atomtronic SQUID
Author: Nalinikanta Pradhan, Rina Kanamoto, M. Bhattacharya, Pankaj K. Mishra
Text_Content: We investigate non-Hermitian Josephson dynamics in an atomtronic quantum interference device (AQUID), formed by a ring Bose Einstein condensate with balanced atomic gain and loss regions and two moving optical barriers. The balanced gain and loss profile establishes a parity time symmetric potential while breaking spatial inversion symmetry, providing the essential ingredients for nonreciprocal Josephson transport. The dynamics are monitored nondestructively through the phase quadrature spectrum of an optomechanical cavity driven by Laguerre Gaussian beams coupled to the condensate. We demonstrate that increasing the local gain and loss strength softens the parity time symmetric collective mode towards an exceptional point, as verified by Bogoliubov de Gennes analysis. The associated coherent population exchange produces an additional characteristic splitting in the cavity output spectrum. For linearly translating barriers, non-Hermiticity provides an additional control parameter for tuning the critical current. When the barriers undergo simultaneous translation and rotation, the rotation induced phase modifies the interference between counter propagating currents, offering further control over the nonreciprocal response. Under periodic barrier modulation, we find more pronounced Shapiro steps in the current voltage characteristics due to the intrinsic parity time symmetric collective mode. Finally, we propose an alternative Hermitian realization using a tilted optical lattice, providing an experimentally accessible route to engineering biased transport and population transfer. Our results establish parity time symmetric atomtronic SQUIDs as a versatile platform for controlling nonreciprocal Josephson transport and collective excitations in driven quantum fluids.

Title: Adversarial risk analysis with fully probabilistic designs
Author: Mario Chacón-Falcón, Tatiana Valentine Guy, Miroslav Kárný, David Rios Insua
Text_Content: Adversarial risk analysis (ARA) informs decision-makers when facing intelligent opponents and uncertain outcomes, enabling an analyst to model beliefs about the opponents' preferences, capabilities, beliefs, and the strategic calculations that opponents employ. Major applications cover reliability and risk analysis of critical infrastructures in presence of adversarial threats. In such domains, ARA mitigates typical common knowledge assumptions of standard game-theoretic approaches. However, ARA entails complex modelling and computations. To alleviate these, we explore its combination with fully probabilistic design (FPD), a control theory methodology supporting an agent in choosing the decision distribution that achieves the outcomes with a distribution closest to its ideal. We use FPD to model and forecast the opponent's decisions within an ARA setting and present how to handle security games within this ARA-FPD framework, covering both single and multiple stage problems.

Title: VASTRA: Efficient Agentic Top-K Interactive Video Analysis
Author: Tushar Tyagi, Aditya Raghavan, Haoran Qiu, Francisco Romero
Text_Content: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable natural language video retrieval, bypassing traditional hand-engineered pipelines. Integrating agentic reasoning frameworks (e.g., ReAct) further advances this paradigm by allowing models to dynamically inspect video content rather than relying on a single visual pass. Applying this pattern naively to video retrieval inherits problems that video systems cannot afford: results vary from run to run under identical conditions, and cost and latency scale with every reasoning step the agent takes rather than with the work the query actually requires. We present VASTRA, an agentic video retrieval system whose execution is dictated by query complexity rather than an open-ended reasoning loop: cheap, reliably answerable queries are ranked directly from pre-ingested summaries, while harder queries trigger targeted verification only where relevance is genuinely uncertain. This keeps control flow external to the model rather than latent in a growing chain of thought, establishing deterministic control flow by construction and end-to-end rank reproducibility under greedy serving.
