Author: Hang Li, Jiaxin Qi, Yan Cui, Yuhua Zheng, Jianqiang Huang
Text_Content: Motivation: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) capture the underlying interactions through which transcription factors (TFs) regulate genes. Based on gene expression data, existing GRN inference approaches generally fall into two categories: graph-based methods, which model the GRN as a whole graph, and pairwise-based methods, which decompose the GRN into individual TF-target gene pairs for modeling. However, each approach exhibits limitations that are precisely the strengths of its counterpart. Graph-based methods tend to overfit due to their reliance on a single training graph, whereas pairwise-based methods benefit from abundant TF-target training pairs. In contrast, pairwise-based methods overlook the global topological structure, which is essential for comprehensively capturing regulatory mechanisms. Results: To address these limitations, we propose scGPL, an end-to-end unified framework that jointly models global regulatory topology and local interactions. scGPL extracts macro-level features from the global regulatory graph and introduces a dynamic, importance-guided subgraph sampling mechanism to capture fine-grained local dependencies. By fusing global representations with subgraph-enhanced local features, our framework bridges the gap between the two paradigms, incorporating essential whole-graph topological dependencies while retaining the data abundance advantage of pairwise methods. Extensive experiments on seven benchmark datasets demonstrate that scGPL consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, with up to 13.7% improvement over the strongest baseline, validating the effectiveness of our integrative design. Availability and implementation: The source code is maintained on GitHub (https://github.com/talent-hang/scGPL), and the datasets and versioned releases are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21608485 for reproducibility.

Title: Additively manufactured ceramic platforms for miniaturized optical frequency references and robust atomic sensor systems
Author: Marc Christ, Sascha Neinert, Conrad Zimmermann, Klaus Döringshoff, Markus Krutzik
Text_Content: Transferring atomic quantum sensors from laboratory-scale physics packages to compact, alignment-free sensor heads suitable for field and space deployment requires a structural platform that combines mechanical, thermal, and optical functionality within a single, manufacturable component. We present such a platform based on additively manufactured technical ceramics: lithography-based ceramic manufacturing is used to fabricate monolithic micro-optical benches with application-specific mounting geometries, while high-precision active alignment and adhesive bonding realize long-term stable optical assemblies through micro-integration. As a first system-level demonstrator, we present a micro-integrated optical frequency reference based on Doppler-free spectroscopy of the rubidium D2 line, integrated within a 6 mL Al2O3 module. A laser stabilized to the reference reaches a fractional frequency instability of $3\times10^{-12}$ at 1 s. We extend the platform to a compact optically pumped magnetometer, exploiting the magnetic cleanliness and tailored thermal properties of high-purity ceramics for a 7 mL sensor head with picotesla sensitivity aimed at space-borne biomagnetometry, and to a micro-integrated optical dipole trap with active MEMS-mirror beam steering for cold-atom manipulation. Together, these demonstrators show that ceramic additive manufacturing and optical micro-integration form a versatile, robust platform for compact atomic sensor systems in field and space applications.

Title: Auditing LLM Pseudo-Label Distillation for Review Informativeness at E-Commerce Scale
Author: M. Emin Dogan, Cansu Er, Aysenur Kulunk, M. Furkan Eseoglu, H. Bahadir Sahin
Text_Content: We study hard-label distillation from Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite to compact encoders on 5.34 million Turkish marketplace reviews. A strict new-SKU temporal test measures teacher fidelity; a separate, teacher-label-blind audit by one company annotator measures editorial agreement. An H3 category prefix slightly improves teacher fidelity on the full new-SKU test. On the 16,000-review chronological audit subset, it instead reduces agreement with both Gemini and the annotator, with a clearer paired difference for CORN than for cross entropy. Thus the context effect depends on the evaluation population, and teacher fidelity alone does not establish editorial alignment. Under the measured offline configurations, a single-L4 student pipeline processes reviews 50.2 times faster than the teacher pipeline.

Title: AnchorMTS: Multi-View Signal Representation and Forecast-Anchored Fusion for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting
Author: Gao Wu, Tingting Xu, Changning Wu, Tengfei Long, Yong Liu, Jiabin Jin, Kexin Zhang
Text_Content: Long-term time-series forecasters typically optimize a single numerical representation, even though the same history exposes complementary geometry, recurrence, and semantic structure. We propose AnchorMTS, which derives self-aligned visual and textual views from each observed window and uses them only to refine a complete numerical forecast. A trainable evidence path produces a candidate forecast, while a parameter-free output projection enforces an exact per-variable bound on its displacement from the numerical anchor. Across six benchmarks and four horizons, AnchorMTS achieves the best macro MSE/MAE (0.336/0.367) among seven supervised baselines and wins 18 of 24 MSE settings against the cellwise baseline envelope; removing the auxiliary path raises macro MSE to 0.340. The projection leaves 95.8% of candidate refinements unchanged while yielding zero bound violations, showing that complementary multi-view evidence can improve forecasting while its final influence remains explicitly controlled.

Title: Analytic Solution to Cumulative Coulomb Scattering in Boltzmann Theory
Author: Tie-Huai Zhang, Wei-Min Wang, Zi-Yan Zhang, Yu-Tong Li, Jie Zhang
Text_Content: In plasmas, frequent soft Coulomb collisions gradually transfer energy and momentum, whereas a single close collision can change both abruptly and redirect a particle. This coexistence can shape runaway-electron avalanches in tokamaks and alpha-particle heating in inertial fusion, yet no first-principles analytic theory has determined how the cumulative statistics evolve under plasma conditions. Fokker--Planck and moment-matched models reproduce average transport but do not determine how scattering evolves from isolated events to cumulative relaxation across plasma conditions. Here we resolve this long-standing problem directly from Boltzmann theory. By asymptotically rescaling the exact angular expansion, we obtain the first quantitative map of the single-collision, core-tail coexistence, and low-order relaxation regimes within a unified Boltzmann framework. The rescaling also provides explicit analytic representations of the angular distribution across these regimes without empirical transition parameters. The theory further shows that small-angle models differ from the Boltzmann distribution even in the forward core, so appending a large-angle tail to a conventional core cannot recover the collision statistics. In fast-electron transport, this full-range redistribution leaves mean energy loss nearly unchanged yet counterintuitively enhances beam concentration and modifies the energy flux delivered to a finite region.

Title: RiSE-Drive: Risk-Sensitive Long-Horizon Candidate Evaluation for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
Author: Yu Zhao, Hongyi Duan, Ming Yin, Hongyuan Zhang, Fan Yang, Hongzhi Wang, Xiubo Liang
Text_Content: End-to-end autonomous driving systems increasingly rely on generating multiple trajectory candidates and selecting one for execution. In this setting, a central challenge is no longer only candidate generation, but how to evaluate candidates according to their long-horizon consequences under uncertainty. Existing methods still mainly use deterministic point scores, heuristic subscores, or single-outcome evaluations, which makes it difficult to capture delayed failures, tail risk, and ranking instability under plausible future perturbations. We present RiSE-Drive, a framework for risk-sensitive long-horizon candidate evaluation in end-to-end autonomous driving. RiSE-Drive first performs candidate-conditioned latent future rollout, then estimates long-horizon outcome distributions instead of single scalar scores, and finally ranks candidates using a tail-risk-aware and perturbation-robust decision criterion. This reformulates candidate scoring from deterministic oracle-style evaluation into distributional outcome assessment with explicit risk control. As a result, the evaluator is encouraged to prefer candidates that are not only strong under nominal conditions, but also reliable under long-horizon rollout and safety-critical deviations. Experiments on the NAVSIM-v1 and NAVSIM-v2 benchmarks, as well as the closed-loop HUGSIM benchmark, show that RiSE-Drive achieves state-of-the-art performance and significantly improves the robustness of candidate selection.

Title: LLM Validation Makes Minimal-Pair Benchmarks Easier for Language Models
Author: Guofang Tang, Zheng Qu
Text_Content: Minimal-pair benchmarks are only as good as their labels, and LLMs are an obvious substitute for costly human validation. We test it on BLiMP (English) and QFrBLiMP (Quebec French), the two public minimal-pair datasets releasing every forced-choice human judgment. Three LLMs validate by forced choice, by rating, and as a panel, scored against human panels of one, three and five judges in two pre-registered phases. On BLiMP, forced-choice validators agree with held-out human majorities more often than five-judge panels, yet catch far fewer pairs whose label humans reject than one judge does. By point estimate, no validator is worth more than one judge. The errors are not random. On both datasets, across 10 open LMs, human-supported pairs that the pre-registered LLM filter flags are 18.9 points harder than those it accepts, in all 70 LM-validator combinations, and harder than pairs a single human judge flags. Filtering thus removes items on which LMs fail but humans do not, raising accuracy more than random removal. A protocol frozen before any output replicates the gap and the lift on Dutch BLiMP-NL. LLM validation makes minimal-pair benchmarks easier for the models they are meant to test; we release code, validator outputs and item-level scores.

Title: Local Modifications of Nearest-Neighbor and Min-Plus Representations
Author: Liliia Redina
Text_Content: We study how changing a Boolean-valued function at $d$ inputs affects the size and precision of its exact representations. Starting from a representation of size $m$, we prove four bounds, two for nearest-neighbor (NN) representations and two for integer min-plus representations. (i) For NN representations on a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n\ge2$, at most $m+2d$ anchors suffice. The coefficient $2$ is optimal: on a three-point domain, changing one value can increase the minimum number of anchors from one to three. (ii) For NN representations on the Boolean cube with rational anchors, let $R$ be the maximum original coordinate bit length, and let $Δ$ be the maximum bit length of the least common denominator of any one original anchor's coordinates. We construct a representation with at most $m+3d$ anchors on a common dyadic grid and coordinate bit length $O(R+Δ+\log(n+1))$. (iii) For integer min-plus representations on the Boolean cube, we give a construction that keeps the original $m$ forms and their labels and adds at most $d$ new forms. Its maximum weight is at most $W+2n$, where $W$ is the largest absolute original coefficient, including constant terms. (iv) For integer min-plus representations on a finite rational domain $X\subset\mathbb{Q}^n$, at most $m+2d$ forms suffice. Their maximum weight is polynomially bounded in $m,d,W,n,|X|$, the coordinate bound, and the common denominator of $X$. The coefficient $2$ is again optimal: on a three-point domain, changing one value can increase the minimum number of forms from one to three. These bounds imply stability under polynomially many changes on the cube for polynomial-size representations, including those with polynomially bounded NN coordinate bit length or min-plus weight.

Title: The Target Is a Predicate: Predicate-State Grounding for Semantic-Level Video Reasoning Segmentation
Author: Yuhuan Hong, Yiming Ren, Zhiqiang Lin, Feize Wu, Xingyun Liu, Yitong Xie, Lei Zhou, Lisheng Wu, Junjie Wang, Yujiu Yang
Text_Content: In this paper, we introduce Predicate-State Video Reasoning Segmentation (PS-VRS), where a query defines a dynamic predicate $P(o,t)$ over objects and time rather than a fixed object identity. Existing methods typically treat the target as permanently active once identified, leading to over-emission of masks during vacant intervals and failure to handle target switching. To address this, we construct PS-Bench, a large-scale benchmark with 2,077 videos and 16,250 queries annotated with explicit active/vacant predicate states, temporal intervals, and pixel masks. We further propose Predicate-State Grounding (PSG), a State-Bind-Emit pipeline that: (1) predicts [ACTIVE]/[VACANT] state tokens; (2) aligns them to video frames via dense cross-modal similarity; and (3) emits masks via SAM2 only for active states. Experiments show that PSG outperforms existing baselines by +9.32 J&F on PS-Bench and significantly reduces false-positive mask emissions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of explicit predicate-state modeling for video reasoning segmentation with dynamic visual witnesses.

Title: Marrying Capacity and Precision for Efficient 2D Gaussian Image Representation
Author: Lin Dong, Qi Ming, Liuqian Wang, Wentao Chao, Yufei Gao, Chengming Liu, Lei Shi
Text_Content: 2D Gaussian representations provide an explicit and efficient way to represent images, but their rate-distortion performance under limited budgets depends critically on how Gaussian capacity and parameter precision are allocated. Existing methods typically optimize these two resources separately, overlooking content-dependent capacity demands and heterogeneous quantization sensitivity. We present CP-GS, a capacity-precision coupled Gaussian splatting framework for budget-aware 2D Gaussian image representation that jointly optimizes capacity allocation and attribute precision under a shared rate constraint. CP-GS first constructs a content-adaptive Gaussian representation by dynamically reallocating a fixed Gaussian budget from redundant regions to areas with higher representation demand. It then introduces hierarchical distortion-aware representation quantization, using efficient rendering-based calibration to allocate precision across Gaussian attributes and further refine it within heterogeneous attribute groups. Finally, it jointly optimizes Gaussian capacity and attribute precision by constructing candidate representations with different Gaussian counts and precision configurations and selecting operating points according to decoded distortion and actual serialized size. Experiments on DIV2K and Kodak show that CP-GS achieves improved rate-distortion performance over representative 2D Gaussian and implicit neural representations across a range of budgets, while maintaining a fixed overall representation budget and low optimization cost. These results demonstrate the benefit of jointly optimizing spatial capacity and parameter precision for compact Gaussian image representation.

Title: Integrating Action Prefix Prediction and Alignment Across Modalities for Multimodal Reinforcement Learning
Author: Sijie Xu, Francisco Cruz
Text_Content: Learning representations from multimodal observations is difficult in reinforcement learning with limited interaction data. Multimodal Joint Predictive Representation combines multimodal latent prediction with contrastive learning across modalities, but its recursive rollout depends on earlier predictions and its pairwise alignment focuses on correspondence between modalities. We propose Improved Predictive Representation, which combines prediction from action prefixes with alignment at the observed anchor based on Contrastive Multimodal learning. At each horizon, it predicts future representations directly from the observed anchor and the corresponding sequence of actions. We evaluate two crop configurations: IPR-S with a minimum retained crop area of 10%, and IPR-H with 50%. Across five DeepMind Control Suite tasks, IPR-H achieves an average return across tasks that is 10.0% higher than the baseline with visual and depth images and 3.4% higher with visual images and position vectors. The relative performance of the two configurations varies across tasks. In Webots, both IPR configurations achieve higher mean final returns than the baseline without LiDAR, but not when LiDAR is available.

Title: Prior Probabilities for Constrained Hypotheses: Invariance, Neutrality, and Model Search
Author: Joris Mulder
Text_Content: When testing hypotheses with equality and inequality constraints using Bayes factors, the hypotheses are commonly assigned equal prior probabilities. The resulting posterior probabilities depend on how the analyst divides the parameter space into hypotheses: splitting one hypothesis into two changes the posterior probabilities of the other hypotheses, and a hypothesis can receive more posterior probability than a hypothesis that contains it. An alternative is considered where the prior probabilities of the hypotheses follow from a single prior distribution on the parameters. Prior probabilities of the equality constrained subspaces are taken from the Bayesian variable selection literature, and prior probabilities of the inequality constrained regions within these subspaces are given by their relative complexities under the encompassing prior. Under this complexity-induced prior, posterior probabilities do not depend on how the hypotheses are divided, are coherent across nested hypotheses, and agree with those from an exploratory model search over the same subspaces. In return, inequality constraints do not increase the posterior probability of a hypothesis relative to the null hypothesis. The prior is therefore suited for analysts who want to test constrained hypotheses without favoring specific constraints a priori, while the potential gain in evidence for the constraints remains quantified by the Bayes factor.

Title: Softness is something you also need! Why compliance helps control: information metrics of a passive walker with compliant ankle
Author: Fabio Bonsignorio, Elisabetta Barletta, Sorin Dragomir, Francesco Esposito, Enrica Zereik
Text_Content: A great gap in adaptivity, flexibility, and dexterity still exists between intelligent robots, whether they are made of rigid or (partially) compliant components, and their naturally evolved animal and vegetal counterparts. One reason could be of `paradigm' nature. On the one hand, most robots (both rigid and soft) are still designed by following a `Cartesian' approach, with top-down control and a clear mind-body separation. Designing artificial agents on the basis of the principles that we observe in biology is not an easy task. The principles of organization of animals and plants rely on morphological computation and emergence of fit behaviors from loosely coupled networks of embodied agents. Modeling and control require radically new approaches. In this paper we briefly recall and explain some seminal mathematical results linking information metrics and dynamics of the agents, already published years ago; we integrate them with some recent methods developed by us and by the community, we highlight some brief remarks about their relevance and we hint to our current and near future work towards finding concrete and efficient ways for the modeling and control of completely or partially compliant artificial agents and for a better understanding of physical intelligence in nature. We present a technical note summarizing phase-space volume calculations for inverted-pendulum and passive-dynamic walking models, following our proposed framework. Starting from the McGeer compass gait, we introduce knee-ankle compliance, foot-rocker effects, and a Ruina-style compass gait with distributed leg inertia. Standard heel-strike maps are derived and used in the estimation of viable phase-space volumes $W(γ)$, based on a state-dependent Monte-Carlo and Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces methods. We show how the methods based on RKHS allow deeper and more subtle analysis.

Title: Polynomial Quantum Recurrent Channels for Matrix Inverse Actions: Deferred-Reset Dynamics and Chebyshev Filtering
Author: Vahid Tavakkoli, Kabeh Mohsenzadegan, Kyandoghere Kyamakya
Text_Content: We develop completely positive, trace-preserving polynomial recurrent channels for quantum solution-state preparation and derive fixed-point and time-varying tracking bounds. Across 2,880 synthetic configurations, resident Chebyshev recurrence improves accuracy-passing snapshot counts in 608 cases, ties in 2,271, and loses in one. A separate 360-scenario cost study shows that fresh recurrence is cheaper in all 184 jointly feasible scenarios (median resident-to-fresh cost ratio: 3.12), while resident recurrence uniquely satisfies accuracy requirements in 74 cases. At a logical noise rate of $10^-4$, neither recurrent method qualifies. Based on exact reduced-density simulations and assumed cost models, our results demonstrate conditional tracking advantages but no general end-to-end speedup or total-cost benefit.

Title: Omni-JEV: Text and Dual-Stream Speech Decisions
Author: Shengzhou Kong
Text_Content: A user utterance does not uniquely determine the next action in full-duplex dialogue: its consequences depend on the assistant's response state and interaction history. Speech activity, utterance completion, and interruption intent provide related evidence, whose implications for a response require an explicit action policy. We formulate this task at collected-segment endpoints and introduce Omni-JEV, which maps text or role-indexed user and assistant-reference speech to probabilities over five interaction actions. An aligned speech-to-speech understanding backbone encodes the acoustic roles separately and shares its candidate readout with text inputs. Bilingual weak supervision supports cross-entropy fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning for probability-sensitive decisions (RLCD). We compare Gaussian-logit and categorical Choice RLCD from the same supervised initialization under matched training exposure, observing different trade-offs between classification and probability quality. Gaussian Omni-JEV achieves test accuracies of 84.08% for audio and 96.55% for text. This common action interface supports decisions about when a full-duplex voice assistant should respond, preserve ongoing speech, interrupt, or resume an interrupted response.

Title: DisasterAgent: An Evidence-Driven Agent for Verifiable Disaster Report Generation From Remote Sensing Imagery
Author: Zhijian Li, Jiawei Song, Chao Ren, Yidan Zhang, Peijin Wang, Xian Sun, Kun Fu
Text_Content: Remote sensing disaster assessment is moving from simple damage classification toward comprehensive report-level analysis. In this setting, responders need not only damage descriptions but also verifiable evidence to guide response and recovery. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) and tool-augmented agents offer strong multimodal reasoning and perception, but they struggle to provide the evidence required for high-stakes verification. To address these limitations, we propose DisasterAgent, an evidence-driven agent that uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow to generate verifiable disaster reports from bitemporal optical imagery. DisasterAgent first invokes a specialized vision expert toolkit in the perception phase to build a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph (STPG), serving as a structured memory to store and organize disaster-induced changes across space and time. Evidence-based Augmentation (EA) then extracts evidence from the STPG, attaching inline citations that form a closed evidence loop from each statement to the supporting visual evidence. Extensive experiments on the DisasterM3 and RSCC benchmarks demonstrate that DisasterAgent consistently outperforms general-domain VLMs, remote sensing-specialized models, and existing remote sensing agents. Notably, compared with the original model, it improves the average score for disaster report generation on DisasterM3 by 13.5\% and ST5-SCS on RSCC by 15.34\%, providing a more accurate and verifiable solution for disaster emergency response. The code will be available at https://github.com/ZhijianLi2003/DisasterAgent.

Title: AI-Adaptive Virtual Reality for STEM: Engagement, Retention, and Learning Outcomes
Author: Srinivasa K G, Akshit Rana, Aman Singh, Kshitij Kumar Singh Chauhan
Text_Content: Virtual Reality (VR) presents a com pelling opportunity to transform STEM pedagogy; however, empirical evidence evaluating AI-driven adaptivity, objective engagement metrics, and long-term knowledge retention remains sparse. This paper proposes and evaluates an AI-adaptive VR based solar system learning module deployed on Meta Quest 2, wherein a machine learning model dynamically adjusts in structional difficulty based on real-time learner interaction logs including dwell time, gaze patterns, and response latency. A controlled between-subjects experiment was conducted involving 120 secondary school students (mean age 14.3 years) across three schools in India, randomly assigned to three conditions: AI adaptive VR, standard VR, and traditional classroom instruction. Engagement was measured objectively through eye-tracking fixation density and heart rate variability (HRV), alongside pre-test, immediate post-test, and delayed post-tests at one week and one month intervals. Statistical analyses encompassing paired t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) reveal that the AI-adaptive VR cohort demonstrated significantly higher knowledge improvement scores (mean gain = 38.4 vs. 31.2 vs. 10.7), superior one-month retention (p < 0.001), and measurably elevated engagement across all biometric indicators. SEM confirmed immersion as a significant mediator between adaptive instruction and knowledge acquisition (\b{eta} = 0.63, p < 0.001). Post-session self-directed learning exploration was recorded at 80% among AI-adaptive VR participants versus 40% in the traditional group. These findings establish an evidence based framework for deploying AI-adaptive immersive learning environments in resource-varied STEM educational contexts.

Title: RF3DGS: Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting with Self-Priors
Author: Qiang Wen, Guotao Meng, Junhong Ruan, Hongyu Liu, Chenyang Lei, Qifeng Chen
Text_Content: 3D reflection removal is crucial in applications demanding high-fidelity visualization, such as museum exhibitions. In this work, we propose Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting (RF3DGS), a novel method for superior reflection removal. RF3DGS exclusively leverages a widely-adopted photometric prior for reflection removal: that the minimum pixel intensity across multi-view images corresponding to the same 3D point strongly correlates with reflection-free information. However, generalizing this principle to a 3D Gaussian Splatting within a multi-view context is non-trivial. To address this, RF3DGS first optimizes a vanilla 3DGS model using a geometric prior to estimate a coarse, reflection-free depth map for each view. Leveraging these depth maps and photometric prior, a 3D warping process aggregates reflection-free information from auxiliary views to construct a clean transmission pseudo-label for a given reference view. This pseudo-label provides a robust self-supervised signal for optimization. We further introduce an Adaptive Twin Rendering (ATR) loss to synergistically utilize this pseudo-label while preserving high-frequency details from the original, reflection-degraded images. By adeptly fusing these internal 3D self-priors with the ATR loss, RF3DGS demonstrates state-of-the-art reflection removal performance across both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we establish the first 3D reflection removal benchmark, based on the Unity rendering engine, for rigorous quantitative evaluation.

Title: From Depth to Safe Depth: Uncertainty-Aware Monocular Perception for Mobile Robot Navigation
Author: Saeid Firouzi Daghigh, Saeed Ayat
Text_Content: Monocular depth foundation models make it tempting to replace depth sensors on mobile robots with a single RGB camera. We show that, used off the shelf, this is unsafe: in a simulated indoor navigation benchmark, a standard Nav2 stack driven by Depth Anything V2 (metric) collides in 63\% of 120 episodes, because the model systematically over-estimates the distance to nearby obstacles. We propose a lightweight plug-in module that turns predicted depth into \emph{safe depth}. A 0.58\,M-parameter head on top of the \emph{frozen} depth model predicts, per pixel, a log-depth correction $μ$ and an uncertainty $σ$, trained with a $β$-weighted Gaussian negative log-likelihood. The navigation stack consumes the one-sided bound $\hat d_{\text{safe}}=d\,e^{μ-kσ}$, where $k$ is set by conformal calibration on a held-out world, and uncertainty also decides which pixels may be treated as floor. The correction halves the depth error (AbsRel $0.262\rightarrow0.134$) and reduces near-range over-estimation from 59.8\% to 12.0\%. In navigation, safe depth raises the success rate from 37\% to 70\% and lowers collisions from 63\% to 3\%, close to the 2\% of ground-truth depth. A constant safety margin calibrated to the same pixel coverage reaches only 30\% success because it freezes the robot; uncertainty-aware safety wins 52 of 56 discordant paired episodes against it. Gains hold on glass, texture-less walls and dark regions.

Title: Unified Far-field and Near-field Codebook Design for XL-array Systems
Author: Chao Zhou, Changsheng You, Liujia Yao
Text_Content: While extremely large-scale antenna arrays (XL-arrays) hold immense promise for next-generation wireless networks, the paradigm shift encompassing new near-field communications renders conventional discrete Fourier transform (DFT)-based Type-I codebooks inefficient. Meanwhile, existing near-field alternatives usually impose prohibitively high storage and/or feedback burdens. To tackle these challenges, we propose in this letter a unified codebook applicable to both far-field and near-field XL-array systems. Our key idea is to express the near-field channel steering vector in an equivalent form, which is a Hadamard product of an angular vector and a curvature-related vector. This new representation allows direct reuse of the legacy Type-I codebook for angle quantization, while only a lightweight auxiliary codebook is newly added for additional curvature quantization. Subsequently, we optimize the auxiliary curvature codebook by maximizing the average beamforming gain given the information of user distribution. By leveraging the local monotonicity of the beamforming gain with respect to curvature mismatch, the optimization problem is further reduced to a quantization-error minimization problem, for which suboptimal curvature codewords are obtained. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed unified codebook achieves near-optimal beamforming performance that approaches its upper bound based on perfect channel state information (CSI), while significantly reducing the required feedback overhead as compared to various benchmark schemes.

Title: FAME-QP: A GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control
Author: Santosh Mohan Rajkumar, Debdipta Goswami, Stephanie Stockar
Text_Content: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.

Title: Beyond Interaction Scores: Selecting Feature Interactions via Independent Replication
Author: Jincheng Gao, Shuo Sun
Text_Content: Learning feature interactions is essential for accurate prediction and interpretable modeling, yet a high interaction score may reflect fitting noise rather than a reproducible pattern. Ranking methods score feature pairs but leave the cutoff to the user; testing methods set the cutoff but rely on repeated model refits or a model of the joint feature distribution. We present LENS, a model-agnostic framework for selecting feature interactions through independent replication. LENS trains two models with the same learning algorithm on disjoint data and accesses them only through predictions. For each feature pair, it removes main effects from the joint-effect surface to isolate an interaction pattern, ranks pairs by its strength, and tests whether the second model reproduces it at a meaningful strength. A single multiple-testing correction determines which pairs to retain, using only two model fits regardless of the number of features. We prove that a replication ratio alone can retain arbitrarily weak patterns shared by both fits, whereas a strength floor restores selection consistency, and we characterize when normalization in Friedman's $H^2$ reverses interaction rankings. On 16 synthetic designs, LENS matches leading model-specific ranking methods (e.g., TreeSHAP) and recovers 91% of material interactions, against 45% for the knockoff-based DIAMOND, without selecting false pairs; with 1,225 candidate pairs and no interactions, it makes substantially fewer false discoveries. On large-scale French motor insurance data, it identifies interactions documented in the actuarial literature and recovers 90% of the deviance gain obtained using all pairs. On two credit datasets, LENS selects few pairs while maintaining or slightly improving predictive performance over the additive baseline.

Title: Time-Varying Photonics: A Review of Theory, Phenomena, and Experimental Platforms
Author: Zhaohui Dong, Xianfeng Chen, Luqi Yuan
Text_Content: Time-varying photonics opens new avenues for controlling waves through engineering material properties in time. In this review, we introduce the basic concepts and theoretical tools for describing temporal interfaces, time-periodic systems, and space-time media, as well as review representative experimental approaches across different photonic and wave platforms. We further discuss characteristic phenomena enabled by temporal modulation, including coherent wave control, parametric amplification, nonreciprocity, and topological effects. This review provides a unified pathway for understanding time-varying photonics and outlines its current challenges and future opportunities in both fundamental physics and practical applications.

Title: Exploiting What NVIDIA Profilers Hide: Fast and Accurate Analytical GPU Performance Modeling
Author: Ziwen Wang, Qi Luo, Kunlin Li, Changxi Liu, Dongsheng Wang, Yun Chen
Text_Content: GPUs have become essential to many fields, including AI and scientific computing. As GPUs grow more complex, the design space of their hardware configurations becomes increasingly large, yet cycle-level simulators remain too slow to explore it. Analytical models make this exploration much faster. However, existing GPU analytical models fall short of accurately predicting performance across hardware configurations, because they re-estimate or scale every stall of a warp on the target configuration. We observe that fixed-latency stalls stay the same across configurations, whereas queueing stalls vary with the pressure on each hardware unit. Based on this observation, we propose ForeSight, a queueing analytical model that reuses the fixed-latency stalls measured on GPU hardware and recomputes the queueing stalls of each hardware unit from its pressure. To provide ForeSight with the counter values of each hardware unit, we build UnitSight, a profiler that recovers these values, which NVIDIA's official profilers hide by aggregating across units. Our evaluation on hardware configurations of nine NVIDIA GPUs shows that ForeSight predicts kernel execution time with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 8.3%, compared with 14.1% for the best baseline. ForeSight also predicts the end-to-end execution time of LLM inference on vLLM with a MAPE of 2.0%. It runs 49x faster than the cycle-level simulator Accel-Sim and faster than interval-based models such as GCoM. With the aid of ForeSight, we explore configurations derived from the H20 GPU for LLM inference and find one with 1.78x its performance/cost.

Title: Recursive memory for prediction and generation
Author: Pengbin Feng, Chunlei Meng
Text_Content: Recurrent and state-space language models compress the past into a state of fixed size. The state must answer questions about the future now, and it must remain useful as new tokens arrive, including tokens the model samples itself. We show that the second requirement can cost far more memory than the first. For a known hidden Markov source with positive transition probabilities, a state of $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ bits answers every question about the future to accuracy $\varepsilon$, however far ahead it looks, because the Bayesian filter forgets its rounding errors. Generating the future is different. When a model feeds each sampled token back into its state, the small errors in its next-token distributions add up, and $T$ tokens can require a state of order $\log(T/\varepsilon)$ bits. The lower bound comes from the KL chain rule: at every step, a model with $K$ states pays for approximating the true next-token distribution by one of only $K$ distributions. The argument applies to any source, including a language model continuing a prompt, and a small-ball estimate makes it tight for two-state sources. The extra $\log T$ disappears if the model keeps private randomness, or if error is budgeted per token, as in perplexity. Statistics of the recent past show the same gap between describing and maintaining. The number of ones among the last $n$ bits takes $\log n$ bits to write down. But if each bit is a noisy copy of the one $n$ steps earlier, tracking that count to a mean-square error $E^2$ well below its variance costs order $n/(1+E^2)+\log n$ bits. Information about each bit must be kept until the bit leaves the window, and a queue holding the counts of recent blocks keeps just enough of it.

Title: Exploring Synchrony for Communication in Modular Neural Networks
Author: Nikolas Willems, Qiyang Sun, Björn W. Schuller
Text_Content: One motivation for modular neural networks is to divide computation across components that learn distinct, reusable functions, which could then be recombined to support compositional generalisation. In practice, modular structure alone does not guarantee that such roles develop, and unrestricted communication between modules can undermine any specialisation that does emerge. This raises the question of how modular communication should be organised. The problem can be viewed as an analogue of the perceptual binding problem, where synchrony has been proposed as a mechanism for coordinating distributed representations. We introduce SyncNet, a modular architecture that separates module content from a dynamical phase state: learnt Kuramoto dynamics evolve the phases, while phase alignment determines communication through a shared channel. We evaluate SyncNet on Sort-of-CLEVR for relational reasoning and on SQOOP for systematic generalisation, where lower pair variety demands more recombination at test time. SyncNet gives the best held-out accuracy of the models compared at the three lowest pair varieties, by 5.1 percentage points at the hardest, and is competitive on Sort-of-CLEVR though below the strongest attention baselines. Test-time overrides show that performance depends on phases that evolve: fixed phases cost as much as no addressing at all, and permuting which module holds which region is nearly as damaging. A content-addressed variant trained from scratch nonetheless matches it, so the benefit appears to come from the modular decomposition rather than synchrony itself.

Title: Mixed Signals: Weight-Space Programming for EEG and ECG
Author: Dara Varam, Taraneh Aminosharieh Najafi, David Atienza
Text_Content: Weight-space programming allows language models to read a trained neural network's weights and edit them. This opens the door to ``training'' by reasoning rather than through gradient descent. Prior work has demonstrated its functionality and promise for game-playing networks and fixing specific failures in language models, even extending to diffusion models. In this work, we present its applicability to models trained on biosignal data, specifically EEG and ECG data. We show that frontier models are not only able to debug specific faults planted in biosignal-based models without being told what these faults are, but are even capable of writing all the weights of a network from scratch, given only the architecture, the task, and a minimal set of training subjects. In particular, in one set of experiments, a language model was able to match standard gradient-descent training using $6\times$ fewer training subjects, through reasoning alone and without any gradient descent step. Networks written by Claude Opus 5.5 also scored higher than classic hand-crafted EEG pipelines (alpha band power, and common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis) when built from the same 5 subjects. We also highlight some of the limitations, which include the inability of language models to improve already well-trained classification models, and their incapacity to reliably recognize, from the weights alone, the task a network was trained on. Overall, our results indicate that weight-space programming can be useful for small networks, such as those deployed on edge devices and wearables, but the concept still requires further investigation before it can be used in practice.

Title: Stochastic Aggregation with Prescribed Resources and Additive Delay
Author: Tianhang Lu, Runtian Ren, Shengcai Liu
Text_Content: We study online aggregation with prescribed resources and additive delay. In this problem, we are given a finite set of resources with purchase costs and a collection of request types, each specifying the resources it requires. Requests arrive over time, and each request can be served immediately or postponed to a later time. A service may serve several pending requests together by purchasing every resource required by at least one of them, paying for each purchased resource only once. These purchases serve only the current batch; resources needed in a later service must be purchased again. A request served $t$ units of time after its arrival incurs delay cost $t$. The objective is to serve all requests while minimizing the sum of resource purchase costs and individual delay costs. We consider a stochastic version of this problem in which requests of each type follow an independent Poisson process of known rate. An online algorithm knows these rates but observes requests only upon arrival. We compare its expected cost with that of an offline optimum that knows the entire realized input and may choose every batch freely. A resource--scale linear program supplies both an offline lower certificate and synchronized service periods. This yields a deterministic online algorithm with polynomial-time preprocessing on rational input and a long-run ratio of expectations below $2.113$. The guarantee applies in particular to rooted multi-level aggregation and prescribed-pair aggregation on trees. Besides, for Poisson TCP acknowledgment, we further characterize the optimal long-run ratio of expectations at every load, showing that its worst-case value is approximately 1.409 and is attained by a deterministic online policy.

Title: A Hardware-Trained Generative Quantum Eigensolver for Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization of Organotin Hydroxides up to 70 Qubits
Author: Kunal Kumar, Kimberlee Keithley, Toshiya Iwamori, Shu Kanno, Ikko Hamamura, Takao Kobayashi, Akira Koseki, Qi Gao, Naoki Yamamoto, Hiroshi Horii, Yuri Kobayashi, Borja Peropadre, Kouhei Nakaji, Toru Imai, Takayuki Osogami
Text_Content: Quantum hardware can provide feedback for training circuit generators beyond the reach of exact classical simulation. We train generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) policies, transformers conditioned on molecular descriptors, to generate the state-preparation circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). Training runs first on a noiseless simulator and then with the IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe inside the loop, at 46 and 70 qubits ($1.2 \times 10^8$ shots for the four main training runs). A classical CCSD(T) reference energy of the training molecules enters only an admission gate and two auxiliary reward terms. During hardware training, a reward penalty prevents collapse to circuits that sample only the Hartree-Fock determinant. Policies trained on transition-metal complexes are applied without retraining to Sn(OH)$_3$-Me and its hydrates, minimal models of organotin photoresists for extreme-ultraviolet lithography, from 32 to 70 qubits. After one round of hardware sampling, followed by classical ranking and recovery of the cached counts with the molecular Hamiltonian and no further QPU calls, 27 of 28 runs at 46-70 qubits are within 15 mHa of the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) reference (median 4.5 mHa), and in all eight runs with an untrained control the trained policy is more accurate. At 56-70 qubits the selected circuits use 34-72 times fewer two-qubit gates than the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) circuit transpiled for the same device. These results demonstrate that circuit generators can be trained with quantum hardware at 70 qubits.

Title: Harnessing collaborative networks for nonparametric quantile learning
Author: Jinyuan Chang, Yue Wang, Heng Lian, Wen-Xin Zhou
Text_Content: Data are increasingly distributed across networked agents that must learn collaboratively without exchanging raw observations or relying on central coordination. Existing decentralized methods largely focus on finite-dimensional models with smooth and strongly convex objectives, leaving nonparametric distributional learning over networks underexplored. We study decentralized nonparametric quantile regression in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. The standard kernel estimator is poorly suited to this setting: the check loss is nonsmooth, while its representer theorem formulation requires a global, data-dependent basis whose dimension grows with the total sample size. We reformulate the estimator using convolution smoothing and shared random features, yielding a differentiable objective with a common, data-independent parameterization of substantially lower dimension. We develop a gradient-adjusted alternating direction method of multipliers algorithm that replaces costly local minimization with network-corrected gradient updates, together with a communication-enhanced variant that selectively transmits updates. We establish nonasymptotic error bounds for the smoothed full-kernel and random-feature estimators, showing that the latter attains the full-kernel rate with suitable bandwidth and feature dimension. We also show both algorithms converge linearly to the random-feature consensus estimator. Simulations and a real data application demonstrate competitive predictive accuracy with substantial computational and communication savings.

Title: Word-Level Alignment of OCR and Ground Truth under Zoning and Reading-Order Errors
Author: Fonseca Cacho, Jorge Ramón
Text_Content: OCR post-processing needs OCR text aligned word by word with its ground truth. Data sets rarely provide that mapping, and a monotone aligner can lose its place when zoning errors permute the reading order. We revisit this problem, the Zoning Problem of our 2019 paper, with a protocol that tests correctness under such permutations. We apply OCR-side reading-order permutations with construction-time word-level gold and score correct-match F1, cascade length and recovery. We compare the 2019 location-aware aligner, a re-anchoring extension of it, a RETAS-style baseline (RETAS-lite), a multi-region aligner that combines unique-word and unique n-gram anchors with chunk-to-window assignment, genalog's RETAS and the original Java RETAS. Experiments use synthetic character noise with block moves, paragraph swaps and column interleaving, historical newspaper reading-order permutations, geometry-derived gold for Tesseract OCR, and a small word-box set. Synthetic tests show where local tracking fails after large displacements and where unique-anchor methods collapse when unique anchors are scarce. On our synthetic boilerplate page the 2019 method had the highest F1 among those tested. Historical newspaper and geometry-derived evaluations carry the limitations of approximate gold and the article-order convention. The first multi-region version has a quadratic scaling cost. Local tracking remains fragile under large reading-order changes; the tested anchor-based methods handle many of those cases but fail when unique anchors are scarce. Approximate gold, the article-order convention, missing residual annotation, and the lack of modern multi-column word-level ground truth remain limitations.

Title: List Update with Per-Page Maximum Delay
Author: Tianhang Lu, Runtian Ren, Shengcai Liu
Text_Content: We study list update with per-page maximum delay. Requests may wait, and one access clears all pending requests of a page at its current list rank, paying their maximum waiting penalty. Each service can change the permutation and therefore the cost of later accesses. We give a strictly $5$-competitive deterministic algorithm: serve a page when the oldest waiting time reaches two thirds of its current rank, then move it to the front. Our main tool is an asynchronous marked-rank coupling that compares different list orders and different service histories. A temporal transfer principle separates this permutation argument from two waiting-cost inequalities. It gives factor $5$ for page-specific superadditive penalties, common calendar rates, and additional hard deadlines; deadlines alone admit factor $3$. Two structural conditions on request-specific penalties give factor $3+2κ$. In particular, nonincreasing request severity retains factor $5$ even with unbounded weight ratios. For linear delay, offline optimization is NP-complete but fixed-parameter tractable in the number of pages. We characterize fixed-list batching, show an $Ω(m)$ gap between the best static order and dynamic reordering, and prove that the optimal deterministic factor for one page is exactly $2$. Counterexamples delineate the threshold rule's scope.

Title: When Covariance Is Not Enough: Kernel-Based Regularization for Single-Cell Counterfactuals
Author: Korbinian Traeuble, Edward de Brouwer, Archit Verma, Doron Haviv, Kipper Fletez-Brant
Text_Content: Counterfactual editing of single cells, predicting how an observed cell would look had one factor been different, enables in-silico screening where experiments are infeasible, but is useful only if the edit is faithful to the individual and not merely to the condition. Concept bottleneck generative models make the effects of interventions interpretable by decomposing a cell's representation into known and unknown factors. Previous work uses a linear cross-covariance penalty to disentangle known and unknown dimensions. We demonstrate that this first-order criterion does not fully separate information when non-linear interactions are present. We first demonstrate the inadequacy of linear cross-factor penalization with simulation experiments with controlled edits and known non-linear covariate effects. We then demonstrate that adding a nonlinear kernel criterion, the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, is able to recover the true intervention effects on simulation data. Finally, we apply the non-linear concept bottleneck model to a complex single-cell RNA-seq dataset and find that it improves the ability to generate counterfactual expression profiles of cells under different tissue environments.

Title: Hierarchical interfacial anchoring for durable perovskite solar cells
Author: Jiaxin Wu, Hongzhuo Wu, Zuhong Zhang, Xiaoyu Guan, Jinbo Zhao, Yuting Guo, Zhihao Li, Zirui Li, Tengyu Ma, Ying Tang, Zhe Li, Weiwei Zuo, Jorge Pascual, Bo Hou, Feng Yang, Xiaoli Pan, Yu Wang, Luyao Wang, Lin-Long Deng, Guixiang Li, Luca Sapienza, Antonio Abate, Meng Li
Text_Content: Although inverted perovskite solar cells now deliver certified efficiencies approaching their single-junction limits, their practical deployment remains constrained by the thermo-mechanical fragility of buried interfaces under realistic temperature fluctuations. Here, we identify thermo-mechanically driven, stress-accumulation-dominated adhesion failure at self-assembled monolayer-based buried interfaces as a critical failure mode in inverted perovskite solar cells. To address this issue, we propose an interfacial robustness design strategy based on a homometallic halide pretreatment, which constructs a chemically compatible and highly anchorable interfacial environment on transparent conductive oxides to guide the ordered assembly of SAMs. This interfacial treatment increases the density of surface hydroxyl species and enables hierarchical multipoint interfacial anchoring dominated by metal-oxygen coordination, with Cl- induced hydrogen-bonding interactions acting cooperatively, thereby enhancing anchoring robustness and improving tolerance to thermo-mechanical stress accumulation. With this interfacial strategy, the devices achieve a power conversion efficiency of 27.3% (26.9% certified) and retain 94% of their initial efficiency after 400 temperature cycles between -40 and 85 degrees C (ISOS-T-3). These results demonstrate that rational regulation of buried interfacial anchoring architectures can simultaneously enhance device efficiency and long-term operational reliability, offering a viable pathway toward high-efficiency and durable perovskite photovoltaics.

Title: Do Language Models Feel the Sentiment? Investigating Emotion Vectors
Author: Ali Hassan Khan, Saad Bin Ather, Muhammad Saif, Maryam Bashir, Hajra Waheed
Text_Content: Emotion vectors are directions in a language model's internal representations that are associated with emotional concepts. Prior work shows that these vectors can influence model behavior, but their role in sentiment classification remains unclear. This study investigates emotion directions in Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Eight directions extracted from GoEmotions are evaluated through sentiment probing, activation interventions, and supervised correction. Emotion-only probes achieve 88.66% and 90.70% accuracy on binary TweetEval. In exploratory matched-ablation experiments, raw emotion-space removal causes 2.39 and 1.10 percentage points more accuracy loss than matched isotropic random-subspace removal for 0.5B and 3B, respectively. All four TweetEval raw and denoised effects are significant after Holm adjustment across eight comparisons. An exploratory SST-2 extension shows smaller raw excess losses of 0.66 and 0.57 points, with no effects surviving Holm adjustment. Frozen sentiment-correction classifiers are also tested on 20,000 Amazon Polarity reviews. Emotion-based correction improves accuracy over uncorrected Qwen, but does not consistently outperform margin-only baselines. These results distinguish sentiment information available in model representations, the effects of changing those representations, and their practical value for classification. They do not establish a uniquely emotional mechanism.

Title: Structural Perturbations and Full Field Evolution in Tapered Spun Ring-Core Fiber Amplifiers
Author: Hassan Asgharzadeh B., Regina Gumenyuk, Marco Ornigotti
Text_Content: We theoretically investigate the complex full-vector modal field evolution in tapered spun ring-core fiber amplifiers subject to structural perturbations, utilizing a combined coupled-mode theory and rate-equation model. To provide a comprehensive characterization, we introduce a normalized complex modal-state fidelity factor that simultaneously incorporates intensity, phase and polarization into a single quantitative measure. We demonstrate that the twist pitch of the structure can be purposely tuned to either suppress or leverage the effect of specific geometrical perturbations. These findings provide insight into the physical conditions governing modal stability, establishing a robust mechanism for highly efficient in-fiber OAM mode conversion.

Title: Plug-and-Play ADMM for Inverse Problems with Flow Matching Denoiser
Author: Dibyanshu Kumar, Magda Gregorova
Text_Content: Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods with generative priors have achieved strong performance in inverse problems, with recent flow matching models enabling fast and scalable reconstruction. However, a key challenge in PnP methods is maintaining consistency between data fidelity updates and the learned generative prior, as data-consistency steps can move iterates away from the flow trajectory. We propose an ADMM-based PnP framework for flow matching priors that enforces stronger consistency between the measurement model and the prior through auxiliary variables and dual updates. In addition, we introduce a trajectory correction mechanism that restores consistency with the flow via a combination of deterministic and stochastic projections. Our method provides a more principled integration of flow priors within PnP frameworks, achieving high-quality reconstructions with reduced computational cost.

Title: Retargetable Compilation for Tensor Kernels via a Unified Layout Abstraction
Author: Likai Ma, Renze Chen, Tianqi Li, Yuhao Luo, Youwei Xiao, Size Zheng, Xiuhong Li, Yun Liang
Text_Content: Modern hardware accelerators achieve high performance through specialized instructions coupled with tightly managed memory hierarchies. These instructions impose strict layout requirements on their operands: where tensor fragments reside, how they are organized, and how parallel units access them. Such instruction-visible layout is critical to kernel performance, as it determines whether instructions execute correctly and how much data movement they incur. However, existing compilers either scatter layout requirements across handwritten programs and local scheduling rules, or provide layout representations and conversions specific to a single class of targets. Both approaches expose the same abstraction gap: the absence of a unified model for instruction layout requirements across backends. This paper presents Arknife, a retargetable compiler that treats instruction-visible layout as first-class instruction semantics. Its central idea is a constraint-based layout algebra: tensor layouts map logical axes to hardware axes spanning parallel levels and memory spaces. Instruction operands declare layout requirements, and target-provided repairs resolve conflicts. Layouts are then solved globally across the program. ISA-specific layout facts are supplied by target-side instruction descriptions rather than hardcoded in the compiler. Retargeting reuses the layout algebra and solver while defining the new target's instructions and their operand requirements. We evaluate Arknife across x86 CPU, Hexagon NPU, and NVIDIA A100 GPU. Arknife matches cuBLAS on A100, and on x86 and Hexagon outperforms vendor-optimized libraries by $2.17\times$ and $3.78\times$ and the retargetable compiler MISAAL by $5.08\times$ and $4.53\times$, respectively.

Title: Multi-Objective Scheduling of LLM-Based Multi-Agent Workflows in Cloud Computing
Author: Goshgar Can Ismayilov
Text_Content: Large language models (LLMs) have been increasingly composed into multi-agent workflows to accomplish complex and multi-step tasks. As the open-weight models continue to close the performance gap with the proprietary ones, model parameters are becoming a less significant source of competitive advantage in the artificial intelligence market. Yet how these models are efficiently scheduled onto distributed infrastructure such as the cloud, with respect to overall latency, monetary cost and resource utilization, remains largely unaddressed in the literature despite being an increasingly critical problem. Existing agentic workflow frameworks mostly focus on output quality and task success rates over popular benchmarks, rarely accounting for execution dynamics of LLM-based agents such as inference latency, computation power of heterogeneous resources, cloud-specific billing period and resource provisioning overheads. Therefore, this paper formulates multi-agent scheduling in cloud computing as a multi-objective optimization problem that jointly minimizes makespan and cost while maximizing resource utilization. Building on this formulation, we propose MO-SAIC (Multi-Objective Scheduling of Multi-Agent Workflows in Cloud Computing), a scheduling framework comprising four multi-objective schedulers with Non-Dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II), Weighted-Sum Genetic Algorithm (W-GA), a multi-objective adaptation of Heterogeneous Earliest Finish Time (MO-HEFT) and a random baseline (RAND). We evaluate the schedulers from the workflow scheduling, multi-objective optimization and system perspectives to measure their overall performance, quality of their Pareto-optimal fronts and impacts of workflow topology, cloud resource composition and scalability parameters. We report the experimental results with their statistical significance via the Wilcoxon test.

Title: Effects of Laser Beam Width and Measurement Noise on Tree Diameter Estimation in Laser Scanning
Author: Jesse Muhojoki, Nuutti Ervasti, Eric Hyyppä, Aapo Erkkilä, Eppu Honkanen, Tuomas Yrttimaa, Mikko Vastaranta, Juha Hyyppä
Text_Content: Laser scanning has been utilized for decades to measure tree structure and geometry. Despite continuous advances in sensor technology, uncertainties arising from scanner characteristics and measurement conditions has remained relevant sources of error. In particular, factors such as laser beam diameter can introduce both systematic and random errors in the reconstructed tree geometry. This study investigates the main sources of these errors in mobile laser scanning (MLS) and quantifies their effects on stem curve (stem diameter) estimation. We discovered through simulations and experiments that the heteroscedasticity (difference in variance in ranging and scan angle) in the measurement noise is a key factor along with the beam width of the lidar, which cause the bias of the diameter estimates to depend not only on distance, but also on the tree diameter. We demonstrated that this bias can be reliably predicted and negated for trees with a diameter at the breast height greater than 10 cm using technical specifications of the sensor without any additional calibration. In experiments, the proposed bias compensation method reduced the root-mean-square error of stem diameter estimates to sub-centimeter level on boreal forest test sites. However, for small trees with diameter below 10 cm, the diameter bias becomes sensitive to the diameter of the tree$\unicode{x2013}$an unknown factor$\unicode{x2013}$and other factors, such as different bark and out-of-roundness of the stem, limiting the precision of lidar for measuring geometry of trees and applicability of the presented method.

Title: Multi-Step Underwater Acoustic Channel Prediction via Dual-Domain Structure Preservation and Pretrained Transformer
Author: Mingjie Cao, Gewei Zhang, Deqing Wang, Lizhao You, Fei-Yun Wu, Liqun Fu
Text_Content: Accurate future channel state information (CSI) is essential for underwater acoustic (UWA) communication because delays associated with signal propagation, feedback, scheduling, and transceiver reconfiguration can render currently available CSI outdated. However, most existing predictors estimate only the next channel state and obtain multi-step forecasts through recursive rollout, which causes prediction errors to accumulate as the multipath structure evolves. The scarcity of sea-trial measurements further limits reliable model training. To address these challenges, we propose LLM4UACP, a dual-domain, structure-preserving framework that adapts a pretrained Transformer for few-shot multi-step UWA channel prediction. LLM4UACP extracts complementary features from the channel impulse response (CIR) and channel frequency response (CFR), aligns them through Fourier-consistent fusion, and encodes the fused representation as delay-time tokens. A pretrained Transformer with a frozen backbone is adapted through Butterfly Orthogonal Fine-tuning to jointly predict multiple future CIRs in a single forward pass, thereby avoiding the error accumulation associated with recursive prediction. Experiments on the measured SO-06 and SO-07 channels show that LLM4UACP achieves normalized mean squared error (NMSE) values of 0.0411 and 0.0399, corresponding to reductions of 88.53% and 85.15%, respectively, relative to the most recent baseline. With only 0.11M trainable parameters, LLM4UACP maintains robust performance across varying prediction horizons and observation-window lengths, limited-data settings, and cross-dataset transfer scenarios.

Title: Linear stability of viscous stratified shear flows with arbitrary equations of state
Author: Benjamin Bugeat
Text_Content: A mathematical framework is developed to analyse the linear stability of viscous stratified flows with arbitrary equations of state. The model accommodates equations of state of the form $p=Φ(T,ρ)$ or $ρ=φ(T)$, together with a set of governing dimensionless parameters. Density stratification is unrestricted, allowing for the study of non-Boussinesq effects. A low-Mach-number approximation is employed to filter out acoustic phenomena. The framework is applied to two viscous stratified configurations of plane Couette flow: a triple-layer density profile supporting the Taylor--Caulfield instability (TCI), and a differentially heated supercritical fluid exhibiting a distinct instability mechanism. Following validation against reference studies, we present new results showing that non-Boussinesq effects weaken the viscous TCI, whilst viscosity can further destabilise the supercritical fluid instability, in contrast to the stabilising influence of buoyancy.

Title: An infrared divacancy color center in bulk hexagonal diamond for quantum communication
Author: Xuanxuan Zhang, Chen-Min Dai, Cong Li, Chunlan Ma, Zenghua Cai
Text_Content: Intrinsic color centers are investigated in bulk hexagonal diamond as potential emitters for fiber-based quantum communication. Hybrid density functional theory and constrained-occupation delta SCF calculations identify five carbon-vacancy and divacancy configurations with stable optical excited states. A comparison of their radiative and nonradiative properties within a three-point configuration-coordinate model identifies the positively charged axial divacancy, VVa1+, as the most promising candidate. It exhibits the highest calculated zero-phonon-line (ZPL) emission rate of 43.9 MHz and ZPL quantum efficiency of 11.8% among the five candidates. Its weak structural relaxation yields a Huang-Rhys factor of 0.395, while a multimode photoluminescence calculation gives a Debye-Waller factor of 69.37%, indicating a dominant zero-phonon contribution. The predicted ZPL at 0.603 eV (2057.3 nm) also has the smallest photon-energy separation from the 1310 and 1550 nm telecom targets among the candidates. These results identify VVa1+ as a promising intrinsic color center for fiber-based quantum communication, with quantum frequency upconversion offering a route from its strong infrared ZPL to the telecom O and C bands.

Title: CIALLO: Learning Shared Intent Representations for Cross-Embodiment Manipulation
Author: Choo Sin Wai, Dake Zhong, Jingye Zhang, Zhifang Liu, Siyao Xiao, Zirong Ding, Yuhong Zhang, Kangjie Chen, Dongbin Zhang, Guorui Song, Guocun Wang, Peng Jiao, Haoqian Wang
Text_Content: Robot demonstrations contain reusable manipulation knowledge, but transferring this knowledge across embodiments requires representations that bridge differences in control interfaces. Action reconstruction alone does not ensure that similar behaviors across robots share a representation. To address this gap, we introduce CIALLO, an action codec that aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a shared space of short-horizon behavioral intent. An embodiment-conditioned decoder maps this intent back to robot-specific actions, allowing a shared representation to support different control interfaces. After pretraining on eight embodiments, CIALLO adapts to a new robot from one recording of at most 10 seconds by updating only its embodiment embeddings. The calibrated codec then remains frozen while a policy learns to predict intent from observations and instructions. We instantiate this policy with Qwen3.5-4B to form Qwen-CIALLO, whose backbone requires no large-scale robot-action pretraining before policy finetuning. With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO achieves 76.7\% average success across real SO-101 and single-arm Piper robots, compared with 70.0\% for fully finetuned $π_0$. In simulation, we additionally finetune the action decoder, achieving 97.3\% success on LIBERO and 52.7\% on RoboTwin 2.0. The LIBERO policy also achieves 80.8\% on LIBERO-Plus without further finetuning. Together, these results support a shared action codec as a transferable control interface that separates embodiment calibration from task learning.

Title: Deterministic, Reproducible Inference in Exact Integer Arithmetic, and Verifiable Distributed Inference as Its Consequence
Author: Sayed Amir Karim
Text_Content: Optimized floating-point inference is not reproducible across environments: the same model on different hardware, compilers or thread counts can produce different bits. We present tritify, an open-source runtime that executes the forward pass of real models -- decoder-only language models, Mixture-of-Experts decoders, and the Segment Anything 2.1 image/video stack -- with the entire run-time path in exact integer arithmetic; floating point is confined to offline quantization and the float reference used for verification. We make three separate claims and verify each. (1) Cross-hardware reproducibility: the integer path produces bit-identical output run to run, across CPU instruction-set architectures, and across CPU/GPU, carried by a reproducing SHA-256 of the output. (2) Decision fidelity: the integer path reproduces the float reference's decision on the models and inputs tested, with the numeric exceptions measured; per-layer fidelity through sixteen layers of OLMoE-1B-7B and of a 106-billion-parameter MoE shows no fidelity cliff. (3) Location independence: a model's computation can be split across instruction sets, CPU and GPU, and networked machines with zero effect on the output bits. GLM-4.5-Air (106,852,251,264 parameters, 427 GB of integer codes) generated its answer across three machines, none of which can hold its integer codes in RAM, bit-identically to a single-host reference. The consequence is verifiable distributed inference: an untrusted server or a fleet of devices runs the model while an open scalar oracle re-derives the exact bytes; a guarantee against a dishonest server is future work. We do not claim a per-device speed-up, bit-equality of floating-valued intermediates, or confidentiality. Code: https://github.com/pelloran-inc/tritify

Title: Kinetic Non-Equilibrium Receptivity Analysis of Hypersonic Flows via a Complex Linearized Unified Gas-Kinetic Scheme
Author: Yue Zhang, Caihong Su, Chao Li, Kun Xu
Text_Content: In the near-space regime, local rarefaction near the leading-edge shock and wall degrades Navier-Stokes-based stability and receptivity analyses due to velocity slip, temperature jumps, and non-equilibrium transport. The unified gas-kinetic scheme (UGKS) provides a multiscale kinetic description spanning continuum to rarefied regimes. Building on this, a complex linearized UGKS (CLUGKS) is developed: first-order perturbations of the discrete UGKS residual are formulated under a time-harmonic assumption with complex amplitudes, converting disturbance equations into a steady elliptic system solved via pseudo-time marching with LU-SGS acceleration. Consequently, kinetic shock structures, wall slip, temperature jumps, and non-Fourier heat fluxes are inherently captured without hybrid coupling. Three benchmarks verify the framework: a standing acoustic wave at an isothermal wall, a Mach 2 normal shock interacting with an obliquely incident acoustic wave, and freestream acoustic receptivity of a hypersonic blunt wedge. The scheme is applied to argon blunt-wedge flows at equivalent altitudes of 40 km and 50 km. At 40 km, UGKS and Navier-Stokes wall responses agree well in period and phase, while wall slip sustains a weakly positive spatial growth rate in UGKS downstream. At 50 km, intensified rarefaction produces a kinetic temperature precursor and a thickened, merged shock layer; while wall-pressure responses remain close, significant deviations emerge in temperature and heat-flux disturbances. These findings show that while continuum models capture dominant wall-pressure signatures under moderate rarefaction, resolving kinetic non-equilibrium across the shock-particularly its thermal footprint-is essential at higher altitudes.

Title: Weighted-AoI-Driven UAV Trajectory and Reporting for Dynamic CKM Tracking
Author: Zeyu Zhao, Yueling Che, Sheng Luo
Text_Content: Existing channel knowledge map (CKM) construction assumes quasi-static environments, failing when channels rapidly decorrelate. This paper investigates continuous online dynamic CKM tracking over an airborne 2D plane via a UAV fleet. We formulate a long-term error minimization problem under UAV mobility and reporting constraints. This problem, however, is intractable with unobservable errors for unmeasured cells. To tackle this, we propose a metric-driven scheduling approach featuring the Weighted-Age of Information (W-AoI). W-AoI evaluates cells by combining exact temporal staleness with spatial uncertainty predicted by a 2D U-Net. We prove that top-$K$ W-AoI selection maximizes the one-slot error reduction bound. Guided by this guarantee, we develop a lightweight greedy trajectory policy incorporating continuous along-path sensing. Simulations demonstrate our method reduces steady-state error by 3.8 dB$^2$ and 4.8 dB$^2$ over AoI-only and FIFO baselines, closely approaching an idealized oracle.

Title: Stress-controlled avoided-crossing evolution of an optical microresonator induced by inter-fibre side coupling
Author: Isha Sharma, Misha Sumetsky
Text_Content: Analogies between quantum mechanics and photonics provide a powerful means of transferring concepts and phenomena between the two fields. Photonic analogues offer a distinctive advantage by allowing us to engineer and continuously vary parameters fixed by the microscopic structure of quantum systems, revealing richer behaviour. Building on these analogies, the recent demonstration of widely tunable microresonators formed by side coupling between optical fibres marked a significant advance in the development of reconfigurable resonant photonic systems. However, those methods offered no direct way to reach the centre of the avoided crossing, where the uncoupled fibre cutoff frequencies coincide and the modes hybridise most strongly. Here, we introduce an additional tuning degree of freedom by axially stretching a straight fibre coupled to a bent fibre. At essentially fixed coupling geometry, this lets us sweep the detuning between their uncoupled cutoff frequencies through zero. As the avoided crossing is approached, the induced microresonator's resonance band widens. Beyond the crossing, the band narrows and, strikingly, appears to "hang" below the stretched fibre's rising cutoff frequency. Our experimental results agree with coupled-mode theory and indicate the feasibility of 100 MHz-scale control of the straight-fibre cutoff frequency and the resonator spectral height over a tuning range of about 100 GHz, using a relative elongation of order $10^{-3}$.

Title: TRUER: Test-Time Reward Correction Using an Error-Aware Rectifier for Reinforcement Learning
Author: Mingxiang Shen, Jinhao Li, Jiaming Xu, Yibo Han, Guohao Dai, Yijia Zhang, Ningyi Xu
Text_Content: Test-time reinforcement learning enables language models to adapt using rewards derived from their own answers. However, majority voting can reinforce incorrect solutions even when correct alternatives are available. Our training audit shows that false positives (incorrect responses receiving positive rewards) dominate reward errors. We focus on a practical regime where ground-truth rewards are difficult to obtain at scale, while a limited labeled source set is available. We introduce TRUER, a framework that uses limited supervision to train a reward rectifier that distinguishes correctness from consensus. To achieve this goal, we train the rectifier with an emphasis on incorrect majorities and correct minorities, targeting cases where consensus and correctness disagree. After that, we freeze the rectifier and use it to correct rewards during subsequent test-time adaptation. By improving reward accuracy and thereby model performance, TRUER consistently outperforms naive TTRL in both metrics across all evaluated configurations.

Title: Toward Autonomous RTL and Synthesis Optimization: Benchmarking and Self-Improving Agents
Author: Wenji Fang, Yao Lu, Jinghua Wang, Zhiyao Xie
Text_Content: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents are creating new opportunities for hardware design optimization. This paper examines three connected directions toward autonomous RTL and synthesis optimization: (1) Realistic benchmarking. We discuss reference-based and open-ended RTL optimization benchmarks that evaluate optimization opportunities under realistic EDA workflows. (2) Tool-grounded RTL optimization. We present Dr. RTL, a multi-agent framework that automates critical-path analysis, RTL rewriting, and implementation-level evaluation, while continuously improving through reusable optimization skills. Evaluated on 20 real-world RTL designs, Dr.~RTL achieves average WNS/TNS improvements of 21\%/17\% with a 6\% area reduction over commercial synthesis. (3) Design-specific synthesis optimization. We explore agent-driven synthesis script tuning and the discovery of executable synthesis algorithms across intermediate representations, technology-independent optimization, and technology mapping.
