A calendar-day based threshold allows for the detection of temperature extremes across all seasons, which may impact several economic sectors, public health and ecosystems. Previous approaches to modeling the occurrences of extreme heat events typically treat heat event duration and the time between heat events separately. We propose modeling the inter-exceedance times (IETs) between extreme heat days, allowing for a unified description within a single model. We consider several candidate distributions for the IETs of extreme heat days and find that the zero-inflated discrete Weibull (ZIDW) distribution clearly provides the best fit according to Pearson's chi-squared goodness-of-fit tests. The ZIDW distribution is a flexible model for count data exhibiting excess zeros as well as over- and under-dispersion: the zero-inflation component captures the pronounced clustering of heat days, while the discrete Weibull component adequately accounts for over-dispersion. Heat days are extracted using both trend-adjusted and non-trend-adjusted thresholds. This allows the analysis of general changes in the occurrence of extreme heat days as well as changes after accounting for the general increase in temperature.

Title: Frequency-selective membrane-based metamaterial filters for low-insertion-loss harmonic crosstalk suppression in sub-harmonic THz receivers
Author: Hui Yuan, Meng Zhang, Almila Kura, Daniel Erni, Hartmut G. Roskos
Text_Content: Parasitic reflections and standing waves fundamentally limit amplitude stability and phase fidelity in coherent continuous-wave (CW) terahertz (THz) systems. We report a complementary metamaterial filter pair designed for frequency-selective isolation at 300 GHz and 600 GHz in sub-harmonic heterodyne architectures. Fabricated on ultra-thin polyimide membranes, the filters provide more than 30 dB stopband isolation while maintaining insertion losses below 1 dB in the passband. System-level coherent-imaging experiments demonstrate effective suppression of spurious-reflection-induced interference effects and improved spectral baseline stability. The filters mitigate wavefront distortions resulting from such interferences and enhance reconstruction robustness. These results establish membrane-based metamaterial filters as compact frequency-selective isolation elements for sub-harmonic heterodyne THz detection and highlight their potential for phase-engineered imaging and sensing applications.

Title: Adapting Small Language Models to Romanized Nepali: Tokenizer Fertility, Reference Likelihood, and Generation Metrics
Author: Pujan Pant, Sagar Newpane, Hari Sitaula, Manish Sakhakarmy
Text_Content: Romanized Nepali, Nepali written in Latin script, is common in digital communication but has no standard spelling and few resources, and it is unclear how reliably small open language models can be adapted to it. We adapt three 2-3B base models from different families, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Gemma-2-2B, with QLoRA on 9,000 instruction examples produced by deterministic transliteration of Nepali instruction data. Each model is trained with one shared recipe and three seeds and evaluated on 1,000 held-out examples with reference-overlap metrics, byte-normalized reference likelihood (bits per byte, BPB), and an output audit, against zero-shot baselines under two prompts. Fine-tuning raises chrF++ from 10-14 to 29.0-30.6 and lowers BPB from 2.23-2.41 to 0.78-0.84; most zero-shot outputs (54-92%) are English-like. Likelihood and overlap disagree on how far apart the models are. Llama-3.2-3B has the lowest BPB in every seed, 0.042 below Qwen2.5-3B (95% CI 0.039-0.046), yet the two cannot be separated on chrF++ (30.51 and 30.61) or BLEU, even with paired item-level tests. Gemma-2-2B, whose tokenizer splits Romanized Nepali words least (2.72 tokens per word), scores worst on every measure. Which model gains most over its zero-shot baseline depends on the zero-shot prompt. In a supplementary comparison with an identical tokenizer, Llama-3.1-8B lowers BPB by 0.053 (0.050-0.056) relative to Llama-3.2-3B, while chrF++ and BLEU rise by only 0.68 and 0.58 points. Lower fertility and higher reference likelihood therefore did not identify the model whose outputs were closest to the references.

Title: Spike-to-Field Mechanisms of Turbulence-Like Dynamics in Spatial Spiking Neural Networks
Author: Zequan Liu
Text_Content: Neural avalanches and turbulence-like brain dynamics are usually measured after neural activity has been coarse-grained into continuous fields, leaving open which spike-level mechanisms can generate these macroscopic observables. We build a spatial leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network and explicitly transform spikes into activity-density and Hilbert phase fields. A delayed, distance-dependent, passive-dendrite regime reproducibly generates turbulence-like field structure, including high-amplitude phase-defect tracks, structure-function scaling, and power-law-favored continuous-field avalanche tails. Controls show that firing rate, vortex count, and avalanche tail fits are individually insufficient: destroying delayed propagation, dendritic filtering, or spike timing suppresses key field signatures, while random-space nulls can retain many mathematical phase defects but show weaker spatial structure and synaptic-delay transfer. Biologically motivated gates further shape the regime: PV-like perisomatic inhibition clamps phase dynamics, SST-like dendritic inhibition and projection-specific inhibitory facilitation preserve long-lived tracks, and a rate-constrained projection-STP regime expresses a roughly 200-ms episode at 12.25 Hz (full-record mean) across 12 seeds. These results use SNNs as a mechanistic testbed for spike-derived brain turbulence observables and show why phase defects and avalanche-like statistics must be interpreted jointly with spatial scaling and spike-level propagation.

Title: Non-Equilibrium Ising-Bloch Transition in Polarization Cavity Solitons
Author: Juan Diego Mazo-Vásquez, Lewis Hill, Flore K. Kunst, Gian-Luca Oppo
Text_Content: Polarization cavity solitons in coherently driven Kerr resonators undergo a sequence of dynamical bifurcations as the cavity detuning is increased. Here we show that a stationary localized state containing an Ising wall first becomes a fixed breather and then develops finite chirality and drift motion through a spontaneous non-equilibrium Ising-Bloch transition. Stability analyses identify the modes responsible for the breathing and the motion, revealing controllable dynamics of polarization cavity solitons.

Title: Towards Reconstructing and Recognizing Objects behind Fragmented Occlusion using Video
Author: Roman Pflugfelder, Michael Lindenbaum, Daniel Cremers
Text_Content: Perceiving objects through fragmented occlusions, such as foliage, is a natural capability of the human visual system but remains a fundamental challenge for computer vision. This work addresses the problem of object reconstruction, or de-occlusion, in the presence of high-density, fragmented occlusions. We propose a reconstruction framework that operates on a sequence of grayscale images of a moving object, acquired by a single camera, either stationary or in motion. The algorithm estimates the object's relative positions across frames by jointly registering the images and optimizing the alignment parameters to maximize the contrast of their average, referred to as the integrated image. This integrated image serves as the reconstructed representation of the object. Experimental evaluations on both synthetic and real video sequences demonstrate the feasibility of accurate reconstruction under occlusion densities exceeding 90%. The proposed approach is competitive with synthetic aperture techniques, which are limited to static objects and require complex camera setup with careful calibration. Furthermore, we show that the integrated image enables reliable object classification under severe occlusion when used as input to standard, off-the-shelf classifiers.

Title: Reconfiguring System-Level Protection Through Bounded Delegation in RISC-V MCUs
Author: Luís Cunha, José Martins, Manuel Rodríguez, Tiago Gomes, Uwe Moslehner, Kai Dieffenbach, Georg Schmalz, Kajetan Nuernberger, Thomas Roecker, Sandro Pinto
Text_Content: MCU-based embedded and cyber-physical systems increasingly require protection policies to change at runtime as resources, software, and system composition evolve. Yet widely used COTS MCU protection mechanisms are still largely designed around statically established policies. While they can restrict which domains modify protection primitives, they generally do not constrain what policy an authorized domain may create. As a result, domains may expand protection rules beyond their intended scope or interfere with boundaries established by other domains. We identify bounded configuration authority as a missing primitive for secure dynamic policy evolution and introduce an ownership-aware model in which explicit ownership and rule containment bound both configuration authority and recursive delegation. Changes to active protection-rule ranges are validated before commit, preserving protection boundaries without extending the normal access-checking datapath. We implement the model in an open-source RISC-V World Checker integrated into a CVA6-based SoC. Our FPGA evaluation shows no degradation in access latency or operating frequency, with 7.1% LUT and 1.2% FF overhead for eight rules. In an OTA update case study, direct reconfiguration under delegated authority reduces policy-transition latency by 89.5% over hypervisor mediation and 94.6% over trusted firmware mediation, while preserving established authority boundaries. All artifacts will be open-sourced to support the evolution of RISC-V specifications and system-level protection designs.

Title: Reducing Cold-Start Latency on the WebAssembly Edge via Locality and Network-Aware Scheduling
Author: Michiel Van Kenhove, Emiel Sucaet, José Santos, Filip De Turck, Bruno Volckaert, Merlijn Sebrechts
Text_Content: Edge computing places computation closer to users and data sources, but introduces heterogeneous hardware, limited resources, and variable network conditions. WebAssembly (Wasm) is increasingly considered for these environments because modules are compact, portable, and quick to start. However, cold-start latency remains a challenge: when a worker node does not yet hold the required artifact, it must fetch it before execution, adding transfer overhead that directly increases the end-to-end (E2E) latency, especially for large artifacts or slow network links. At the same time, the geographical distance between the requester and the assigned worker independently contributes to latency through network routing overhead. Together, artifact locality and network proximity do not always point to the same placement decision, and naive scheduling strategies fail to account for either. This work extends a Wasm-native edge orchestrator with state-aware scheduling strategies that jointly optimize for both objectives. Evaluation on a Raspberry Pi testbed with emulated regional network latency shows that a hybrid scheduler combining cache-state and network-proximity signals reduces mean E2E latency by up to 40.8% compared to a default round-robin baseline. Artifact locality-aware placement is most effective when artifacts are large or repeatedly requested, while network-aware placement dominates when artifacts are small and routing latency has a larger relative effect, but combining both objectives consistently yields the lowest E2E latency across diverse edge workloads.

Title: Better Bounds For Graph Reconstruction
Author: Antoni Buraczewski, Paweł Gawrychowski
Text_Content: The goal in graph reconstruction problems is to learn an initially unknown graph using only a few queries of a specific type. Possibly the most natural query type is retrieving the distance between any two vertices of a connected, undirected, and unweighted graph. For a bounded-degree graph on $n$ vertices, Kannan, Mathieu, and Zhou [TALG 2018] showed a randomized algorithm that uses only $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{3/2})$ such queries. On the lower bound side, it is only known that any randomized algorithm needs $Ω(n\log n)$ queries. We make a significant step forward to bridging these bounds by designing a randomized algorithm that uses $n^{4/3+o(1)}$ queries. This requires extending the original approach based on Voronoi diagrams into a recursive procedure that partitions a cell into smaller cells. While such a recursive approach has been used in the related graph verification problem, in the more general graph reconstruction problem we need to operate without knowing the graph, which requires a new (and more technical) approach.

Title: Type-logical grammars and formal languages
Author: Richard Moot
Text_Content: We show that type-logical grammars with the standard rules for product, associativity, extraction and infixation have an NP-complete fixed recognition problem, adapting a construction for first-order linear logic from Pshenitsyn (2025), who already showed that grammars in first-order linear logic are closed under intersection and therefore not semilinear and not mildly context-sensitive. We strengthen these results and shown that grammars in first-order linear logic can simulate the quasi-linear grammars of Book \& Greibach (1970), the grammars recognised in non-deterministic linear time (NSPACE(n) or. NLIN). I argue that NLIN is an interesting class of formal languages as well, and a useful upper bound on the time complexity of formalisms used for natural language, just like LOGCFL is a useful upper bound on the space complexity. Taken together this means that first-order linear logic can be seen as the logic of non-deterministic linear-time string languages, graph languages and automata.

Title: Analytic $GW$-Bethe--Salpeter Gradients with Quasiparticle Response in the Resolution of the Identity
Author: Christof Holzer
Text_Content: Analytic nuclear gradients for excited states from the Bethe$-$Salpeter equation (BSE) in the static screening approximation are presented within this work. The response of the screened interaction to nuclear displacements is treated within the resolution-of-the-identity (RI) approximation, in close analogy to RI random phase approximation gradients, and is folded into the Lagrangian formalism of time-dependent density functional theory gradients. Quasiparticle gradients enter via the full analytic derivative of the corrections for RI contour-deformation $G_0W_0$ and ev$GW$, also taking into account that incomplete quasiparticle spectra are typically supplied. Comparisons to earlier approaches using a geometry-independent fixed quasiparticle correction are made. For the latter, the orbital-rotation terms are derived exactly, too. The implemented gradient scales as $\mathcal{O}(N^4)$, and the three-index integrals are processed in batches with a memory demand of $\mathcal{O}(N_\mathrm{aux}^2 + N_\mathrm{occ}^2 N_\mathrm{aux})$. Excited-state geometries of a set of small molecules are compared to EOM-CCSD references and to TD-DFT. It is shown that the full quasiparticle gradient removes most of the systematic underestimation of the bond lengths in singlet excited states. A comparison along the C$-$C stretch of acetylene shows that the neglected derivative of the quasiparticle corrections is modest, but becomes erratic for $G_0W_0$ near poles of the self-energy, which ev$GW$ avoids.

Title: Bias in Method-of-Moments Heritability Estimation Under Model Misspecification
Author: Jonathan Gal, Sriram Sankararaman, Saharon Rosset
Text_Content: Method-of-Moments (MoM) based approaches for estimation of variance components --- heritability and beyond --- are central in computational genetics due to their flexibility in addressing diverse and complex models while minimizing assumptions, and ease of computation and approximation in biobank-scale data. MoM are closely related to other important methods in this area like LD-score regression. A fundamental, highly debated question relates to the bias inherent in MoM estimates of variance components when the fitted model is misspecified: since the true underlying model is unknown, the fitted model may be missing some of the components from the true model or contain superfluous ones. We offer a general mathematical formulation of this bias and investigate its properties. This leads to novel insights about the sign and the magnitude of the bias in settings of interest and allows extensions and re-interpretation of previous MoM results in the literature. One case study we pursue is in estimating gene-environment interaction variance components (GxE). We prove that when omitting environment-specific noise components (NxE), the resulting GxE estimates are strictly upward biased, even when no true interaction exists. In another case study, we consider heritability estimation, when the genetic variance components are incorrectly partitioned (such as using a single genome-wide component instead of chromosome-specific components). We derive explicit expressions for the bias in the estimate of genome-wide heritability and its dependence on LD scores within and between components. For example, if all components have the same average LD score, the misspecified heritability estimate is still unbiased.

Title: A Dual-Frequency-Constrained Structure-Function Kirchhoff Model for Near-Nadir Ocean Backscatter -- Part I: Theoretical Framework
Author: Alexey S. Mironov, Frédéric Nouguier, Bertrand Chapron
Text_Content: Most operational near-nadir geophysical model functions (GMFs) are empirical and fitted one radar band at a time, and do not explain the difference between Ku and Ka band. This paper derives a backscatter model in which one local description of the sea surface serves both bands. The near-nadir Kirchhoff integral is written in terms of the elevation difference between two surface points separated by a horizontal lag. The surface then enters through the structure functions of that difference, and the scattering kernel selects the lags each band samples, about 2.5-1.4 cm at Ku and 1.0-0.5 cm at Ka band. Geometric optics is recovered as the quadratic, isotropic limit, without a spectral cutoff. With a logarithmic second-order structure function, one wind-dependent log-slope sets both the incidence shape and the Ku-Ka shape difference, and band transfer reduces to evaluating one curve at a second lag. Same-footprint dual-frequency radar data show that one band alone does not determine this transfer. The log-slope is the level of the short-wave saturation range and grows about as the square of the wind speed; a physical short-wave spectrum reproduces this growth but overestimates the level. Dual-frequency radars thus measure the centimetre-scale roughness level, although they do not separate a scale-dependent structure function from non-Gaussian surface statistics. A companion paper delivers and evaluates the resulting GMF, KuKa-Mod.

Title: Graph-Guided Bayesian Factor Analysis: A Fast Integrated EFA-CFA Approach for High-Dimensional Data
Author: Shitao Fan, Lizhen Lin, Zhenyao Ye, Shuo Chen
Text_Content: Factor analysis has been central to the analysis of high-dimensional biomedical data. However, existing exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis methods face several limitations: less interpretable factor findings, difficulty in identifying which variables can and cannot be represented by low-dimensional factors, challenges in estimating the covariance among factors, and maximum-likelihood fits that break down when variables outnumber subjects. We propose graph-guided Bayesian factor analysis (gg-BFA) to address these gaps. We first use a Bayesian model to explore and learn the latent graph structure, identifying which variables can and cannot be represented by low-dimensional factors and how many factors are needed. A dense-subgraph search proposes partitions of the variables into communities, each defining one factor, and a forward stepwise search compares their fractional variational posteriors and stops when the evidence lower bound first decreases. We show that this search recovers the true communities even when the number of variables grows much faster than the sample size. We then develop a confirmatory Bayesian model whose variational posterior of the covariance contracts at the parametric rate up to a logarithmic factor, yielding posterior inference for the factors and their covariance, as well as predictions of missing values. Its four members range from a community mask to several cross-loadings per variable. In five biomedical panels, the complete analysis took under ten minutes each on one GPU, and cross-loadings improved held-out covariance and the prediction of masked measurements. In TCGA Kidney, six of the first eight factors were enriched for known pathways, and 190 of the 210 factor correlations had 95% credible intervals excluding zero. Overall, gg-BFA is computationally fast and provides interpretable factor analysis findings and reliable inference results.

Title: Continuous-Time Set-Transformers for Asynchronous WiFi-IMU Indoor Localization
Author: Mohamed Bachar, Ilyass Abouelaziz, Yuehua Ding
Text_Content: Indoor localization commonly combines WiFi received signal strength indicator (RSSI) fingerprints with inertial measurements. However, these sensor streams are sampled asynchronously at different rates; therefore, observations rarely align in time and may be missing or stale. Most existing methods resample the data onto a shared clock and process each modality using a separate branch. We instead present a continuous-time transformer that represents observations as an unordered set of timestamped tokens. Each token encodes its measurement, modality, and elapsed time since acquisition. A single attention block jointly fuses information across modalities and time, avoiding both resampling and modality-specific branches while remaining invariant to token order. During training, we randomly mask entire modalities and individual observations, enabling the model to operate under missing or outdated inputs. We validate the modality-specific encoders on their respective benchmarks and evaluate the fused model on both simulated and real datasets, including a crosssession dataset collected on unseen days. The proposed approach improves upon an open WiFi fingerprinting baseline under cross-session drift, remains competitive with learned fusion and dead-reckoning baselines, and degrades gracefully as observations become missing or stale. These results suggest that a single continuoustime transformer provides a practical framework for indoor localization from asynchronous sensors.

Title: Learning Global Equilibria in Non-Concave Prospect Theoretic Games
Author: Ashok Krishnan K. S., Lilou Malfoy, Helene Le Cadre, Ana Busic
Text_Content: Human agents in non cooperative games often exhibit non rational behaviour. Prospect theory provides a behavioural framework to capture how agents perceive gains and losses under risk, but, its incorporation into games typically leads to non concave and non convex utility functions, making equilibrium computation challenging. In such cases, it is difficult to obtain algorithms that have global convergence behaviour. This paper proposes a learning algorithm which uses minorization-maximization (MM). Under a proximal Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition on the potential function, we establish global convergence of the algorithm to a potential-maximizing Nash equilibrium. We further show how the structure of the MM minorizer can be used to enable a distributed implementation of the algorithm. With additional noise injection, the individual updates of the agents can be obscured, while still ensuring global convergence.

Title: Creative Intent as an Evolving Shared State: Supporting Cross-Stage Human-AI Video Co-Creation
Author: Yuhang Jin, Mengfei Chen, Hanwei Zheng, Songruoyao Wu, Kejun Zhang
Text_Content: As generative AI becomes increasingly involved in video creation, creators face challenges in expanding, translating, and negotiating creative intent across stages. We therefore view creative intent as an evolving shared state throughout human-AI co-creation. A multi-stage design was employed: semi-structured interviews with 12 creators informed 3 design goals, followed by expert co-design and the development of VideoMaker. VideoMaker organizes creation into a six-stage workflow that progressively translates creative intent. At key stages, creators negotiate with AI through the Seed Panel, explicitly confirming, revising, and updating intent. A shared AI Agent, supported by the Multi-style Script Library and Cinematic Language Knowledge Base, enables differentiated expansion of initial intent and faithful translation. A within-subjects study with 30 participants showed that VideoMaker effectively supported the expansion and cross-stage translation of creative intent, with stronger intent preservation, while negotiated boundaries between creator-confirmed intent and AI initiative remained difficult to sustain.

Title: Double Blind Evals: Resolving the Dual Confidentiality Dilemma in AI Safety Auditing
Author: Andrew Trask, Sol Messing, Vai Pahwa, Pegah Maham, Rene Kolga, Austin Frantz, Andrew Tash, Kate Thomas, Sean McGregor, George Balston, Patricia Paskov, Miles Brundage, Akriti Vij, Bennett Hillenbrand, Alexandros Karargyris, Tin Acosta, Joel Fenster, Madeleine Elish, Rasmi Elasmar, Myriam Khan, Koen van der Veen, Rasswanth S, Sameer Wagh, Stephen Gabriel, Pedro Werneck, Lacey Strahm, Kevin McDonough, Ronnie Falcon, Kristian Lum, William Isaac
Text_Content: AI safety evaluations often involve sensitive prompts and proprietary models. Evaluators want to keep their evaluation prompts secret from model owners to prevent purposeful or incidental data leakage, ensuring longer usefulness of their benchmark. Model owners in turn wish to keep their proprietary model weights and inference code within their own secure infrastructure to protect their IP. We present a way forward for "double-blind evals", which provide cryptographic guarantees that an evaluator's prompts are not shared with the model owner, while simultaneously maintaining the confidentiality of the model weights and inference code. To accomplish this, we use secure enclaves that encrypt data in RAM at the hardware level. In a world-first pilot, we test this approach by evaluating a proprietary Google DeepMind model (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite) against a selection of the private AILuminate benchmark corpus, using an NVIDIA H100 secure enclave on Google Cloud Platform, and using OpenMined's PySyft to maintain data and model privacy. We believe this effort marks the first use of this technology to provide mutual secrecy for one organization's frontier-class proprietary model weights and another organization's closed benchmark.

Title: Direct Conditioning of Audio Diffusion Transformers on fMRI Reveals Cortical Contributions to Sound Reconstruction
Author: Matteo Ciferri, Tonio Weidler, Matteo Ferrante, Nicola Toschi, Elia Formisano
Text_Content: Reconstructing audio from brain activity remains challenging. Existing brain-to-audio pipelines typically map neural responses to predefined stimulus representations before synthesis. While recent work in the visual domain has explored direct conditioning on brain activity, this approach has not yet been extended to audio diffusion models. We introduce MAAS (Multi-Area Auditory Synthesis), an end-to-end framework that conditions a pretrained audio diffusion transformer on ROI-wise fMRI responses without first supervising a decoder to predict an external stimulus representation. MAAS uses region-specific projections and learned brain tokens to condition Stable Audio through a dedicated cross-attention pathway. On a 7T fMRI dataset, we demonstrate consistent improvements over baselines, including two-stage fMRI-to-latent conditioning, across both acoustic and semantic evaluation metrics. In addition, we introduce a fidelity metric grounded in a computational model of auditory neural processing, which allows us to quantify the contribution of individual auditory cortical regions to reconstructed audio representations.

Title: Reducing Provers in Distributed Quantum Verification
Author: Alex Della Schiava, Atsuya Hasegawa, François Le Gall, Harumichi Nishimura
Text_Content: In the distributed quantum Merlin-Arthur ($\mathsf{dQMA}$) model introduced by Fraigniaud, Le Gall, Nishimura, and Paz (ITCS 2021), a network of quantum computers verifies a global property with the aid of a quantum proof supplied by an untrusted prover. While the nodes are computationally unbounded, the challenge is to limit proof size and the communication required for verification. In this paper, we consider the model of Hasegawa, Kundu, and Nishimura (PODC 2024), where the proof must be unentangled across nodes, and define its extension to $k$ unentangled provers, denoted by $\mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$. In this setting, we investigate the proof size per node and the communication costs of reducing the number of provers. Our first result reduces the number of provers from $k$ to two, doubling the proof size without additional communication. Moreover, with four additional rounds, we can reduce the number of provers from $k$ to one, using at most three times the original local proof size plus a logarithmic term in the number of nodes. Finally, we establish amplification for perfectly complete protocols. In this regime, a single prover suffices with a constant-factor overhead in our reductions, yielding $\mathsf{dQMAS} = \mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$.

Title: Consistent Mapping for Fluid Structure Interaction with Geometrically Nonlinear Isogeometric Beams
Author: Juan Ignacio Camarotti, Ricky Aristio, Roland Wüchner
Text_Content: Isogeometric beam formulations provide an efficient reduced-dimensional representation of slender structures, combining accurate geometry and high-order continuity with few structural degrees of freedom. Their application to fluid--structure interaction (FSI) requires transferring motion and loads between the one-dimensional beam centerline and the surrounding fluid interface. While mapping strategies exist for conventional finite element beams, geometrically nonlinear isogeometric formulations require operators consistent with their spline-based kinematics and distinct descriptions of cross-sectional rotation. This work develops consistent beam-to-surface mappings for geometrically nonlinear isogeometric Bernoulli and Timoshenko beams in partitioned FSI. Fluid-interface points are attached to the beam in the reference configuration and reconstructed using the nonlinear kinematics of each formulation. Consistent linearization yields a configuration-dependent mapping operator whose transpose ensures work-conjugate load transfer. The formulations are verified through analytical deformation tests, convergence studies, and virtual-work checks, and evaluated in beam-based adaptations of the Mok and Turek--Hron benchmarks and the Goland wing flutter benchmark. The results confirm accurate interface reconstruction and work-conjugate load transfer under large deformations, while demonstrating the applicability of both beam formulations to coupled FSI problems.

Title: Unmasking Four Knapsack Problems in the Traveling Thief Benchmark
Author: Mohammed Mizan Alanazi, Mahdi Khemakhem
Text_Content: The traveling thief problem (TTP) asks a thief to choose a tour and a packing together, and the benchmark of 9,720 instances of Polyakovskiy et al. (2014) is the standard test set for comparing TTP heuristics. We show that four of these instances are not TTP instances at all. Their files give a renting rate of 0.00, so the tour has no effect on the objective and each instance reduces to a 0-1 knapsack problem. One of them belongs to the 60 categorized instances on which new methods are usually compared, and on it five of nine published methods report exactly the same value. The cause is the format of the files, which keep the renting rate with two decimals, while the rule of the generator gives a rate close to 0.003 on these instances. The same rounding may shift the rate of 949 other instances by more than 1%. Since the tour and the packing used by the generator were not published, the original rates cannot be recovered. We therefore define new rates with the same rule, applied to a fully specified reference solution that we publish, and we show with a published heuristic that the corrected instances behave as TTP instances again. We also give reference results on the corrected instances and recommendations for future studies. Finally, we present ttplib, a new open-source Python library that loads any of the 9,720 instances, including the corrected ones, without downloading the whole benchmark.

Title: Fairness in Explainable AI Narratives: Decomposing Social Disparities in LLM-Generated Explanations
Author: Wannes Van den Bulck, Sofie Goethals, David Martens
Text_Content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate technical explainable AI (XAI) artefacts such as SHAP into explanatory narratives (XAINs) for lay users. In high-risk domains, these explanations are often the main resource through which individuals can understand and contest adverse decisions. Yet LLMs are known to reproduce social bias, even from proxy variables alone, and fairness in XAINs remains unstudied. Because XAINs are bound to a ground-truth artefact, fairness concerns not only what a narrative says and how, but also whether it is equally faithful across social groups. We introduce fairness in XAINs as a new field of research and propose a framework that generates narratives under three conditions (protected attribute disclosed, withheld, or counterfactually swapped), allowing five comparisons that pinpoint the cause of disparities. We apply it to adversely classified instances from four datasets in credit scoring, education and employment, generating narratives with five LLMs, and evaluate faithfulness, feature coverage and sentiment. We find significant disparities across all datasets, metric families and models, arising in two ways. Faithfulness disparities result from feature values: LLMs make plausible but false statements, triggered by values that are unequally distributed across social groups. Feature coverage and sentiment disparities stem from the protected attribute itself: once it is disclosed, LLMs give less explanation to, or frame more negatively the narratives of, groups that have historically been discriminated against or are stereotypically associated with worse outcomes. A more faithful model removes the faithfulness disparities, and withholding protected attributes mostly removes the others, but neither suffices on its own. Fairness in XAINs should therefore be audited separately from the predictive model and its XAI artefact.

Title: TRACE: Adaptive Trust-Region Bayesian Optimization for Open-Ended Molecular Design
Author: Madhav R. Muthyala, Mahsa Askari, Farshud Sorourifar, Evan Zhou, Joe Gauthier, Joel A. Paulson
Text_Content: Optimizing molecules under small evaluation budgets requires deciding both where in chemical space to search and which candidate within that region to evaluate. We introduce Trust Region Adaptive Chemical Exploration (TRACE), a framework for open-ended molecular Bayesian optimization (BO), where candidates are generated on demand rather than selected from a fixed library. TRACE combines an objective-free graph-perturbation mechanism with a fixed, chemistry-aware Gaussian process (GP) surrogate using fragprints, a representation combining molecular fingerprints and fragment descriptors. Rather than learning the search geometry itself, TRACE makes the scale of chemical exploration explicit through a Tanimoto-similarity threshold controlling chemical extent and a cardinality budget controlling candidate-search breadth. A simple success/failure controller expands or contracts both quantities during optimization, while the GP and acquisition function select which admissible molecules to evaluate. Across six challenging molecular optimization benchmarks under matched 1,000-evaluation budgets, TRACE achieves the strongest overall sample efficiency as measured by the best molecule found as evaluations accumulate. Crossed ablations on two objectives further show that adaptive region control contributes beyond the proposal mechanism, while its benefit depends on the proposal distribution. We further apply TRACE to the stability of iron phthalocyanine (FePc), a non-precious molecular electrocatalyst whose degradation can involve loss of the Fe center. Using a first-principles density functional theory (DFT) workflow designed for accurate energy evaluation, TRACE increases the computed thermodynamic resistance to Fe dissolution from 0.42 to 2.59 eV over 80 designed evaluations.

Title: Spin-valve effect through electrostatic coupling
Author: Jan Phillips, Joaquín Fernández-Rossier
Text_Content: We propose a spin-valve effect in which an insulating magnetic van der Waals multilayer controls the conductance of an adjacent non-magnetic conductor by electrostatic coupling, without transport-electrons entering the magnetic layers. The coupling is induced by the variations of the electronic structure when the relative orientation of the magnetization of adjacent monolayers changes from parallel to antiparallel, modifying both the dielectric constant and band alignment. We consider two types of coupling and device concepts: charge transfer to a graphene monolayer and capacitive coupling in a single-electron transistor. We use density functional calculations to assess the magnitude of the effect in various materials, including CrI$_3$, CrBr$_3$, CrCl$_3$ and NiBr$_2$. We predict magnetoresistance ratios in the range of 1.14-1.20 for the charge-transfer device and up to $10^3$ in the single-electron transistor.

Title: AgentOPSD: Turn-Level Credit Assignment via Recursive Belief Revision
Author: Yizhuo Li
Text_Content: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards ordinarily spreads a single advantage over a whole trajectory, a granularity too coarse to isolate the few decisions on which success in a long, multi-turn interaction actually turns. Privileged self-distillation supplies denser supervision, but it leaves unanswered how a set of local teacher-student discrepancies should be converted into credit along a sequence. We introduce AgentOPSD, a critic-free scheme that assigns credit recursively, one interaction turn at a time. Inside a turn, the token-level log-probability gaps between a skill-conditioned self-teacher and the student are summed, and that sum acts as evidence in a recursive Bayesian update carried out in log-odds space; the resulting revisions reallocate the outcome-derived advantage across turns through a multiplier that is bounded and preserves its sign. With Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B as policy backbones on ALFWorld, the method improves consistently on GRPO and on self-distillation baselines, and attains 89.1% success at the 7B scale. Ablations attribute the gain to aggregating evidence at turn boundaries and to making the belief revision depend on history, rather than to the local gap by itself.

Title: Effects of pulse durations in atom interferometry with double Raman diffraction
Author: Nadja Augst, Albert Roura
Text_Content: Double Raman diffraction is a key enabling technique for future space missions relying on atom interferometry that offers enhanced sensitivity and intrinsic suppression of systematic effects. This diffraction mechanism naturally arises when employing a retro-reflection configuration in microgravity, but then accelerations can no longer be determined through a frequency-chirp scan. As a consequence, measurements become much more sensitive to systematic effects associated with pulse timing and duration. Indeed, the finite pulse duration can introduce additional phase shifts and small modifications of the arm trajectories, which are critical sources of error in high-precision measurements. In this work, we present the first complete analytical results of these effects for double Raman diffraction, building upon previous work for single diffraction and extending the standard literature. Our analysis determines the impact of finite pulse durations on the full interferometer sequence, quantifying the shifts of the atomic wave packets' trajectories and the acquired phases. The description relies on a comprehensive framework describing matter-wave propagation in terms of central trajectories and centered wave packets, and can be easily incorporated into relativistic treatments. Furthermore, we make use of group theoretic methods that are particularly useful when accounting for residual accelerations and frequency chirps, which are also relevant for ground-based applications. Our study includes time-dependent accelerations and frequency chirps, gravity gradients, retardation effects, AC Stark shifts induced by the Raman pulses, and external forces such those due to magnetic fields or temperature gradients in the black-body radiation.

Title: Vendor-Agnostic Pseudocontinuous Arterial Spin Labeling Using Pulseq: Cross-Vendor Quantitative Evaluation
Author: Jianing Zhang, Jun Wang, Joseph G. Woods, Shaoyou Ye, Shuai Ming, Hongwei Li, Wei Hu, Wei Wei, Xiaohu Li, Thomas W. Okell, Yang Ji
Text_Content: Purpose: Inter-scanner variability in cerebral blood flow (CBF) quantification limits reproducibility in multi-center arterial spin labeling (ASL) studies. We developed and validated a vendor-agnostic pseudo-continuous ASL (PCASL) sequence using the open-source Pulseq framework, and assessed its extensibility to advanced perfusion imaging. Methods: A vendor-independent PCASL sequence was implemented in Pulseq and deployed on 3T scanners from Siemens, GE, and United Imaging. Seven healthy volunteers underwent single-post-labeling-delay (PLD) PCASL on all platforms, including test-retest scans. An in-house adapted Siemens vendor-based PCASL sequence served as reference. Reproducibility was assessed using within-subject coefficient of variation (CVwithin), root mean square error (RMSE), regional CBF correlation, and voxel-wise variation ratio maps. Multi-PLD PCASL and planning-free VE-PCASL were implemented as proof-of-concept extensions. Results: Mean gray matter (GM) CBF was similar across implementations. Test-retest GM CVwithin was below 4% on all platforms; Siemens-Pulseq had the lowest value (2.65%), versus 3.64% for the native sequence. GM RMSE between Siemens-Vendor and Pulseq implementations was comparable to test-retest RMSE, and all inter-scanner CVwithin values were below 3%. Voxel-wise variation ratio distributions were centered near 100%, suggesting cross-vendor variability comparable to physiological baseline fluctuations. Multi-PLD and VE-PCASL ran successfully on all platforms, yielding consistent CBF/ATT maps and vascular territory delineations. Conclusion: Pulseq-based PCASL enables vendor-agnostic perfusion imaging with low inter-scanner variability. This open-source approach provides a reproducible, standardized solution for multi-center ASL studies and facilitates deployment of advanced ASL techniques in clinical research.

Title: Covert System Identification Under Timing Constraints: A Static Linear Model and Its Detectability Implications
Author: Victor Mattos, Guilherme Sobreira, Amit Bhaya, Alan Oliveira de Sá, Charles B. Prado, Raphael Machado, Gaurav Srivastava, Daniel S. Menasche
Text_Content: This paper studies covert system identification in cyber-physical systems, where an attacker infers plant dynamics while attempting to remain stealthy. We introduce a lightweight static linear model in which the time to execute a setpoint change is proportional to the commanded speed difference. On a Siemens PROFINET testbed this gain captures the drive's ramp response accurately but not its terminal overshoot. That omitted transient becomes the attacker's main exposure: on real traces, the residual left by the linear masking procedure is detected by two anomaly monitors, Process-Aware Stealthy-Attack Detection (PASAD) and the CUSUM change detector. Across the cascade identification and staircase attack strategies defined in the paper, the stealth boundary relates to the plant's own settling transients, a structural limit for this class of models under the adopted detector-calibration regime. Comparison against dynamic models obtained by N4SID, trained at multiple excitation amplitudes, shows that the evaluated N4SID models do not improve stealth over the structure-informed ramp model. Since per-cycle computation is negligible for both procedures, the binding trade-off is not inference cost but whether the attacker can acquire and refresh a model without injecting detectable perturbations.

Title: Stylization as Geodesic Navigation on Diffusion Manifolds
Author: Yan Li, Zehao Li, Xinlong Sun, Fuchen Long, Xi Chen, Wenhan Luo, Yike Guo
Text_Content: Facial stylization asks for a delicate transformation: the image should look unmistakably artistic, yet the person should remain unmistakably the same. Existing training-free and instruction-driven methods often fail to expose such control, either drifting away from identity or producing only weak stylization. We introduce Stylus, a training-free framework that treats facial style transfer as navigation on the curved latent manifold of a pretrained diffusion model. Rather than interpolating in flat Euclidean space, \method refines the interpolated content--style point by lowering a ratio-weighted discrete geodesic energy under the pullback metric, made tractable by a rank-one power-iteration approximation of the Jacobian. This principle drives two complementary controls: content--style latent interpolation for smooth semantic fusion, and self-attention query optimization for spatially adaptive style injection. The resulting dual-control mechanism provides continuous, fine-grained control over stylization strength while preserving identity-critical facial structure, all without additional training. Experiments show that Stylus achieves the strongest identity and content preservation at competitive stylization strength.

Title: From Likelihood Convergence to Parameter Convergence in POMDPs
Author: Jack Zhang, Saurabh Amin, Jiawei Zhang, Patrick Jaillet
Text_Content: Likelihood-based methods are widely used to learn the parameters of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). While finite-sample guarantees for policy suboptimality exist for certain POMDP subclasses, analogous guarantees for parameter recovery remain less well understood. For any candidate POMDP parameter, we bound its parameter recovery error in terms of its likelihood gap to the ground truth, the structural conditioning of the observation and transition kernels, and the behavior policy used to collect data. The bound applies in both the undercomplete and overcomplete regimes, with the latter following naturally from the undercomplete analysis. Because the result applies to any sufficiently good candidate, it yields finite-sample guarantees for the maximum-likelihood estimator and any procedure producing a parameter with controlled likelihood gap. This is particularly useful for near-optimal learning in infinite-horizon POMDPs, where existing approaches largely rely on model-based planning with accurate transition and observation kernel estimates. The bound separates the contributions of the behavior policy and model, showing how data-collection choices, including action coverage, and their effects on mixing can accelerate parameter learning.

Title: Evaluating Cross-Signal Coherence in Mammography Vision-Language Models
Author: Rebeca Nam, Chase M. Fensore, Christian A. Fauria-Robinson, Judy Gichoya, Joyce C. Ho
Text_Content: As vision-language models (VLMs) move toward interpreting medical images directly, their outputs increasingly include not just a label but a stated confidence and a written justification. Yet the field still predominantly evaluates VLMs using just accuracy. We evaluate the coherence between answer, confidence, and explanation across four VLMs on breast density and BI-RADS categorization, using two mammography datasets. We perform controlled perturbations of the question, multiple choice option orders, and the images and assess changes in the three outputs. Our results suggest confidence does not decrease even as the mammography image is changed. Shuffling the options also changes most VLMs' answers. Notably, there are cases where a model's own stated reasoning contradicts its final answer, a distinction accuracy alone cannot capture but one that governs whether an AI-generated answer can be trusted.

Title: Ab Initio Molecular Dynamics-Guided Machine-Learning Potentials for Mapping Nitric Oxide Interactions with Oxygen-Covered Graphite
Author: Yaideny Rodriguez Linares, Gilberto A. Alou Angulo, Samuel Del Fré, Maurice Monnerville, Alejandro Rivero Santamaría
Text_Content: Exploratory ab initio molecular dynamics is used to construct machine-learning interatomic potentials for NO interactions with highly oriented pyrolytic graphite at 33\% bridge-site oxygen coverage. Representative configurations sampled across surface temperatures and incidence energies provide reference energies and forces for training and validation. The selected potential enables relaxation of 300 adsorption configurations and construction of spatial and angular interaction maps. These maps reveal increasingly restricted attractive regions during vertical approach and reduced short-range repulsion upon molecular reorientation. The resulting adsorption geometries and interaction landscapes guide further first-principles sampling toward refining potentials for NO oxidation dynamics.

Title: Text2NGAC: a multi-LLM pipeline for NGAC policy extraction with mutation-based verification
Author: Ayesha Habib, Huixiang Zhang, Dan Zhu, Waiz Haider
Text_Content: Access-control policies are written in natural language but enforced as formal models, and translating them into NIST Next Generation Access Control (NGAC) graphs remains unsolved: prior systems cover only subsets of the NGAC model, and none verify the graphs they extract. We present Text2NGAC, a pipeline of cooperating large language models that disambiguates each sentence before extraction, escalates uncertain sentences to a multi-model ensemble, and checks the resulting graph with a five-strategy verifier whose own effectiveness is measured by controlled mutation testing. To our knowledge it is the first system to extract all four NGAC relationship types - associations, prohibitions, event-response obligations, and assignments - from real-world policy documents. Three results anchor the evaluation. The verifier detects 99.7% of 918 injected mutants and every structural fail-open fault, and the fault classes it misses are characterized and weighted by security consequence rather than left unexamined. The extracted graphs are enforceable: one corpus's graph loads unmodified into the NIST reference implementation, which reproduces all 55 access decisions the graph entails and fires an extracted obligation end-to-end. Extraction reaches 97.3-99.6% exact-tuple-match accuracy on the 714 scored sentences of four real corpora, far above three reproduced baselines on matched metrics, and paraphrase probes with semantic re-scoring bound the pipeline's sensitivity to rewording. Reported accuracy is wording- and benchmark-specific, adversarial input is outside the verifier's guarantees, and the intended deployment is extraction plus structural verification feeding expert review. A complete two-tier reproducibility artifact accompanies the paper.

Title: More Papers, Not More Output: Collaboration and Publication Trends among Early-Career Researchers
Author: Christian Leibel
Text_Content: Concerns about publication pressure often assume that early-career researchers now produce more papers than comparable researchers did in the past. However, publication counts may give a misleading impression of individual publication output because research has become increasingly collaborative. Researchers can list more papers on their CVs not only by producing more work themselves, but also by working with more coauthors and sharing credit for the same papers. Whether the collaboration-adjusted output of early-career researchers has increased over time has rarely been examined empirically. This study addresses this gap by analysing publication records from more than 200,000 early-career researchers at Western research institutions across five major science, engineering, and health fields between 1996 and 2024. Recent cohorts appear on more papers than earlier cohorts, but they also work in much larger research teams. Once publication credit is divided among coauthors, collaboration-adjusted output remains stable or declines across all fields. These findings show that research evaluation metrics that ignore collaboration are increasingly poorly aligned with how scientific work is produced. Rising publication counts alone should therefore not be taken as evidence that early-career researchers are producing more individual publication output.

Title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Privacy-Enhanced Computing Through Register Renaming
Author: Ahmed Nematallah, Stefanos Kaxiras
Text_Content: Privacy-Enhanced Computing (PEC) is a mechanism to hide program secrets from the outside world without paying the cost of fully-homomorphic encryption. Previous work has developed hardware mechanisms to achieve this goal but they require a dedicated processor enclave where all computations are done, requiring duplicate ALU resources and limiting the performance of PEC-utilizing applications due to not being able to access the full compute resources of the processor (e.g., multiple execution units and vector units), or not being able to execute PEC instructions in parallel and out-of-order. In this work, we introduce HPS-PEC (Hidden in Plain Sight PEC), a novel method of utilizing existing infrastructure in the CPU to achieve PEC with minor modifications to the architecture. We show that, across 25 VIP-Bench benchmarks and with a 7-cycle QARMA-64 cipher, HPS-PEC runs encrypted code at 3.41x the execution time of unprotected native code (geometric mean), of which 1.03x is the cost of data-oblivious code itself, and is 1.26x faster than a Sequestered Encryption (SE) unit while utilizing under a third of its dedicated area. Our method keeps plaintext out of reach of every instruction, as an enclave does given a correctly functioning renamer and register file, which every program already depends on.

Title: Modeling and Estimation of a Towed Marine System
Author: Josef Matouš, Simon Hoff, Damiano Varagnolo, Marius S. Rundhovde, Kristin Y. Pettersen, Martin Saska
Text_Content: This paper addresses the modeling and state estimation of a towed marine system consisting of two autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs), a pair of umbilical cables, towfish, and a trailing loop cable. Inspired by the existing literature, we employ a lumped-mass modeling approach for the cables and towfish, capturing the essential dynamics while maintaining computational tractability. A Lyapunov-based analysis is conducted to verify the stability and convergence properties of the proposed model. Building on this model, we propose two state estimation methods, namely a reduced-order observer and a perfect-measurement extended Kalman filter (PMEKF), using only the measurements from the ASVs' onboard sensors. Numerical simulations and experimental results are provided to validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

Title: LawKAN: Group-Law Layers for Composition -- When Imposing a Known Law Pays Off
Author: Anna Mishchenko, Nikolai Gavrilin
Text_Content: Many tasks compose transformations by a known rule: chained rotations in robotics and navigation. Learned models relearn it, compounding error; classical estimators hardcode it and miss hardware deviations. We impose the known structure and learn only the remainder: an exact non-commutative group law sits in the node of a self-contained layer, its edges learn local increments, and a zero-initialized correction psi learns unknown deviations of the law. A pre-training criterion predicts exact representability. On fixed-angle SU(2) composition, a 54-parameter dense edge is the most accurate dense model, at 27x fewer parameters than the strongest fixed-matrix baseline, and lies 0.05 deg above the Bayes floor. On real robot arms, an isolated 306-parameter psi reaches 1.12-1.14 mm versus 1.29-1.33 mm for Gauss-Newton at N >= 60, and the recipe transfers across three vendors and two protocols. The recipe matches classical fits where the data obey the law and loses where the imposed law is not the task's.

Title: Distinguishing thyroid nodule malignancy using digital palpation
Author: Brendan M. Unikewicz, Joseph E. Bonavia, Ekaterina L. Koelliker, Abigail Klein, Katie C. Spaeth, Hannah M. Varner, S. Kiana Naghibzadeh, Yoav Horev, Sareh Parangi, Tal Cohen
Text_Content: Accurate pre-operative diagnosis of thyroid nodules remains a major clinical challenge. Current diagnostic techniques rely on fine-needle aspiration and demonstrate high rates of inconclusive results, often leading to avoidable thyroidectomies with lifelong implications. Here, we introduce a mechanics-based diagnostic method that leverages Digital Palpation to determine malignancy and identify tissue subtypes in human thyroid nodules. From a cohort of patients undergoing thyroidectomies, we evaluated ex vivo thyroid specimens and processed the resulting mechanical data from 36 tests in 10 thyroid nodules. Principal Component Analysis reveals that these experimental results are distributed within a three-dimensional space of interpretable scalar features reflecting tissue grittiness, strength, and toughness, which map closely to descriptions of malignant and benign nodules given by clinicians. Our results further demonstrate that malignant nodules exhibit distinct mechanical signatures compared to their benign counterparts. This revealed a statistically significant difference (p = 9 x 10^-4) and separability (95% lower-bound Hedges' g = 1.08) between benign and malignant nodules along a direction in principal component space representing effective stiffness. Preliminary clustering patterns were also observed among malignant subtypes, including follicular, oncocytic, and papillary thyroid carcinomas. Together, these results highlight the potential of Digital Palpation as a novel mechanics-based method for tissue characterization and motivate its further development toward diagnostic applications.

Title: GHiML: VLM-Guided Hierarchical Multi-Label Learning with Applications to Benthic Imagery
Author: Isaac Xu, Devi Ayyagari, Martin Gillis, Benjamin Misiuk, Craig J. Brown, Thomas Trappenberg
Text_Content: Vision language models (VLMs) encode substantial expert knowledge within their weights, yet their direct application to specialised classification domains such as benthic imagery remains limited. Meanwhile, vision transformers trained on these tasks rely predominantly on low-level visual latents (colours, textures, and shapes) that lack the higher-level reasoning humans employ for identification. We propose Guided Hierarchical Multi-Label (GHiML) learning, a pipeline that extracts conceptual latent variables from a VLM conditioned on training data, generates sample-relevant captions grounded in those variables, and fuses the resulting textual embeddings with image embeddings via cross-attention and a per-node gated router. We also introduce the inverted HML score ($d_{\mathrm{inv}}$), a similarity score that evaluates hierarchical multi-label predictions through graph traversal distance and a cardinality penalty, providing an interpretable alternative to existing measures, which are insensitive to realistic degradations in sparse, deep hierarchies. Experiments on BenthicNet, FathomNet and iNaturalist show that the router improves macro $F_1$ over the vision-only baseline by up to 6.7 pp and $d_{\mathrm{inv}}$ by up to 21.1 pp on in-domain benthic data, with gains persisting under distribution shift. Ablations locate the contribution of the text itself: on the multi-label biotic hierarchies, removing the per-sample text signal degrades $d_{\mathrm{inv}}$ while leaving macro $F_1$ unchanged, consistent with text acting through prediction cardinality rather than node discrimination, whereas iNaturalist, whose annotations are single-label, loses 18.7% of macro $F_1$. Our results support the hypothesis that VLMs contain exploitable specialised knowledge that, when appropriately elicited, can augment classification in domains where direct visual learning is insufficient.

Title: WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?
Author: Yuhang Chen, Jiheng Li, Jiale Wang, Zai Wang, Guangyue Liu
Text_Content: Video world models conditioned on an input video make it possible to explore real, recorded dynamic scenes, enabling re-shooting of footage, free-viewpoint replay, and real-to-sim environments for embodied agents. Such uses require the generated rollout to stay faithful to the recorded world, yet existing benchmarks start from a single image or a text prompt, and video-conditioned generation is evaluated mainly on perceptual quality and camera following. These evaluations do not directly assess whether exploration preserves subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency upon revisiting a location. We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos of real and AI-generated content in three difficulty tiers (3-25 s), paired with camera routes given as keyboard actions, and evaluates six dimensions with 24 human-validated sub-metrics. Benchmarking eight models, we find that as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics, and that none keeps revisited places consistent. We further propose WanderLand, a training-free framework that conditions each frame of a frozen model on the same-instant source and, on revisits, on its own earlier static content. WanderLand improves five models on every dimension, by up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.

Title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery
Author: Weimin Wu, Han Liu
Text_Content: We propose SciMARS, a framework for recursive task-local adaptation of multi-agent harnesses in closed-loop scientific discovery. Multi-agent systems coordinate analysis, experimental design, and verification as scientific evidence evolves. However, two problems limit their effectiveness: (i) without shared memory, agents lose observations and repeat work; (ii) fixed role procedures, handoffs, and memory policies perpetuate mistakes despite retained evidence. We address these problems with a shared evidence graph and separate component editors. SciMARS adapts roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory adds a third editor for how agents record, retrieve, and receive evidence. Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next harness. We evaluate scientific discovery through experimental-data replay and a digital twin. SciMARS + Memory resolves 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 attempts on Autonomous Science Bench, compared with 8/18 and 1/18 for the base multi-agent team. On ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld, it solves 14/38 and 11/20 tasks, compared with 11/38 and 5/20 for the base team. These results support combining shared memory with harness adaptation across scientific and interactive tasks.

Title: A Strict Upper Bound for Three-Point Weighted Selection in Planar Vector-Valued Regression
Author: Sergey Volkov
Text_Content: We prove $F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)<11/6$ for minimum-Frobenius-norm least-squares regression with two input and two output coordinates, improving the upper bound $15/8$. More precisely, a universal $\varepsilon_0>0$ satisfies $\mathcal T_3\le(5/6-\varepsilon_0)E$ for every finite residual frame. The proof combines an exact scalar certificate, rigidity of equality in planar selection, and a compactness argument that controls disappearing weights. Together with the known lower bound, this gives $13/8\le F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)<11/6$. No numerical value of $\varepsilon_0$ is claimed.

Title: Beyond the Document: Compiled Context and Governed Agents for Any Work Product
Author: James Rhodes, George Kang
Text_Content: A document preserves the visible result of professional work but often discards the research, calculations, assumptions, evidence, and authorization boundaries behind it. We study a different unit of delivery: a Portable Agent Format (PAF) package that carries a work product together with compiled context, evidence, provenance, and rules for subsequent interaction. To test whether this context remains useful beyond the process that produced it, we evaluate four new packages, created after the hosted and offline readers were fixed: an investment proposal, fund research, financial-statement analysis, and an engineering incident review. Two packages were produced by specialized agents and two through a general-purpose assistant's packaging skill. Across 400 frozen questions and 12,000 evaluated responses, a hosted governed reader succeeds on 96% of questions versus 86% with instructions plus raw-file retrieval (Holm-adjusted p < 10^-7). On the 260 answerable questions per condition, success is 94% versus 79%; the gap varies by package. Source-material chat and instructions alone reach 48% and 74% overall. A separate 0.8-billion-parameter offline reader succeeds on 69% overall, but 54% on answerable questions. Its -1 response rate is 2.9%, combining materially wrong and unauthorized answers, versus 56% with the source and instructions alone. Ablations suggest advantages for the integrated selector and package-adapted writer, without isolating representation from training effects. The same run exposes a failure: offline retrieval resolves none of the 40 historical-record questions in one financial-data package. These findings support treating compiled knowledge as part of the delivered work product, while leaving independent standards interoperability and end-to-end governance conformance unproven.

Title: Memory in biological Lévy walks from the dynamic-entropy formalism
Author: Adriano Barra, Andrea Ladiana
Text_Content: Lévy walks are recognized by the histogram of their flight lengths, while the renewal hypothesis on which the textbook model rests, that every flight is drawn afresh, is seldom tested. We test it with the dynamic-entropy formalism. Maximizing the causal entropy of a sequence of logarithmic flight lengths at fixed lagged correlations yields a chain of continuous spins on a compact interval, whose depth, selected by the data, tells a renewal walker from a Markovian one and from one with a longer memory. With one lag the chain is exactly solvable. A duality that exchanges long and short flights locates a first-order condensation of the flights at the upper cutoff, with the logarithmic range of the flights in the role of system size, and a positive memory makes the histogram heavier-tailed than the rule that generates each flight. For groups, the same construction separates the memory of each individual from delayed interactions and from drives common to all units, which an analysis of the group average confounds, and it gives the collective speed a critical point. On open data, renewal is rejected in seven of ten conditions of Drosophila larvae and in every termite, whose memory reaches a few flights back and lowers the exponent of the histogram by more than half a unit below that of the one-step rule. Wild baboons align with where their nearest neighbors, those ahead above all, were heading 10 to 30 s earlier, and homing pigeons are coupled across their small flocks. Zebrafish T cells, a negative control, remember their own speed, but no delayed coupling between the speeds of different cells survives the controls.

Title: Teamknitt: Configuring, Observing and Intervening in LLM-Agent Teams through the Lens of Dynamical-Systems and Human-Team Theory
Author: Goran Mitevski
Text_Content: Most frameworks for teams of large language model (LLM) agents fix the team's shape inside the software: who talks to whom, how much is passed along, and what a human can do once a run has started. Human-team research has long asked those questions: where team phenomena live (in members or in their interaction), how team-level properties arise, and what separates what a team does from how a team is. I propose using that theory as the organizing lens for configuring, observing and intervening in LLM-agent teams, without assuming its findings transfer. I introduce teamknitt, a framework and open reference implementation in which a user configures a team of 1-16 AI agents for task completion, solution generation, achieving a goal or a research mission; selects one of fourteen deterministic routing topologies or a custom directed graph; chooses a sharing profile that limits what may travel along permitted routes; and binds sources, representations, work dependencies, handoffs and an expertise directory. The recorded process can be observed through non-system views (member reports and behavior) and system views (distributed problem-solving, differentiated transactive memory, interactive coordination, team dynamics). Interventions are explicit and human-led: reviewed reconfiguration between runs, planned disturbances, and private feedback, pause, resume or stop applied at dependency-wave boundaries, with "queued", "applied", "assembled", "understood" and "improved" kept as separate claims. Emergent states such as trust and shared understanding are declared unmeasured. This is an idea and system-description paper with falsifiable hypotheses on topology, information flow and intervention timing, including whether the fractal scaling of communication output between members, and between members on different models, relates to task and team performance. No comparative result is reported.

Title: Learning inexact alternating minimization for convex problems with quadratic coupling
Author: Paul Häusner, Jevgenija Rudzusika, Jens Sjölund, Ozan Öktem
Text_Content: Alternating minimization is a standard tool for optimization problems with two coupled variable blocks. Its cost is dominated by the inner subproblem solvers, which rarely have a closed-form solution. In this paper, we propose to learn an inexact alternating scheme in which neural networks approximate the subproblem solution at each iteration. For convex problems with quadratic couplings between the variable blocks that satisfy a quadratic growth condition, we derive a worst-case bound on the optimality gap that exposes the per-iteration error that each network is trained to minimize in a greedy fashion. Combining the bound with a PAC-Bayes argument, we obtain a fixed-horizon, high-probability bound on the expected optimality gap over the distribution of problem instances. We apply the learned scheme to robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction with dictionary regularization where we achieve a 5x-13x speedup over the inexact first-order baseline at matched accuracy. A brief end-to-end fine-tuning stage extends this up to 30x and outperforms other learned schemes. The code is available at https://github.com/paulhausner/learned-alternating-minimization.

Title: Dynamic Graph Indexing for Label-Filtered Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
Author: Mengxu Jiang, Zhi Yang, Fangyuan Zhang, Yin Yang, Sibo Wang
Text_Content: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) over high-dimensional vectors is a core primitive in modern retrieval systems. In practice, objects are often also associated with labels (e.g., attributes or keywords), and retrieval must combine vector similarity with explicit label-based filtering, giving rise to label-filtered ANNS. This task is challenging because label filtering and ANNS favor very different index structures, selective filters fragment the admissible search space, and updates complicate index maintenance. To address these challenges, we propose DYLAN, a dynamic composite index for label-filtered ANNS supporting containment, overlap, and their conjunctions and disjunctions. DYLAN organizes label sets by shared prefixes in a frequency-ordered trie and selectively shares HNSW-style graph indices across trie-induced subsets, so that each trie region has a constant-factor covering index while each object participates in only logarithmically many indices. To mitigate fragmentation, DYLAN performs a cross-region multi-graph search that exploits ancestor-level indices as bridges between otherwise isolated trie regions. To support insertions, it adopts a threshold-based maintenance scheme that rebuilds shared indices only when necessary, yielding low amortized update cost. Extensive experiments with real data show that DYLAN consistently improves query throughput at comparable recall, by up to two orders of magnitude on challenging label-rich datasets, while retaining competitive memory, construction, and update costs.

Title: ML Models Are Not Ciphers: Power Analysis for Weight Extraction Is Harder Than You Think
Author: Mohammed Qaiss, Peter Horvath, Michal Shagam, Lejla Batina, Zhuoran Liu, Eyal Ronen, Mahmood Sharif, Yuval Yarom
Text_Content: Can power-analysis techniques reveal secret weights of machine-learning models? Multiple recent works demonstrate proof-of-concept attacks that can partially recover such weights. To that end, these works build on techniques from cryptographic engineering, treating the model as a ``cipher'' and its secret weights as keys. We question the basic assumption behind such straightforward adaptations of cryptographic attacks and highlight the challenges arising when applying past techniques to fully recover all layers of deep neural networks. Unlike past works, which extract only a few weights, typically from shallow layers, we investigate the recovery of complete networks. Moreover, we target fully trained and functional models, rather than untrained, randomly initialized networks. To focus on fundamental challenges, we assume an unrealistically strong side-channel adversary that can directly observe the output of the leakage model without any added noise. With this adversary, we show that machine-learning models differ significantly from cryptographic implementations, giving rise to unique challenges that have not been observed in the prior art. We observe two main differences between machine-learning models and ciphers. First, in contrast to the high-diffusion nonlinear integer arithmetic prevalent in cryptographic schemes, machine-learning models tend to use limited-precision floating-point arithmetic and low-diffusion linear operations. We show that these operations introduce difficulties in weight recovery, often requiring an unexpectedly large number of traces, even under ideal channel conditions. Second, we observe that, unlike ciphers, which aim to increase the data entropy, machine-learning models aim to reduce it. This reduces data variability as the algorithm progresses, hampering weight recovery in deep layers of the model. (details can be found in the paper)

Title: Entropy: the Route from the Gaussian Field to the Statistical Mechanics of the Thermal Radiation
Author: Arnaldo Spalvieri
Text_Content: Maximum Entropy or canonical typicality applied to the electromagnetic field can provide starting points for arriving at the Bose distribution of the photon numbers of thermal radiation, but they rely on statistical postulates whose experimental testability is controversial. Here we start from experimentally verifiable assumption of Gaussianity of the electromagnetic field. We analyze the field by projecting it onto orthonormal time-frequency basis functions with unitary bandwidth duration product that represent field's orthogonal time-frequency modes. Through the Glauber-Surashdan representation, we see that the joint density operator of the modes in the photon number basis factorize into diagonal density operators with geometric coefficients of individual modes, while the mean photon occupations of the modes remains still unknown. The independent imposition of Clausius' relation on each one of the entropies and energies of the modes leads to Bose's mean photon occupancy. Thus, our main claim is that for the first time Bose statistics is recovered in the paper under explicit, experimentally verifiable statistical assumptions, without assuming any statistical postulate that is not directly experimentally verifiable. From the mean occupation numbers, the Boltzmann distribution of the energy of matter particles of the material that generates/absorbes the radiation is then derived by retracing in the backward direction the Einstein-Feynman detailed balance.

Title: K-prop: Deep Online Learning by Backpropagating Temporal Kernels
Author: Bingkun Liu, Paul Haider, Federico Benitez, Mihai A. Petrovici, Walter Senn
Text_Content: Self-recurrence represents an important component for temporal processing in neural networks, both artificial and biological, where it appears naturally in the form of leaky integration. However, due to the complex temporal dependencies of the gradient, an efficient and effective method of online training is still lacking. Here we propose K-prop, a novel online learning method for leaky neural networks. It dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. K-prop also outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. We further analyze how its sole approximation affects gradient quality and identify conditions under which K-prop remains accurate and effective.

Title: Perceived Agency During Agent-Avatar Control Transitions in Virtual Reality
Author: Jingyi Zhang, Anthony Steed
Text_Content: Prior beliefs about whether a virtual human (VH) is controlled by a human or a computer can shape how users interpret and respond to its behaviour. As emerging hybrid VH systems allow control to transfer between human operators and computer programs during an ongoing interaction, it remains unclear whether perceived agency updates with the actual controller or continues to reflect users' prior beliefs and first impressions. We investigated this question in a within-subject VR study with 24 participants across four conditions: always computer-controlled, computer-to-human, human-to-computer, and always human-controlled. We designed an interaction task in which participants acted as interviewers, asking the VHs a fixed set of questions. Before each interaction, participants were informed whether the VH was human- or computer-controlled, matching the actual controller at the beginning, but were unaware of possible control transitions. We found that perceived agency was strongly influenced by the controller presented at the beginning of the interaction, with no evidence of updating following the control transitions.
